docs.title: Preventing Zone.Identifier Files in Linux
docs.text: Zone.Identifier files can appear in repositories when Windows attaches security metadata to files downloaded from the internet. When working with Linux tools through WSL, Git, or Docker, these metadata streams may appear as real files and pollute the project directory.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Work inside the Linux filesystem instead of Windows-mounted paths.

    Store projects inside the WSL Linux home directory:

    ~/projects/my-repo

    Avoid storing repositories in Windows-mounted locations such as:

    /mnt/c/Users/<user>/projects

    Linux filesystems do not support Windows Alternate Data Streams, so Zone.Identifier files are not created.

  2. Clone repositories inside WSL.

    Run Git commands from the Linux shell:

    git clone https://github.com/example/repo.git

    Avoid cloning repositories through Windows Explorer or Windows Git clients.

  3. Download files using Linux tools.

    Download files from inside WSL using tools such as:

    curl -O https://example.com/file.tar.gz

    or

    wget https://example.com/file.tar.gz

    Files downloaded in Linux do not receive Windows security streams.

  4. Edit files using WSL-aware editors.

    Use editors that interact directly with the Linux filesystem:

    • Visual Studio Code with the Remote – WSL extension
    • vim
    • nano

    Avoid editing project files through Windows Explorer under \\wsl$.

  5. Extract archives inside Linux.

    Extract downloaded archives using Linux tools:

    tar -xzf archive.tar.gz

    Avoid extracting archives using Windows Explorer before moving them into the repository.

  6. Block metadata files in Git.

    Add rules to .gitignore:

    Thumbs.db
desktop.ini
*.Zone.Identifier

    This prevents accidental commits if the files appear.

  7. Remove existing Zone.Identifier files.

    If metadata files already exist in a repository, remove them:

    find . -name "*:Zone.Identifier" -delete

    Verify the working tree afterwards:

    git status

docs.title: Note
docs.text: Windows creates Zone.Identifier using the Mark of the Web security mechanism. When files are downloaded or copied from external sources in Windows environments, the metadata may appear as separate files when accessed from Linux tooling. Keeping repositories entirely inside the Linux filesystem prevents the issue.

docs.title: Renaming WSL Username and Home Directory
Renaming WSL Username and Home Directory
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Use this to rename a WSL Linux user account (login name and /home/<username> directory) to a new name, e.g. /home/<OLD-USERNAME> to /home/<NEW-USERNAME>.

Warning: This changes your login account, not just a folder. Close every terminal, editor, and tool using the account first — VS Code Remote-WSL windows, other WSL terminals, background services — before running these commands. usermod refuses to run cleanly (or leaves things half-changed) on a user with active processes.

docs.title: Step 1: Close Everything Using the Account
docs.text: Close all WSL terminals and any VS Code Remote-WSL windows connected to the distro.

docs.title: Step 2: Stop the Distro
docs.text:
From Windows PowerShell (not WSL):

wsl --terminate <YOUR-DISTRO>

docs.title: Step 3: Start a Root Shell
docs.text:
Start the distro logged in as root instead of the normal default user, so no processes are attached to the account you're renaming:

wsl -d <YOUR-DISTRO> -u root

docs.title: Step 4: Rename the Account and Move the Home Directory
docs.text:
Inside the root shell:

usermod -l <NEW-USERNAME> -m -d /home/<NEW-USERNAME> <OLD-USERNAME>
  • -l <NEW-USERNAME> renames the login from <OLD-USERNAME> to <NEW-USERNAME>.
  • -m -d /home/<NEW-USERNAME> moves the home directory's contents and updates the account record to point at the new path.

docs.title: Step 5: Rename the Matching Group (If One Exists)
docs.text:
Ubuntu's default setup creates a group with the same name as the user. Rename it too, if present:

getent group <OLD-USERNAME> && groupmod -n <NEW-USERNAME> <OLD-USERNAME>

docs.title: Step 6: Check for a Default User Setting
docs.text:
cat /etc/wsl.conf

If it has a [user] section with default=<OLD-USERNAME>, update that value to <NEW-USERNAME>.

docs.title: Step 7: Restart WSL
docs.text:
exit
wsl --shutdown
wsl -d <YOUR-DISTRO>

You should land in /home/<NEW-USERNAME> as the new user.

docs.title: After Renaming
docs.text: Anything that hardcoded the old /home/<OLD-USERNAME>/... path needs a review afterward — project config files, SSH config, git config, and any tool (including Claude Code itself) that stores its own settings under the old home directory.

Commands that start with ~/ or / use an absolute path — they target a specific location regardless of where you currently are in the terminal.

You do not need to cd to the target directory first.

Even if your current working directory is somewhere else, such as:

The command will still delete the correct folder because ~/ always resolves to your home directory.

docs.title: How Paths Work
docs.text:
Prefix Type Resolves to ~/ Absolute (home) /home/<your-username>/ / Absolute (root) The root of the file system ./ or no prefix Relative The current working directory

Warning: rm -rf deletes permanently with no confirmation. Always double-check the path before running it.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
When creating a bilingual documentation site (English and Japanese), specific configuration steps are required to ensure proper language switching and prevent automatic configuration overrides.

This memo describes the required settings.

docs.title: Step 1: Turn Off Automatic Reconfiguration
docs.text:
If you are using Material’s i18n switching feature, disable automatic reconfiguration to prevent the configuration from being rewritten.

Add the following to your mkdocs.yml:

reconfigure_material: false

docs.title: Why this is required
docs.text:
• Prevents automatic modification of language and navigation settings
  • Ensures manual bilingual configuration remains intact
  • Avoids conflicts with custom language paths and alternate links

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Alternate Language Links
docs.text:
Add the following section to define the alternate language versions of your site:

extra:
  generator: false
  alternate:
    - name: EN
      link: /REPO_NAME/
      lang: en
    - name: JA
      link: /REPO_NAME/ja/
      lang: ja

docs.title: generator: false
docs.text:
Optional but recommended.

  • Removes the generator meta tag
  • Produces cleaner HTML metadata

docs.title: alternate
docs.text:
Defines alternate language versions.

Each entry includes:

docs.title: name
docs.text:
Display label for the language:

name: EN
name: JA

docs.title: link
docs.text:
URL path to the root of that language version.

Replace REPO_NAME with your repository name:

/my-docs/
/my-docs/ja/

docs.title: lang
docs.text:
Language code:

en
ja

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
reconfigure_material: false

extra:
  generator: false
  alternate:
    - name: EN
      link: /my-docs/
      lang: en
    - name: JA
      link: /my-docs/ja/
      lang: ja

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
To create a bilingual site:

  1. Turn off automatic reconfiguration
  2. Configure alternate language links

These settings ensure proper language switching and stable configuration behavior.

docs.title: Deploying with gh-deploy
docs.text: mkdocs gh-deploy is a built-in MkDocs command that builds your site locally and pushes the generated files directly to the gh-pages branch. This method does not use GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Warning

Do not use mkdocs gh-deploy if your repository is configured to deploy using GitHub Actions. Choose one deployment method and use it consistently:

  • GitHub Actions > automated deployment on push
  • mkdocs gh-deploy > manual deployment from your local machine

Mixing both methods can cause confusion.

docs.title: When should you use gh-deploy?
docs.text:
Use this method if:

  • You do not want to use GitHub Actions
  • You prefer manual deployment
  • You want the simplest possible setup
  • You are working on a small personal project

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When you run:

mkdocs gh-deploy

MkDocs will:

  1. Build the site locally
  2. Create (or update) the gh-pages branch
  3. Push the built site to GitHub
  4. Publish it via GitHub Pages

docs.title: Setup requirements
docs.text:
1. GitHub Pages must be configured to use:

    Deploy from a branch

  2. Select:

    • Branch: gh-pages
    • Folder: / (root)

    You can configure this in:

    Settings > Pages

docs.title: Deploy the site
docs.text:
From the project root (where mkdocs.yml exists), run:

mkdocs gh-deploy

For a clean rebuild:

mkdocs gh-deploy --clean

docs.title: Updating the site
docs.text:
After modifying your documentation:

mkdocs gh-deploy

That’s it. You do not need to manually:

git add .
git commit
git push

because gh-deploy handles the deployment branch automatically.

docs.title: How this differs from GitHub Actions
docs.text: GitHub Actions mkdocs gh-deploy Automatic on every push Manual command No local build required Builds locally No gh-pages branch needed Uses gh-pages branch CI-based Local deployment

docs.title: Deployment timing
docs.text: After running mkdocs gh-deploy, it may take 20–60 seconds for the site to update. If changes do not appear immediately, refresh the page.

docs.title: Displaying the Revision Date at the Bottom
Displaying the Revision Date at the Bottom
docs.text: Display the Git revision date in the default Material footer area using mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized-plugin.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Add the plugin to requirements.txt.

    mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized-plugin

    Pin MkDocs to 1.x:

    mkdocs<2

  2. Enable the plugin in mkdocs.yml.

    plugins:
  - i18n:
      # your existing i18n configuration
  - git-revision-date-localized:
      type: date
      timezone: Asia/Tokyo
      custom_format: "%Y-%m-%d"
      fallback_to_build_date: true
  - search
  - glightbox

  3. Configure GitHub Actions to fetch full history.

    In .github/workflows/deploy.yml:

    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  with:
    fetch-depth: 0

    Install dependencies:

    - run: pip install -r requirements.txt

  4. Install git in the Docker image.

    Update Dockerfile:

    FROM python:3.12-slim

RUN apt-get update \
  && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git \
  && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /mkdocs
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["mkdocs", "serve", "-a", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

  5. Allow Git to read the mounted repository.

    Add after installing git:

    RUN git config --system --add safe.directory /mkdocs

  6. Rebuild and run.

    docker build --no-cache -t my-mkdocs .
docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

  7. Verify the result.

    Open:

    • http://localhost:8000/kb/
    • http://localhost:8000/kb/ja/

    Confirm that the revision date appears in the bottom metadata area (clock icon section).

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
If the message “Unable to read git logs… Falling back to build date” appears:

  • Ensure .git exists in the mounted directory.
  • Confirm safe.directory /mkdocs is configured.
  • Confirm fetch-depth: 0 is set in GitHub Actions.

If a MkDocs 2.0 compatibility warning appears, verify:

mkdocs --version

Ensure the version is 1.x and mkdocs<2 is pinned in requirements.txt.

docs.title: Displaying the Revision Date at the Top
Displaying the Revision Date at the Top
docs.text: Display the Git revision date at the top of each page using Material for MkDocs. Hide the default footer date and exclude the home pages.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Enable theme overrides in mkdocs.yml.

    theme:
  name: material
  custom_dir: overrides

  2. Create the override file.

    Create:

    `overrides/main.html`

  3. Add the template logic.

    {% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}

  {% set is_home = page.file.src_path.endswith("index.md") %}

  {% if page.meta.git_revision_date_localized and not is_home %}
    <div class="page-date">
      {% if config.theme.language == "ja" %}
        最終更新日: {{ page.meta.git_revision_date_localized }}
      {% else %}
        Last updated: {{ page.meta.git_revision_date_localized }}
      {% endif %}
    </div>
  {% endif %}

  {{ super() }}

{% endblock %}

    This:

    • Displays the revision date above the page content.
    • Hides the date on en/index.md and ja/index.md.
    • Switches the label based on the active language.

  4. Create the stylesheet.

    Create:

    `docs/stylesheets/extra.css`

  5. Add the styling and hide the footer date.

    .page-date {
  font-size: 0.8rem;
  color: #888;
  margin-bottom: 0.5rem;
  font-weight: 400;
}

.md-source-file {
  display: none;
}

    This:

    • Styles the top date as metadata.
    • Removes the default footer revision block.

  6. Register the stylesheet in mkdocs.yml.

    extra_css:
  - stylesheets/extra.css

  7. Rebuild the Docker image.

    docker build --no-cache -t my-mkdocs .
docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
Do not create overrides/partials/content.html with:

{% extends "partials/content.html" %}

This causes a recursion error because the override extends itself.

Verify:

  • The date appears at the top of normal pages.
  • The date does not appear on index.md.
  • The footer revision block is no longer displayed.

docs.title: Fixing "The following pages exist in the docs directory, but are not included in "nav" configuration:"
Fixing "The following pages exist in the docs directory, but are not included in "nav" configuration:"
docs.text:
terminal
The following pages exist in the docs directory, 
but are not included in “nav” configuration:
  - en/tools/docker/docker_troubleshoot_01.md
  - ja/labor/index.md
No fix is needed.

You should only care if you expect the page to appear in the menu but it doesn’t.

docs.title: Fixing "GET /ja HTTP/1.1" Code 302
docs.text:
terminal
"GET /ja HTTP/1.1" code 302

No fix is needed.

This happens because:

  • /ja redirects to /ja/.
  • This is a standard behavior in MkDocs.

docs.title: Fixing "GET /ja/sitemap.xml HTTP/1.1" Code 404
docs.text:
terminal
"GET /ja/sitemap.xml HTTP/1.1" code 404

This happens because:

  • MkDocs does not generate sitemaps by default.
  • Material tries to probe for them.
  • Browser/devtools sometimes request them automatically.

To fix this, you can:

  • Ignore them, or
  • Add a sitemap plugin later if you care about SEO

docs.title: Hosting a Private MkDocs Site on Synology NAS
Hosting a Private MkDocs Site on Synology NAS
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide shows how to serve a static MkDocs site from a Synology NAS on your local network using Web Station, so the site is always accessible without running mkdocs serve.

Requirements:

  • Synology NAS running DSM 7
  • MkDocs project in WSL2 on Windows 11
  • Admin access to DSM

docs.title: Step 1: Install Web Station
docs.text:
1. Open Package Center on the NAS.
  2. Search for Web Station.
  3. Click Install.

After installation, Web Station automatically creates a Default Portal on port 80. No new portal needs to be created.

docs.title: Step 2: Verify Shared Folder Permissions
docs.text:
1. Open Control Panel → Shared Folder.
  2. Select web → Edit → Permissions.
  3. Confirm your user account has Read/Write access.

docs.title: Step 3: Install cifs-utils in WSL2
docs.text: sudo apt-get install cifs-utils

docs.title: Step 4: Mount the NAS Web Folder in WSL2
docs.text:
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nas-web
sudo mount -t cifs //192.168.x.x/web /mnt/nas-web -o username=<YOUR-VALUE>,uid=1000,gid=1000

Replace 192.168.x.x with your NAS IP address. Enter your NAS password when prompted.

Note: To find your NAS IP, open Control Panel → Network → Network Interface tab.

Note: This mount does not persist after a reboot. Repeat this step each time you restart WSL2.

docs.title: Step 5: Build and Sync the Site
docs.text:
.venv/bin/mkdocs build
mkdir /mnt/nas-web/kb
rsync -av --delete site/ /mnt/nas-web/kb/

The mkdir line is only needed the first time.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify
docs.text: Open a browser and go to http://192.168.x.x/kb/. The site should load.

docs.title: Updating the Site
docs.text:
Each time you update content, run the following steps:

  1. Mount the NAS web folder (skip this step if WSL2 has not been restarted since the last sync):
sudo mount -t cifs //192.168.x.x/web /mnt/nas-web -o username=<YOUR-VALUE>,uid=1000,gid=1000
  1. Build the site:
.venv/bin/mkdocs build
  1. Sync the build output to the NAS:
rsync -av --delete site/ /mnt/nas-web/kb/

docs.title: Migrating MkDocs from Docker to venv
Migrating MkDocs from Docker to venv
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Move an existing MkDocs project from a Docker-based setup to a lightweight Python virtual environment (venv) on WSL2.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• WSL2 running Ubuntu
  • An existing MkDocs project set up with Docker
  • Git configured and connected to GitHub

docs.title: Step 1: Identify Files to Copy
docs.text:
From your Docker project folder, copy the following:

Item Description docs/ Markdown content overrides/ Custom theme overrides mkdocs.yml Site configuration requirements.txt Plugin and dependency list .git/ Git history .github/ GitHub Actions workflows

Leave these behind:

Item Reason Dockerfile Docker-specific, no longer needed site/ Generated output — MkDocs will rebuild it

docs.title: Step 2: Check for Unexpected Files
docs.text:
Run the following to inspect your project folder:

ls -la ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs/

If you find an unrecognised file, check its contents before deleting:

cat ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs/<filename>

To delete it:

rm ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs/<filename>

docs.title: Step 3: Create the New Folder
docs.text: mkdir -p ~/projects/python/mkdocs

docs.title: Step 4: Copy Files with rsync
docs.text:
Use rsync to copy everything across, excluding Docker-specific files and the generated site/ folder:

rsync -av \
  --exclude='Dockerfile' \
  --exclude='site/' \
  ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs/ \
  ~/projects/python/mkdocs/

docs.title: Step 5: Set Up the venv
docs.text:
Navigate to the new folder:

cd ~/projects/python/mkdocs

If python3-venv is not installed, install it first:

sudo apt install python3-venv

Create and activate the virtual environment:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

(.venv) will appear at the start of your terminal prompt when the venv is active.

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Site Locally
docs.text:
mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser to confirm the site looks correct.

docs.title: Step 7: Test the GitHub Workflow
docs.text:
Make a small edit to any file in docs/, then commit and push:

git add .
git commit -m "test: verify new venv setup"
git push

Check the Actions tab in your GitHub repository to confirm the deployment workflow completes successfully.

docs.title: Step 8: Remove the Old Docker Folder
docs.text:
Once everything is confirmed working, delete the old project folder:

rm -rf ~/projects/docker/python/mkdocs

Warning: rm -rf is irreversible. Double-check the path before running.

docs.title: Publishing a Docker-Based Site to GitHub Pages
Publishing a Docker-Based Site to GitHub Pages
docs.text: This guide assumes you build and preview MkDocs inside Docker, and publish to GitHub Pages using GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A GitHub account
  • A MkDocs project folder that contains:
  • mkdocs.yml
  • docs/ (your Markdown pages)
  • Docker installed locally (for preview/build)
  • Git installed locally (for pushing to GitHub)

docs.title: 1) Create a GitHub repository
docs.text:
1. Log in to GitHub.

  2. Click New to create a repository.

  3. Set the following options:

    • Repository name: Any name
    • Description: Any description
    • Choose visibility: Public (required for free GitHub Pages on personal accounts)
    • Add README: Off (optional)
    • Add .gitignore: No (optional)
    • Add license: No (optional)

  4. The repository is created.

docs.title: 2) Preview the site locally
docs.text:
1. In the project root folder in VS Code, run:

    docker run --rm -it \
  -p 8000:8000 \
  -v "$(pwd)":/mkdocs \
  my-mkdocs \
  mkdocs serve -a 0.0.0.0:8000

    Tip

    Make sure your Docker image my-mkdocs is already built.

  2. Open the local site:

    http://localhost:8000

docs.title: 3) Initialize git and push the files to GitHub
docs.text:
1. In the project root folder in VS Code, run:

    git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial MkDocs site"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/REPO_NAME.git
git push -u origin main

    Note

    • If you already ran git init, skip it.

    • If origin already exists, update it:

      git remote set-url origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/REPO_NAME.git

docs.title: 4) Add a GitHub Actions workflow to build and deploy
docs.text:
1. Create the workflow folder in the project root:

    mkdir -p .github/workflows

  2. Create and open the workflow file:

    nano .github/workflows/deploy.yml

  3. Add the following content:

    name: Deploy MkDocs

on:
  push:
    branches: ["main"]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: "pages"
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.x"

      # Install the same plugins used locally
      # Prefer: pip install -r requirements.txt

      - run: |
          pip install \
            mkdocs \
            mkdocs-material \
            mkdocs-static-i18n \
            mkdocs-glightbox

      - run: mkdocs build

      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: site

      - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

  4. Commit and push the workflow:

    git add .github/workflows/deploy.yml
git commit -m "Add GitHub Pages deployment workflow"
git push

  5. Open the Actions tab and confirm that the workflow completes successfully (green ✅).

docs.title: 5) Enable GitHub Pages (use GitHub Actions as the source)
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Pages.

  2. Under Build and deployment > Source, select GitHub Actions.

  3. The site should be available at:

    https://YOUR_USERNAME.github.io/REPO_NAME/

    Note

    Changes are published after the GitHub Actions workflow completes. If updates do not appear immediately, wait for the green ✅ in Actions and refresh the page.

docs.title: Publishing a Site Using GitHub Pages
Publishing a Site Using GitHub Pages
docs.text:
1. Connect your project to GitHub.

    terminal
    git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial MkDocs site"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/your-repo-name.git
git push -u origin main

  2. Deploy to GitHub Pages.

    terminal
    mkdocs gh-deploy

    Note

    This command:

    • Builds your site
    • Creates a gh-pages branch
    • Pushes the static HTML to that branch
    • GitHub Pages serves it automatically

  3. Enable GitHub Pages in your GitHub repository: Go to Settings → Pages, then set:

    • Source: Deploy from a branch
    • Branch: gh-pages / root

  4. Your site will be available at:

    https://yourusername.github.io/your-repo-name/

docs.title: Rebuilding the MkDocs Docker Image Only When Needed
Rebuilding the MkDocs Docker Image Only When Needed
docs.text: Use this guide to decide when you must run docker build before docker run for your MkDocs container.

docs.title: What this guide does
docs.text:
• Explains when a rebuild is required
  • Explains when a rebuild is not required (because you mount the repo with -v $(pwd):/mkdocs)
  • Provides a simple repeatable workflow

docs.title: When you must rebuild
docs.text:
Rebuild the image when you change something that affects what’s installed inside the image:

  • Dockerfile (example: adding git, safe.directory, changing CMD, changing base image)
  • requirements.txt (adding/removing/upgrading Python packages)
  • Anything else that is only applied during docker build (system packages installed with apt-get, etc.)

Run:

docker build -t my-mkdocs .

Use --no-cache only when you want to force a completely fresh build (useful after dependency changes or when you suspect caching issues):

docker build --no-cache -t my-mkdocs .

docs.title: When you do not need to rebuild
docs.text:
Because you run with a bind mount:

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

You do not need to rebuild when you change files that are read directly from the mounted repo at runtime, such as:

  • Markdown content in docs/**
  • CSS in docs/stylesheets/** (example: extra.css)
  • Theme overrides in overrides/** (example: overrides/main.html)
  • mkdocs.yml (config changes are picked up when MkDocs reloads)

In these cases, do this instead:

  • Refresh the browser (hard refresh if needed)
  • If live reload does not pick it up, stop the container and run docker run ... again

docs.title: Recommended workflow for local editing
docs.text:
1. Start the container:

    docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

  2. Edit files (.md, .css, overrides/*.html, mkdocs.yml).

  3. If you changed Dockerfile or requirements.txt, rebuild and restart:

    docker build -t my-mkdocs .
docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

docs.title: Note
docs.text: If you ever remove the -v $(pwd):/mkdocs mount and rely only on COPY . . inside the image, then every content/CSS/HTML change will require a rebuild.

docs.title: Understanding the Docker Run Command
docs.text:
This guide explains the meaning of the following Docker command and how image names like mkdocs-dev and my-mkdocs affect behavior.

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs mkdocs-dev

docs.title: 1. Basic structure of docker run
docs.text:
General syntax:

docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE_NAME [COMMAND]

Example:

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs mkdocs-dev

Components:

Part Meaning docker run Start a new container OPTIONS Configure container behavior IMAGE_NAME The environment to run COMMAND Optional override command

docs.title: --rm
docs.text:
--rm

Meaning:

  • Automatically deletes the container after it stops

Why useful:

  • Keeps system clean
  • Avoids unused container buildup

Without --rm:

Container remains after exit.

With --rm:

Container is deleted automatically.

docs.title: -it
docs.text:
-it

This is combination of:

-i   (interactive)
-t   (terminal)

Meaning:

  • Allows interactive use
  • Shows logs and output in your terminal
  • Lets you press Ctrl+C to stop

Required for development servers like MkDocs.

docs.title: -p 8000:8000
docs.text:
-p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT

Example:

-p 8000:8000

Meaning:

  • Maps port from container → host machine

Structure:

host:container

Result:

Browser → localhost:8000 → Docker container port 8000

This allows you to open MkDocs in your browser:

http://localhost:8000

docs.title: -v $(pwd):/mkdocs
docs.text:
-v HOST_FOLDER:CONTAINER_FOLDER

Example:

-v $(pwd):/mkdocs

Meaning:

Mounts your current directory into the container.

Breakdown:

Part Meaning $(pwd) Your current folder on host /mkdocs Folder inside container

Result:

Your files → available inside container

Example:

Host:

/home/user/docs

Container:

/mkdocs

MkDocs reads files from /mkdocs.

Changes update instantly.

docs.title: 3. Image name
docs.text:
Final part of command:

mkdocs-dev

This is the Docker image name.

Docker images are like:

  • Templates
  • Environments
  • Preconfigured systems

They contain:

  • OS
  • Python
  • MkDocs
  • plugins
  • themes

docs.title: 4. Example: mkdocs-dev vs my-mkdocs
docs.text:
Two commands:

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs mkdocs-dev

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

Difference:

Only the image name:

Image Meaning mkdocs-dev Image named mkdocs-dev my-mkdocs Image named my-mkdocs

They may contain different:

  • MkDocs version
  • plugins
  • themes
  • Python version

Example:

mkdocs-dev:

MkDocs only

my-mkdocs:

MkDocs + Material theme + plugins

docs.title: 5. Visual diagram
docs.text:
Your Computer

/docs folder
   │
   │ mounted via -v
   ▼
Docker Container

/mkdocs folder
   │
   │ served by MkDocs
   ▼
Port 8000 inside container
   │
   │ mapped via -p
   ▼
localhost:8000 on your computer

docs.title: 6. Real example workflow
docs.text:
Step 1: Build image

docker build -t my-mkdocs .

Step 2: Run server

docker run --rm -it -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/mkdocs my-mkdocs

Step 3: Open browser

http://localhost:8000

docs.title: 7. Summary table
docs.text: Part Meaning docker run Start container --rm Delete container after stop -it Interactive terminal -p 8000:8000 Map ports -v $(pwd):/mkdocs Mount folder mkdocs-dev / my-mkdocs Image name

docs.title: 8. Key concept summary
docs.text:
Docker image = Environment

Docker container = Running instance of image

Your command means:

"Run MkDocs inside Docker, use my current folder, and show it on localhost:8000"

docs.title: 9. Check available images
docs.text:
docker images

Example output:

REPOSITORY   TAG
mkdocs-dev   latest
my-mkdocs    latest

docs.title: 10. Stop container
docs.text:
Press:

Ctrl + C

Container is removed automatically because of --rm.

docs.title: Understanding the MkDocs 2.0 Warning
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This warning is from the Material for MkDocs team, alerting you about the upcoming MkDocs 2.0 release. It's not an error — your setup is working fine — but it's a heads-up worth paying attention to.

docs.title: What's Happening
docs.text:
MkDocs 2.0 is a new major version of the underlying framework, but the Material for MkDocs team is warning that it's essentially incompatible with the current ecosystem:

  • The plugin system is being removed, so any plugins you use will break
  • The theming system is being rewritten, so Material's theme itself won't work
  • There's no migration path from MkDocs 1.x projects
  • It's currently unlicensed and has a closed contribution model

docs.title: What You Should Do (For Now): Nothing
docs.text: This is a warning about a future version, not something that's broken today. Your current Docker setup with Material for MkDocs is fine. The team is essentially signaling they won't be supporting MkDocs 2.0, and advising users not to upgrade when it releases.

docs.title: Longer Term
docs.text:
• Stay on MkDocs 1.x with Material for MkDocs for the foreseeable future
  • Watch the Material for MkDocs blog/repo — they may announce an alternative path or their own fork
  • Pin your MkDocs version in your Dockerfile or requirements.txt (e.g. mkdocs>=1.5,<2.0) to avoid accidentally pulling in 2.0

You can read the full analysis at the URL in the warning if you want the complete picture from the Material team's perspective.

docs.title: Understanding MkDocs Packages
docs.text: Package Description mkdocs The core engine — turns Markdown into a website. mkdocs-material Theme: beautiful typography, dark mode, search, icons, diagrams (including Mermaid!), callouts, tabs, grids — the works. mkdocs-awesome-pages-plugin Lets you organize pages in folders without manually declaring everything in mkdocs.yml. mkdocs-glightbox Adds a sleek lightbox for images — perfect for documentation with screenshots or diagrams.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Page File
docs.text:
Create the new documentation page inside the docs/ directory:

docs/outlook.md

MkDocs automatically detects files in docs/, but they will not appear in navigation unless added to mkdocs.yml.

docs.title: Step 2: Add the Page to Navigation in mkdocs.yml
docs.text:
MkDocs only shows pages in the left navigation if they are included in the nav: section.

Example:

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Outlook: outlook.md

If your site is bilingual, make sure to add the page in both language configs if applicable.

docs.title: Step 3: Commit and Push Both the New File and the Config Change
docs.text: Both the page file and the mkdocs.yml change must be committed and pushed. Otherwise, the page may exist but will not appear in navigation.

docs.title: Method 1: Commit Everything (Most Common)
docs.text:
git add .
git commit -m "Add Outlook page"
git push

docs.title: Method 2: Stage Only the Files You Changed
docs.text:
git add docs/outlook.md mkdocs.yml
git commit -m "Add Outlook page to nav"
git push

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
The key point is:

mkdocs.yml must be committed and pushed for navigation changes to appear.

If you updated configuration such as navigation or language links, commit and push:

git add mkdocs.yml
git commit -m "Update navigation or fix language switch links"
git push

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
After pushing:

  • The new page will appear in the left navigation
  • The site will rebuild automatically
  • The updated configuration will be applied
  • GitHub Pages (or your deployment target) will publish the updated site

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
To update the site:

  1. Create the page file in docs/
  2. Add the page to nav: in mkdocs.yml
  3. Commit and push both the page and the config

Configuration changes do not take effect until they are committed and pushed.

docs.title: Viewing Deployment Errors
docs.text: You can view deployment errors from the Actions tab in your repository.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Go to your repository on GitHub.

  2. Click the Actions tab, then select the workflow run that shows a failed status (❌).

  3. In the workflow details, click build-deploy.

  4. Review the logs to identify the error.

docs.title: Tip
docs.text:
• Expand individual steps to see detailed error messages.
  • The error message is usually shown in the step marked with a ❌ icon.

docs.title: Commenting Out Lines
docs.text: Use the default keyboard shortcuts to comment code.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. To add or remove a single-line comment, press:

    Ctrl + Q

  2. To add or remove a block comment, press:

    Ctrl + Shift + Q

docs.title: Note
docs.text: Cmd + / is commonly used to toggle comments in editors such as Visual Studio Code and Sublime Text, but it is not the default shortcut in Notepad++.

docs.title: Enabling Comment Shortcut for AutoHotkey
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Enable line commenting (;) using Ctrl+Q for AutoHotkey scripts in Notepad++.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Notepad++ installed
  • AutoHotkey installed

docs.title: Step 1: Download the AutoHotkey UDL
docs.text:
Download the User Defined Language (UDL) file for AutoHotkey from:

  • Repository: jNizM/ahk_notepad-plus-plus
  • File to download: userDefineLang_AHK.xml

docs.title: Step 2: Import the UDL into Notepad++
docs.text:
1. Open Notepad++.
  2. Go to Language → User Defined Language → Define your language…
  3. Click Import.
  4. Select the downloaded userDefineLang_AHK.xml file.
  5. Restart Notepad++.

docs.title: Step 3: Enable the AutoHotkey Language
docs.text:
After restarting Notepad++:

  1. Go to Language → User Defined Language.
  2. Select AutoHotkey.

Syntax highlighting should now be applied to .ahk files.

docs.title: Step 4: Use the Comment Shortcut
docs.text:
1. Select one or more lines in your AutoHotkey script.
  2. Press Ctrl+Q to toggle comments.

This inserts or removes ; at the start of each selected line.

docs.title: Troubleshoot: Shortcut Not Working
docs.text:
If Ctrl+Q does not work, verify the shortcut mapping:

  1. Go to Settings → Shortcut Mapper.
  2. Search for comment.
  3. Confirm that Toggle Line Comment is assigned to Ctrl+Q. If not, double-click the entry to reassign it.

docs.title: Alternative: Comment Without UDL
docs.text:
If you prefer not to install the UDL, you can comment lines manually by adding ; at the start:

; F9::
; {
;     Send "docker run ..."
; }

Or use multi-cursor editing to comment multiple lines at once:

  1. Hold Alt+Shift.
  2. Press ↓ to extend the cursor across multiple lines.
  3. Type ; to insert it on each line simultaneously.

docs.title: Responding to the Notepad++ Updater Hijack Incident
Responding to the Notepad++ Updater Hijack Incident
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Notepad++ updater was reportedly hijacked. See the official announcements:

  • Official incident update
  • Official security clarification

The attack targeted organisations rather than individual users, but the following precautions are recommended:

  1. Uninstall your current version and install the latest version from the official site.
  2. Run a quick malware scan with Windows Defender or your antivirus software.
  3. Delete any previously downloaded Notepad++ installers to avoid accidentally using them.
  4. Until further notice, update Notepad++ manually rather than using the built-in updater.

docs.title: Setting Default Language for New Documents
Setting Default Language for New Documents
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

By default, every new tab opens as plain text (.txt). Notepad++ has a Default Language setting that controls the syntax highlighting applied to new, unsaved documents — this guide shows where to find it and where it falls short for languages like Markdown.

docs.title: Step 1: Open a New Document
docs.text: Start with a new document open. Notice the tab is untitled and has no real extension until you save it.

docs.title: Step 2: Open Preferences
docs.text: Go to Settings → Preferences... in the menu bar.

docs.title: Step 3: Go to the New Document Page
docs.text:
In the Preferences dialog, select New Document from the left-hand list. Here you can set the default line-ending format, encoding, and — most relevant here — the Default language dropdown.

Warning: The Default language dropdown only lists Notepad++'s built-in lexers. Some languages — including Markdown in many Notepad++ installs — are implemented as a User Defined Language (UDL) instead of a built-in lexer, and UDLs do not appear in this dropdown at all. If your Markdown support shows as "User Defined language file - Markdown (preinstalled)" in the status bar, this setting can't target it.

For Markdown specifically, see Add a New File Format to the Windows 11 New Menu for a reliable workaround using the Windows "New" context menu (via PowerToys New+) instead.

docs.title: Setting Default Save Folder
docs.text: Configure a fixed folder for all new files in Notepad++.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open Settings → Preferences.

  2. Select Default Directory.

  3. Under Default Open/Save file Directory, select the third option (custom directory).

  4. Click the … button.

  5. Choose the target folder (for example, D:\notepad-pp).

  6. Click Close.

New files will now default to this folder when you select Save.

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
If Follow current document is selected, Notepad++ saves files in the same folder as the active tab.

If Remember last used directory is selected, it uses the most recently saved folder instead.

Use the custom directory option to enforce one fixed location for all files.

docs.title: Converting a Python Script to an Executable
Converting a Python Script to an Executable
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A guide to packaging .py files into a standalone Windows .exe using Nuitka — with steps to eliminate antivirus false positives.

Note: PyInstaller is popular, but executables it produces are frequently flagged as malware by antivirus engines on VirusTotal. Nuitka compiles Python directly and, with the right configuration, produces clean binaries.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.9 (via Conda recommended)
  • Visual Studio Build Tools with the MSVC v14.2 component installed
  • Conda or pip for environment management
  • (Optional) osslsigncode for digital signing

docs.title: Set Up a Clean Virtual Environment
docs.text:
Nuitka compiles everything in your Python environment into the binary. A bloated environment means a bloated .exe. Start fresh.

conda create -n nuitka python=3.9
conda activate nuitka

Then install only the packages your script actually needs:

pip install <your-dependencies>

Note: Run your script in this minimal environment first to confirm it works before compiling.

docs.title: Install Nuitka
docs.text:
pip install nuitka

Note: If false positives become an issue after a Nuitka version becomes widely adopted, try pinning to a slightly older version: 

pip install nuitka==<older-version>

docs.title: Build the Executable
docs.text:
Run the following command from your project directory, replacing your_script.py with your script name:

python -m nuitka \
  --msvc=14.2 \
  --lto=no \
  --standalone \
  --onefile \
  --onefile-tempdir-spec=my_app_tempdir \
  --plugin-enable=pylint-warnings \
  --plugin-enable=tk-inter \
  --windows-disable-console \
  --windows-product-name="MyApp" \
  --windows-file-description="My Application" \
  --windows-product-version=1.0.0.0 \
  --windows-company-name="YourCompany" \
  --windows-icon-from-ico=C:\path\to\icon.ico \
  your_script.py

docs.title: Understand the Build Flags
docs.text:
Flag Purpose --msvc=14.2 Use the MSVC compiler. Less common than MinGW64, which reduces false positive rates. Alternatives: --clang, --mingw. --lto=no Disables Link Time Optimization. Speeds up the build. --standalone Bundles all dependencies into a dist/ folder. --onefile Compresses the dist/ folder into a single .exe. --onefile-tempdir-spec=<name> Sets where the .exe extracts itself at runtime. Without this, it extracts to %TEMP%. The folder is deleted automatically on exit. --plugin-enable=tk-inter Required if your script uses tkinter. --windows-disable-console Suppresses the console window at runtime. Note: print() statements will cause issues — comment them out before building. --windows-product-name Sets the product name in the executable's metadata. --windows-file-description Sets the file description in metadata. --windows-product-version Sets the version string (format: 0.0.0.0). --windows-company-name Sets the company name in metadata. --windows-icon-from-ico Assigns a custom icon to the executable.

Note: MSVC and Clang require installation via Visual Studio Installer → Modify → Individual Components. If you still get false positives, try recompiling with each of the four compilers (msvc, clang, mingw64, mingw) to find the cleanest result.

docs.title: Reduce False Positives
docs.text: Even a well-built Nuitka binary can trigger antivirus warnings. Check your result on VirusTotal and use the following strategies if needed.

docs.title: Strategy 1 — Fill in Executable Metadata
docs.text:
Antivirus engines treat anonymous binaries with more suspicion. Always set:

--windows-product-name
--windows-file-description
--windows-product-version
--windows-company-name

docs.title: Strategy 2 — Switch Compilers
docs.text:
Recompile using a different compiler. Each one produces a slightly different binary signature:

--msvc=14.2
--clang
--mingw64
--mingw

docs.title: Strategy 3 — Use an Older Nuitka Version
docs.text:
As a Nuitka version becomes more commonly used (including by malware authors), detection rates rise. Pinning to an older version can help:

pip install nuitka==1.x.x

docs.title: Sign the Executable
docs.text: Digital signing is the most effective solution. In testing, signing reduced a VirusTotal result from 13 detections to 0.

docs.title: Tools Needed
docs.text:
• A certificate (.crt / .key), either self-signed or from a CA
  • osslsigncode — an open-source cross-platform signing tool

docs.title: Sign the Executable
docs.text:
osslsigncode sign \
  -certs your_cert.crt \
  -key your_key.key \
  -in your_app.exe \
  -out your_app_signed.exe

Note: You can also use signtool.exe (from the Windows SDK) with a .pfx certificate as an alternative.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text: Issue Detail Japanese (multibyte) folder names Signed onefile .exe files fail to extract if there are Japanese or other multibyte characters in the folder path. Unsigned executables are unaffected. Workaround for path issue Use the unsigned dist/ folder directly instead of the onefile .exe, or ensure the extraction path contains only ASCII characters. print() with --windows-disable-console Console output has no target, which can cause crashes. Comment out all print() calls before building. Persistent false positives Occasionally one detection may remain even after signing. No known complete fix; rotating compilers and Nuitka versions is the best mitigation.

docs.title: Creating an Executable from a Python Script
Creating an Executable from a Python Script
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Recommended Tool: Nuitka
docs.text:
Nuitka compiles Python source code into a native C-based executable. The resulting binary runs without requiring Python to be installed on the target machine.

Note: PyInstaller is a popular alternative, but executables it produces are frequently flagged as malware by antivirus engines. Nuitka compiles Python directly and produces cleaner binaries.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python installed
  • A C compiler (on Windows, Nuitka will prompt to install the MinGW-w64 compiler automatically if none is found)

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Install Nuitka.

    pip install nuitka

  2. Compile the script into a standalone executable.

    python -m nuitka --standalone --onefile your_script.py
    Option Description --standalone Includes all dependencies so the executable runs on machines without Python --onefile Packages everything into a single .exe file

  3. Find the output executable in the current directory (e.g., your_script.exe on Windows).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The first build takes longer than PyInstaller because Nuitka compiles Python to C and then compiles the C code.
  • For GUI apps, add --disable-console to suppress the terminal window.
  • To package the resulting executable into a Windows installer, see Create an Installer for a Python App.

docs.title: Creating an Installer for a Python App
Creating an Installer for a Python App
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Creating an installer packages a Python application into a standalone executable that end users can install without needing Python or any dependencies pre-installed.

docs.title: PyInstaller
docs.text:
Bundles a Python app and its dependencies into a single executable. Works on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

pip install pyinstaller
pyinstaller --onefile your_script.py

The output is placed in the dist/ folder.

docs.title: Inno Setup
docs.text:
A free Windows installer builder. Use it after PyInstaller to wrap the executable into a proper Windows installer (.exe) with install/uninstall support, shortcuts, and a setup wizard.

Typical workflow:

  1. Use PyInstaller to produce the standalone executable.
  2. Download and install Inno Setup.
  3. Create an Inno Setup script (.iss) that points to the executable and any supporting files.
  4. Compile the script to produce the final installer .exe.

docs.title: cx_Freeze
docs.text:
An alternative to PyInstaller that also produces standalone executables. Useful when PyInstaller is not compatible with a specific package.

pip install cx_Freeze

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Inno Setup is Windows-only. For macOS, consider tools like create-dmg or py2app.
  • Always test the generated installer on a clean machine to catch missing files or dependencies.

docs.title: Adding Multiple Images to a Markdown File
Adding Multiple Images to a Markdown File
docs.text:
When you drag multiple images into a Markdown file in VS Code, they are inserted on a single line like this:

![Photo](img/00-images/room01-01.jpg) ![Photo](img/00-images/room01-02.jpg) ![Photo](img/00-images/room01-03.jpg)

But often you want each image on its own line:

![Photo](img/00-images/room01-01.jpg)
![Photo](img/00-images/room01-02.jpg)
![Photo](img/00-images/room01-03.jpg)

You can fix this instantly using Find and eeplace with regular expressions.

docs.title: Step 1: Open Find and Replace
docs.text:
Press:

  • Windows / Linux: Ctrl + H
  • Mac: Cmd + H

This opens the Replace panel.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable Regular Expression Mode
docs.text:
Click the .* icon (Use Regular Expression), or press:

  • Alt + R (Windows/Linux)

Make sure the .* icon is highlighted.

docs.title: Step 3: Enter Find and Replace Patterns
docs.text:
Find:

\s!\[

Replace:

\n![

docs.title: Step 4: Click Replace All
docs.text:
Click:

Replace All

Result: Every image will move to its own line.

docs.title: Why this works
docs.text:
Pattern Meaning \s matches a space ![ matches the Markdown image start \n inserts a newline

So this converts:

(space)![

into

(newline)![

docs.title: Faster alternative (more precise)
docs.text:
This version only affects Markdown images:

Find:

\)\s+!\[

Replace:

)\n![

This ensures replacement only happens between images.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Before:

![Photo](img/a.jpg) ![Photo](img/b.jpg) ![Photo](img/c.jpg)

After:

![Photo](img/a.jpg)
![Photo](img/b.jpg)
![Photo](img/c.jpg)

docs.title: Optional: Assign a keyboard shortcut
docs.text:
You can speed this up by recording a macro using an extension like:

  • Multi Command
  • Macros

Then run it with one shortcut.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Quick version:

  1. Press Ctrl + H
  2. Enable .*
  3. Find: \s!\[
  4. Replace: \n![
  5. Click Replace All

docs.title: Fixing Python Interpreter Path Not Found in VS Code
Fixing Python Interpreter Path Not Found in VS Code
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

When VS Code shows a warning about python.defaultInterpreterPath pointing to a path that no longer exists, the Python interpreter VS Code was previously configured to use has been deleted or moved.

Common causes:

  • You deleted a virtual environment folder.
  • You uninstalled or moved a Python installation.
  • The project was opened on a different machine with a different folder structure.

docs.title: Fix: Select a New Interpreter
docs.text:
1. Open the Command Palette:

    • Windows/Linux: Ctrl+Shift+P
    • Mac: Cmd+Shift+P

    If the shortcut doesn't work, go to Help → Show All Commands in the menu bar.

  2. Type Python: Select Interpreter and press Enter.

  3. Select the interpreter you want to use from the dropdown. VS Code marks the recommended one with a Recommended label.

Label What It Means Recommended System Python installed from python.org Conda Python from an Anaconda/Miniconda environment (path shown) A specific virtual environment

VS Code updates the setting automatically and the warning disappears.

docs.title: Understanding the Setting
docs.text:
python.defaultInterpreterPath stores the file path to a python.exe (Windows) or python (Mac/Linux) executable. VS Code uses this interpreter for:

  • Running scripts
  • IntelliSense and code completion
  • Linting and formatting
  • The integrated terminal

docs.title: Default Installation Paths
docs.text: Source Typical Path python.org (Windows) ~\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python3xx\python.exe python.org (Mac) /usr/local/bin/python3 Miniconda/Anaconda C:\ProgramData\miniconda3\python.exe Virtual environment <project_folder>\venv\Scripts\python.exe (Windows)

docs.title: Edit the Setting Manually (Alternative)
docs.text: If the Command Palette approach does not work, edit the setting directly.

docs.title: Method 1: Edit in Settings UI
docs.text:
1. Go to File → Preferences → Settings (or Ctrl+,).
  2. Search for python.defaultInterpreterPath.
  3. Clear the existing invalid path and enter the correct one, or leave it blank to let VS Code auto-detect.

docs.title: Method 2: Edit settings.json
docs.text:
1. Open the Command Palette → Open User Settings (JSON).
  2. Find the line: 
    "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "D:\\old\\path\\to\\python.exe"
  3. Update or delete it.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• If you are using a virtual environment, activate or recreate it before selecting it as the interpreter.
  • python.defaultInterpreterPath is a fallback — once you select an interpreter for a workspace, VS Code stores it separately and uses that instead.
  • To check which interpreter is currently active, look at the status bar at the bottom-left of the VS Code window.

docs.title: Moving Files Safely in Linux or WSL Using VS Code
Moving Files Safely in Linux or WSL Using VS Code
docs.text: Avoid accidental folder replacement when moving files in Linux or WSL.

docs.title: Restore overwritten files
docs.text:
If a folder was accidentally replaced and changes were not committed:

  1. Open a terminal at the repository root.

  2. Run:

    git restore .

  3. Verify:

    git status

    Confirm that the working tree is clean.

docs.title: Understand Linux folder behavior
docs.text:
In Linux and WSL, moving a folder with the same name can replace the existing folder instead of merging it.

Example behavior:

mv new_folder existing_folder

If both names match, the original folder may be replaced.

docs.title: Copy file contents instead of replacing the folder
docs.text: cp -r source_folder/* existing_folder/

docs.title: Move a single file
docs.text: mv source_folder/file.md existing_folder/

docs.title: Commit before major changes
docs.text:
git add .
git commit -m "Checkpoint before refactor"

This allows safe recovery if a mistake occurs.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: Linux file operations behave differently from Windows folder merging. Use terminal commands instead of drag and drop when folder names are identical.

docs.title: Opening Linux and Windows Folders in VS Code (WSL)
Opening Linux and Windows Folders in VS Code (WSL)
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

When using VS Code with WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux), you can open both Linux folders and Windows folders in the same workspace.

docs.title: Opening a Linux Folder
docs.text:
Linux folders live under your home directory (~/) inside WSL. To open one:

  1. Go to File → Open Folder...
  2. Navigate to your folder (e.g., ~/projects/myproject)
  3. Click OK

The title bar will show [WSL: Ubuntu], confirming you are in the Linux environment.

docs.title: Opening a Windows Folder
docs.text:
Windows drives are mounted under /mnt/ inside WSL:

Windows Path WSL Path C:\ /mnt/c/ D:\ /mnt/d/ E:\ /mnt/e/

To open a Windows folder, use the WSL path format. For example:

  • Windows: D:\projects\my-project
  • WSL path: /mnt/d/projects/my-project

docs.title: Opening Multiple Folders with a Workspace
docs.text: You can open both a Linux folder and a Windows folder at the same time using a Multi-root Workspace.

docs.title: Setting Up a Workspace
docs.text:
1. Open your main folder in VS Code.
  2. Go to File → Save Workspace As...
  3. Enter a name (e.g., myworkspace.code-workspace) and click OK.
  4. Go to File → Add Folder to Workspace...
  5. Enter the path of the second folder (Linux or Windows) and click Add.

Both folders will appear as separate roots in the Explorer sidebar.

docs.title: Reopening a Workspace
docs.text: Double-click the .code-workspace file in your file explorer, or use File → Open Workspace from File... inside VS Code.

docs.title: Previewing Markdown Files
docs.text:
VS Code has a built-in Markdown preview. After opening or editing a .md file:

  • Press Ctrl+Shift+V to open the preview in a new tab.
  • Press Ctrl+K V to open the preview side by side.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Accessing Windows files (/mnt/d/...) from WSL works fine for reading and editing, but can be slightly slower than working with files inside WSL (~/...).
  • For simple file types like Markdown, the performance difference is not noticeable.
  • Claude Code can access both Linux and Windows paths and can edit files in either location.

docs.title: Previewing Markdown Side-by-Side
docs.text: Press Ctrl + K, then V.

docs.title: Replacing an Imported Image
docs.text: Replace an existing image file in an MkDocs project without changing the Markdown reference.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Locate the image file used in the Markdown document.

    Example:

`![Architecture](img/images/diagram.webp)`

The file is stored in:

`docs/images/diagram.webp`

  2. Edit the image using an external image editor.

    Examples:
- Crop unnecessary whitespace.
- Adjust dimensions.
- Export as `webp` if needed.

  3. Export the edited image using the same file name.

    Ensure the file name matches exactly:

`diagram.webp`

  4. Replace the original file in the project directory.

    Overwrite:

`docs/images/diagram.webp`

  5. Refresh the MkDocs development server.

    If using:

`mkdocs serve`

Perform a hard refresh in the browser:

`Ctrl + Shift + R`

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
• Keeping the same file name avoids updating Markdown references.
  • If the browser cache prevents updates from appearing, rename the file and update the Markdown reference.
  • When using Docker with bind mounts, file replacement is detected automatically.
  • Store the project inside the WSL Linux filesystem for consistent permissions and performance.

docs.title: Protecting Your Email When Trying Unknown Services
Protecting Your Email When Trying Unknown Services
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

When signing up for an unfamiliar or potentially suspicious service, avoid using your real email address. Here are three approaches to protect your privacy.

docs.title: 1. Disposable Email Services
docs.text:
The quickest option — no registration required.

Service Notes Temp Mail Popular and easy to use 10 Minute Mail Inbox self-destructs after 10 minutes Guerrilla Mail Lets you choose your own username

Generate a random email address, paste it into the service, and check the temporary inbox for any verification emails. Once you close the tab, the address is gone.

Warning: Do not use these for important accounts. If you get locked out, you won't be able to recover your password since the email no longer exists.

docs.title: 2. Plus Addressing (Gmail / Outlook Alias Trick)
docs.text:
Useful when you want to track whether a service sells your data.

If your email is yourname@gmail.com, sign up as:

yourname+servicename@gmail.com

Emails will still arrive in your normal inbox. You can then set up a filter to delete or label them automatically. If you start receiving spam at that specific address, you'll know exactly who shared your data.

docs.title: 3. Privacy-Focused Email Relay Services
docs.text:
For a more permanent and private solution:

  • Apple Hide My Email (iCloud+ users) — Generates unique random addresses that forward to your real inbox. You can delete any address at any time.
  • Firefox Relay — Similar concept, available without Apple devices.
  • ProtonMail — A privacy-focused email provider as an alternative main address.

docs.title: Recovering Data With Disk Drill
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Disk Drill is a data recovery utility for Windows and macOS developed by CleverFiles. It is designed to recover deleted or lost files from hard drives, USB flash drives, SSDs, memory cards, mobile devices, RAID arrays, and other sources.

docs.title: What It Can Recover
docs.text:
Disk Drill supports nearly 400 file formats and all commonly used file systems. It can recover:

  • Personal and business documents
  • Photos, videos, and music
  • Files from internal, external, and virtual hard drives
  • Files from memory cards, iPhones, iPads, and Android devices
  • Data from RAID arrays, Windows Storage Spaces, and NAS devices

It can also reconstruct damaged RAID arrays.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Recovery Vault — a background service that remembers metadata and properties of deleted files, allowing restoration with original file names and folder locations
  • Recovery during scan — restore files while a scan is still in progress without waiting for it to finish
  • Recovery chances prediction — automatically calculates and displays the likelihood that each file is recoverable
  • Session saving — scan sessions and backup progress are saved automatically, so you can pause and resume without starting over

docs.title: Pricing
docs.text: Disk Drill lets you recover up to 100 MB for free. A paid Pro upgrade unlocks unlimited recovery. Free access includes permanent use of the data protection tools such as Recovery Vault.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: Disk Drill uses non-destructive algorithms that recover data without performing any write operations on the source drive.

docs.title: Visualizing Disk Usage on Windows
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Before backing up or cleaning up your system, it helps to see what's actually taking up space. This guide covers the best tool to visualize disk usage on Windows.

docs.title: Why Visualize First?
docs.text:
Blindly deleting files is risky. Visualizing disk usage lets you:

  • Instantly identify the largest files and folders
  • Make informed decisions about what to delete
  • Reduce backup size and time before copying to NAS or external storage

docs.title: WizTree (Windows)
docs.text:
⚡ Recommended — the fastest disk analyzer available for Windows.

WizTree reads directly from NTFS's MFT (Master File Table), bypassing the normal file system layer. This lets it scan even multi-terabyte drives in seconds.

docs.title: Download
docs.text: Item Details Official site https://www.diskanalyzer.com/ License Free for personal use Platform Windows 7 / 8 / 10 / 11

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Download and install WizTree from the official site.
  2. Launch WizTree and select the drive you want to scan (e.g. D:).
  3. Click Scan.
  4. The treemap view renders immediately — large rectangles = large files.
  5. Click any rectangle to reveal the full file path.
  6. Sort the file list by Size to find the top offenders.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Right-click any file in the list → Open Containing Folder to locate it quickly.
  • Use the Files tab (not just the treemap) to sort all files by size across the entire drive.
  • Filter by extension (e.g. .iso, .vhdx, .bak) to find specific file types.

Note: Always double-check before deleting. Some large files (e.g. page files, hibernation files) are system-managed and should not be removed manually.

docs.title: Suggested Workflow
docs.text:
# Step-by-step cleanup workflow

1. Scan D: with WizTree
2. Sort by Size (largest first)
3. Identify candidates for deletion:
   - Old installer files (.exe, .msi, .iso)
   - Unused virtual machine images (.vhdx, .vmdk)
   - Redundant backups or archives (.zip, .tar, .bak)
4. Delete or move to cold storage
5. Re-scan to confirm free space

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Once you've cleaned up Windows, consider also checking:

  • WSL disk usage — WSL2 virtual disk files (ext4.vhdx) can grow very large and do not shrink automatically even after deleting files inside Linux.
  • NAS / backup size — re-scan after cleanup to confirm how much you've saved before starting your backup job.

docs.title: Migrating PicPick Portable Settings to a New Version
Migrating PicPick Portable Settings to a New Version
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

PicPick Portable doesn't use the Windows registry. Every setting — capture options, hotkeys, auto-save folder, JPEG/WebP quality, screen recorder options, editor behavior — lives in a single plain-text file called picpick.ini, sitting right next to picpick.exe in the portable folder.

Because both the old and new versions read that same file at startup, you can usually skip re-entering all your settings by hand: just close the old version, copy its picpick.ini into the new version's folder, and launch the new one.

docs.title: When This Works Well
docs.text:
• You're upgrading between two portable builds (not the installed/MSI version, which stores settings in the registry instead).
  • The version jump is small (e.g. a patch/point release like 7.6.0 → 7.6.1). The ini format is very likely unchanged.
  • You're not relying on anything version-specific that got redesigned (see Caveats below — e.g. Screen Recorder settings moved out of the main Options dialog into their own panel in some versions, but they're still stored in the same ini file under a [ScreenRecorder] section).

docs.title: Step 1: Locate the Old Version's ini File
docs.text:
It's in the same folder as the old picpick.exe — for example:

\\<YOUR-NAS>\<YOUR-FOLDER>\picpick-portable\picpick.ini

or wherever your old portable copy lives. If you don't see it, the old version may never have had a setting changed/saved yet — the ini is only written the first time you open Program Options and click OK (or change something the app auto-saves, like window position).

docs.title: Step 2: Completely Close the Old PicPick
docs.text:
This step matters: PicPick keeps its current settings in memory and writes them back to picpick.ini on exit. If you copy the file while it's still running, your copy can get overwritten with stale data.

  • Right-click the PicPick icon in the system tray (under the ^ hidden icons arrow if needed) and choose Exit.
  • Double-check it's gone: open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) and confirm there's no picpick.exe process left under Apps or Background processes.

docs.title: Step 3: Back Up the New Version's ini (Optional)
docs.text:
The new portable folder will already have generated its own default picpick.ini the first time you ran it. Rename it just in case you want to compare later:

picpick.ini  →  picpick.ini.default.bak

docs.title: Step 4: Copy the Old ini into the New Folder
docs.text:
Copy picpick.ini from the old portable folder into the new one, replacing (or renaming over) the default file:

<new-picpick-portable-folder>\picpick.ini

docs.title: Step 5: Launch the New Version
docs.text: Double-click the new picpick.exe. It should start with your old settings already in place — auto-save folder, hotkeys, capture options, recording settings, and so on.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify
docs.text:
Open Options (hamburger menu → Options, or the gear icon in Screen Recorder for recording-specific settings) and click through each tab to confirm things landed correctly:

  • General — startup behavior, language, color theme
  • Editor — hide-before-capture, background color, etc.
  • Capture — multi-monitor, sound, magnifier
  • File Name / Auto Save — naming pattern and save folder
  • Images — JPEG/WebP quality
  • Hotkeys — all your custom key combos
  • Screen Recorder settings (gear icon in the recorder toolbar) — output folder, FPS, quality, audio

Note: If Windows complains that a hotkey "cannot be registered" when you save (this can happen even with a legitimately-copied ini, if another app is temporarily holding that key combo), choose No when asked whether to change it — that keeps your intended combo in the file rather than resetting it.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Different major versions: if you're jumping across a bigger version gap, new settings keys may have been added or renamed. Copying the ini should still work — PicPick will just fall back to defaults for any keys it doesn't recognize — but it's worth doing the verification pass in Step 6 rather than assuming a perfect match.
  • Window position / recent files: the ini also stores things like the editor window's last position and size ([Placement]) and per-toolbar layout ([QATBar...]). These will carry over too, which is usually desirable but worth knowing.
  • No ini file yet: if the old version never had its Program Options dialog opened/saved, there may be no meaningful picpick.ini to copy — in that case it's just using PicPick's defaults already, and there's nothing to migrate.

docs.title: Adding a Second SSD to Synology DS720+
Adding a Second SSD to Synology DS720+
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Notes from installing a second M.2 SSD (4TB WD Red SA500) alongside an existing 2TB SSD in a Synology DS720+, and setting it up as an independent storage volume via DSM.

  • NAS: Synology DS720+ (two M.2 NVMe/SATA SSD slots)
  • Existing setup: one 2TB SSD, already running as Storage Pool 1 / Volume 1
  • New drive: WD Red SA500 2.5" 4TB SSD, installed in the second slot

Installing the drive physically is not enough on its own — Windows won't show any change, since the new drive isn't part of a Windows-visible volume yet. Everything else happens inside DSM Storage Manager.

docs.title: Step 1: Install the SSD into a Drive Tray
docs.text:
Before the drive can be recognized, mount it in one of the NAS's drive trays (cassettes):

  1. Remove an empty cassette from the NAS.

  2. Remove the two side rails from the cassette.

  3. Remove the yellow "Remove Before Installing" sticker covering the SSD's connector terminal.

  4. Screw the SSD into the cassette at all four corners.

  5. Slide the cassette back into the NAS.

docs.title: Step 2: Confirm the Drive Is Detected
docs.text: Log in to DSM (http://find.synology.com or the NAS's IP address) and open Storage Manager → HDD/SSD. Both drives should appear, healthy.

docs.title: Step 3: Decide How to Use the New Drive
docs.text:
A brand-new SSD doesn't automatically merge into the existing 2TB volume. Options:

  • Separate, independent volume (used here) — the 4TB drive becomes its own storage pool and volume, showing up alongside the existing one.
  • RAID 1 mirror — requires destroying and rebuilding the existing single-drive volume, and with a 2TB + 4TB pair, usable capacity is capped at 2TB (the smaller drive). Generally not worth it unless redundancy matters more than capacity.

docs.title: SSD Cache vs. Storage Volume
docs.text: The DS720+'s two M.2 slots can be used either as normal storage (each slot holds its own volume) or as SSD cache for spinning HDDs, where the SSD doesn't appear as its own drive but instead transparently accelerates reads and writes to HDD volumes. This guide covers using the M.2 slot as a standalone storage volume, not as cache.

docs.title: Step 4: Create a New Storage Pool
docs.text:
Note: The Action button on the HDD/SSD page only has drive-level tools (Benchmark, Secure Erase, Configure Write Cache) — it does not create pools.

  1. In the left sidebar, go to Storage → Storage Pool 1 (the existing pool's page).
  2. Click Create → Create Storage Pool.

docs.title: Step 5: Choose the RAID Type
docs.text:
For a single drive, only Basic or JBOD make sense (SHR also technically works with one drive, but Basic is simpler and standard for a single disk).

The Storage pool description field is optional — safe to leave blank.

docs.title: Step 6: Select the Drive
docs.text:
Select the new drive (Drive 2). DSM may show a warning:

"This drive is not supported for storage pool use. Refer to the compatibility list for supported drives."

This warning is expected for third-party (non-Synology-branded) drives like the WD Red SA500 — it is not a blocker. The drive works fine; DSM just cannot guarantee full validation and health-reporting support, and may show occasional compatibility notifications.

docs.title: Step 7: Run a Drive Check
docs.text: Choose Perform drive check (not the default "Skip"). For a brand-new drive, a full surface scan up front is worth the extra time — it catches bad sectors before you start storing data, rather than discovering them later.

docs.title: Step 8: Confirm and Apply
docs.text:
Review the summary (RAID type: Basic, Drive 2, ~3.7TB estimated capacity, drive check enabled) and click Apply.

This starts the drive check and pool initialization, which can take over an hour for a full scan on a 4TB drive.

docs.title: Step 9: Create the Volume
docs.text:
Once the drive check completes, Storage Pool 2 shows Healthy with free capacity (3.6TB in this case).

Click Create → Create Volume.

docs.title: Allocate Capacity
docs.text: Storage Pool should default to the new pool (Storage Pool 2). Click Max to allocate the full available capacity, unless you want to reserve space. Volume description is optional.

docs.title: Choose File System
docs.text: Keep Btrfs (recommended) — it supports snapshots, shared folder quotas, and data integrity checksums, which ext4 doesn't.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text: Leave Encrypt this volume unchecked, unless the volume will hold sensitive data and you're specifically concerned about physical theft of the NAS. Reasons to skip: performance overhead (the DS720+ lacks AES-NI hardware acceleration) and permanent data loss risk if the Encryption Key Vault/key is ever lost.

docs.title: Confirm and Apply
docs.text:
Review the summary (Storage pool, allocated capacity, file system) and click Apply.

Volume creation is much faster than the storage pool's drive check. Once done, Volume 2 appears healthy with free space.

docs.title: Step 10: Create a Shared Folder on the New Volume
docs.text:
A volume alone isn't accessible from Windows — you need a shared folder on it.

Open Control Panel → Shared Folder. Existing shared folders (all on Volume 1) are listed here.

Click Create → Create Shared Folder (not "Mount Hybrid Share Folder" — that's for Synology's cloud-linked Hybrid Share feature, unrelated).

docs.title: Basic Information
docs.text:
• Name: shared folder names must be unique across the entire NAS (they're all top-level network shares), not just per volume. Pick something new — reusing a name that already exists on Volume 1 isn't allowed. This guide uses <YOUR-FOLDER>-2 as a counterpart to an existing <YOUR-FOLDER> shared folder on Volume 1.
  • Location: change from the default (Volume 1) to Volume 2.
  • Enable Recycle Bin: leave checked (recommended).

Note: System-generated folders like homes, ActiveBackupforBusiness, web, web_packages are created by specific DSM services/packages (User Home Service, Active Backup for Business, Web Station) the first time each is enabled, and stay on whichever single volume they were pointed to. Adding a new volume does not cause DSM to recreate them there — no need to avoid those names when naming a new folder.

docs.title: Additional Security Measure
docs.text: Leave Skip selected. Encryption has the same tradeoffs as at the volume level; WriteOnce/WORM is only relevant for compliance scenarios requiring files to be locked from editing/deletion for a retention period.

docs.title: Advanced Settings
docs.text:
• Enable data checksum for advanced data integrity: worth enabling for general file storage — it's one of the main benefits of Btrfs (self-healing, detects corruption). Skip it only if this folder will host a database, VM, Surveillance Station recordings, or be an Active Backup for Business target (per DSM's own note), since checksums add overhead in those cases.
  • Enable shared folder quota: optional, leave unchecked unless you want to cap this folder's size within the volume.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: The wizard's permissions step lets you assign per-user access. Defaults (based on existing group permissions) are usually already correct — confirm your account shows Read/Write before finishing.

docs.title: Step 11: Verify the Result
docs.text:
Back in Control Panel → Shared Folder, the new folder appears in the list. Expanding it shows the configured settings (Recycle Bin enabled, Data Integrity Protection enabled, no quota).

To double check permissions later: select the folder, click Edit → Permissions tab. Confirm your account(s) show Read/Write.

docs.title: Step 12: Access from Windows
docs.text:
The new shared folder is now reachable at:

\\<NAS-IP-or-name>\<YOUR-FOLDER>-2

Enter that path in File Explorer's address bar, or map it as a network drive via This PC → Map network drive.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Two independent storage pools, volumes, and shared folders on the DS720+:

Storage Pool Volume Shared Folder Original Storage Pool 1 (2TB SSD) Volume 1 <YOUR-FOLDER>, homes, backup, web, web_packages, ActiveBackupforBusiness New Storage Pool 2 (4TB SSD) Volume 2 <YOUR-FOLDER>-2

    Note: Spaces are allowed, but hyphens and underscores are not.
