docs.title: Backing Up Documents from Android to Synology NAS
Backing Up Documents from Android to Synology NAS
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide explains how to back up documents and other files from an Android phone (e.g., Google Pixel) to a Synology NAS using a Synology Drive sync task. The sync task uploads files from the phone to the NAS. Files you delete from the phone afterward stay on the NAS, so you can treat the phone storage as temporary and manage everything on the NAS.

Note: For screenshots specifically, see Backing Up Screenshots Automatically with Synology Photos instead — no manual sync task or file-moving needed.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Sync Task Settings
docs.text:
1. Open Synology Drive on your phone.

  2. Tap More → Backup and Sync Tasks.

  3. Tap Sync Tasks.

  4. To create a new task, tap the + icon. To change an existing task, tap its ⋮ icon.

  5. Tap Edit task.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure the Sync Task
docs.text:
Set the following values on the Edit task screen:

Setting Value Remote path on the server A folder on your NAS, e.g., My Drive/Backup/<YOUR-FOLDER> Local path A folder on your phone, e.g., Internal storage/Documents/<YOUR-FOLDER> Mode Upload only Keep locally deleted files on the server On

  1. Tap Mode.

  2. Select Upload only. Files go from the phone to the NAS, and changes on the NAS do not affect the phone.

  3. Under File conflict resolution, turn on Keep locally deleted files on the server. This setting keeps files on the NAS after you delete them from the phone.

  4. Tap DONE.

Warning: If Keep locally deleted files on the server is off, deleting a file from the phone may also delete it from the NAS.

docs.title: Step 3: Move Files into the Sync Folder
docs.text:
Only files inside the local path are uploaded. Move the files you want to back up into that folder.

  1. Open the Files app and tap Images (or another category).

  2. Select the files you want to back up.

  3. Tap ⋮ → Move to, then open Documents.

  4. Open the sync folder.

  5. Tap Move here.

docs.title: Step 4: Run the Sync
docs.text:
The sync task runs automatically over Wi-Fi. To run it immediately, use either method:

  • Tap the task's ⋮ icon, then tap Sync now.
  • Use Focused Backup and Sync as described below.

docs.title: Using Focused Backup and Sync
docs.text:
1. Connect your phone to Wi-Fi and a charger.

  2. Tap More → Focused Backup and Sync.

  3. Tap Enable. Keep Synology Drive in the foreground until the sync finishes.

  4. When Backup and sync completed appears, tap Done.

docs.title: Step 5: Delete the Originals from Your Phone
docs.text:
1. Confirm the files appear in the remote folder on your NAS.

  2. In the Files app, select the original files in the sync folder and tap the trash icon.

The files remain on the NAS.

Note: Test with one or two files first. Sync them, delete them from the phone, sync again, and confirm they are still on the NAS.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Action on Phone Result on NAS Add file to the sync folder Uploaded Edit file Updated Delete file Kept (when Keep locally deleted files on the server is on)

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use a dedicated local folder for synced files so the sync behavior stays predictable.
  • Use a dedicated NAS folder to avoid mixing with other files.
  • Enable versioning on the NAS (Synology Drive Admin Console) to protect against accidental edits and file corruption.
  • If the NAS holds your only copy, keep a second copy of it elsewhere, for example with Hyper Backup.
  • Avoid editing the same files from multiple devices at the same time.

docs.title: Backing Up Your Obsidian Vault with Synology Drive
Backing Up Your Obsidian Vault with Synology Drive
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Synology Drive is the recommended tool for backing up a specific folder like your Obsidian Vault. This guide walks you through the full setup.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Synology Drive Server on Your NAS
docs.text:
1. Log into DSM (your NAS web interface).
  2. Open Package Center.
  3. Search for Synology Drive Server.
  4. Click Install.

This turns your NAS into a private cloud, similar to Google Drive.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable Your Home Folder
docs.text:
1. Go to Control Panel.
  2. Open User & Group.
  3. Go to the Advanced tab.
  4. Enable User Home Service.

This creates a personal folder for your account (usually /home/Drive).

docs.title: Step 3: Install Synology Drive Client on Windows 11
docs.text:
1. Download Synology Drive Client from the Synology website.
  2. Install it on your PC.
  3. Launch the app.

docs.title: Step 4: Connect to Your NAS
docs.text:
1. Click Start Now.
  2. Enter your NAS IP address (e.g., 192.168.x.x), username, and password.
  3. Click Next.

If you are on the same local network, the connection is usually straightforward.

docs.title: Step 5: Choose "Backup Task"
docs.text:
When prompted, select Backup Task, not Sync Task.

Note: Backup Task is safer for Obsidian. It is a one-way upload (PC to NAS) and avoids sync conflicts.

docs.title: Step 6: Select Your Obsidian Vault Folder
docs.text:
Set the local and remote folders:

Local folder (on your PC):

C:\Users\<username>\Documents\Obsidian Vault

Remote folder (on your NAS):

/home/Drive/Obsidian Backup

You can rename the remote folder if you prefer.

docs.title: Step 7: Set the Backup Mode
docs.text:
Choose one of the following:

  • Continuous backup — backs up automatically whenever files change (recommended for Obsidian)
  • Scheduled backup — runs at a fixed interval (e.g., hourly or daily)

Use Continuous backup for Obsidian to keep your notes protected in near real-time.

docs.title: Step 8: Enable Versioning
docs.text:
Turn on File versioning and set a retention count such as 10–20 versions.

Note: Versioning lets you recover notes that were deleted, overwritten, or corrupted.

docs.title: Step 9: Finish Setup
docs.text:
1. Review your settings.
  2. Click Apply.

Your Obsidian Vault is now automatically backed up to your Synology NAS.

docs.title: Tips for Obsidian
docs.text:
Do:

  • Use Backup Task, not Sync Task.
  • Keep versioning on.

Avoid:

  • Syncing the same vault with multiple tools at the same time.
  • Using two-way sync unless you fully understand how it handles conflicts.

docs.title: Optional: Combine with Active Backup for Business
docs.text:
For full coverage, pair Synology Drive with Active Backup for Business:

Tool Purpose Synology Drive Protects your Obsidian notes with versioning Active Backup for Business Protects your entire PC

docs.title: Changing the UI Language of Synology Photos
Changing the UI Language of Synology Photos
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Synology Photos app does not have a built-in language setting. The display language follows the system language of your Android device.

To display the app in English, change the system language of your phone:

Synology Photos does not support Android's per-app language setting, so there is no way to change its language independently.

docs.title: Checking the IP Address of Your Synology NAS
Checking the IP Address of Your Synology NAS
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Use Synology Assistant to connect to your NAS and find its local IP address via DSM.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A smartphone with an authenticator app set up for DSM login approval
  • Synology Assistant installed on your computer

docs.title: Connect via Synology Assistant
docs.text:
1. Open Synology Assistant on your computer.
  2. Select your NAS from the server list.
  3. Click Connect.
  4. Enter your ID and password to log in to DSM.
  5. Check your phone — you will be prompted to approve the login.
  6. Approve the login on your phone.

docs.title: Find the IP Address in DSM
docs.text:
1. After logging in, open Control Panel.
  2. Go to Info Center.
  3. Select the Network tab.
  4. Check the status of each LAN section (Connected / Disconnected).
  5. Note the IP address of the Connected LAN — this is your NAS's local IP address.

Tip: The IP address shown here is your NAS's local network address (e.g. 192.168.1.100). You can use this to access DSM directly in a browser without QuickConnect.

docs.title: Checking Storage on Synology DS720+
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Managing storage on your NAS is essential for maintaining performance and ensuring backups have enough room to grow. This guide covers the three best ways to monitor your DiskStation's capacity.

docs.title: Method 1: Quick View via Storage Manager
docs.text:
The fastest way to see a high-level summary of your total, used, and available space.

  1. Log in to DSM (DiskStation Manager).
  2. Open the Main Menu (top-left corner) and launch Storage Manager.
  3. Select Storage from the left-hand sidebar.
  4. Click on the Volume you wish to inspect.

Note: Look for the "Used/Total" bar. If you have multiple volumes, check each one individually.

docs.title: Method 2: Granular Breakdown via Usage Details
docs.text:
If you are using the Btrfs file system (standard for the DS720+), you can see exactly which services (like Synology Drive or Snapshots) are consuming space.

  1. Go to Storage Manager → Storage.
  2. Click the three dots (...) icon on the specific volume.
  3. Select Usage Details.
  4. A categorized list appears showing space taken by:
    • Shared Folders
    • Snapshots
    • System Databases (e.g., Synology Photos, Drive)
    • Swap files

docs.title: Method 3: Deep Dive via Storage Analyzer
docs.text: To find specific large files, duplicates, or space-hogging file types, use the Storage Analyzer package.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Open the Package Center.
  2. Search for Storage Analyzer and click Install.

docs.title: Running a Report
docs.text:
1. Open Storage Analyzer.
  2. Go to Report Profile and click Create.
  3. Follow the wizard to select which volumes to analyze.
  4. Once the report is generated, select it and click View Report.

Key Features:

  • Large Files: Identifies files exceeding a specific size.
  • Duplicates: Finds identical files that can be safely deleted.
  • File Groups: Shows a breakdown by type (Video, Image, Audio, etc.).

docs.title: Troubleshoot Missing Space
docs.text:
If the used space is significantly higher than your actual file size, check the following:

  • Drive Versioning: Synology Drive keeps versions of files. Check the Admin Console in Drive to limit versions.
  • Recycle Bins: Empty them via Control Panel → Shared Folder → Action → Empty all Recycle Bins.
  • Snapshots: If using Snapshot Replication, old snapshots can occupy significant space until they rotate out.

docs.title: Create a Task

docs.title: Configure the Task

  3. In the Task Settings tab, select the recycle bins and file types to delete.

  4. If needed, click Advanced Settings for additional options.
  5. Click OK, then Yes in the confirmation dialog.

docs.title: Steps

docs.title: Hiding the Homes Folder in Synology DSM
Hiding the Homes Folder in Synology DSM
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The homes shared folder appears alongside home when you connect as an administrator. You can hide it from Windows Explorer without affecting its functionality.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: homes is an admin-level shared folder. When you log in with administrator privileges, both home and homes are visible. Regular users see only their personal home folder by default.

docs.title: Step 1: Hide the Folder via Network Preview
docs.text:
1. Log into DSM.
  2. Go to Control Panel → Shared Folder.
  3. Select homes from the list and click Edit.
  4. On the General tab, check Hide this shared folder in "Network".
  5. Click Save.

After saving, homes no longer appears when browsing the NAS from Explorer. It remains accessible by direct path.

docs.title: Alternative: Use a Standard User Account for Daily Tasks
docs.text: If your everyday PC account is a regular user (not in the administrators group), homes is already invisible — only your personal home folder appears. Creating a separate standard account for daily use keeps the interface clean and improves security.

docs.title: Warnings
docs.text: Warning: Do not hide or delete the home folder. It is your personal access point for the NAS, and removing it breaks smartphone photo backup destinations.

docs.title: Running Claude on Synology NAS via Docker and API
Running Claude on Synology NAS via Docker and API
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide shows how to run Claude-powered workflows on a Synology NAS using Docker and the Anthropic API.

docs.title: 📌 Overview
docs.text:
Since Claude Desktop cannot run on Synology, the best approach is:

  • Run a lightweight app in Docker
  • Connect it to Claude via the Anthropic API
  • Use it for automation, chat interfaces, or file processing

docs.title: ✅ Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Synology NAS with Container Manager (Docker) installed
  • An Anthropic API key
  • Basic familiarity with Docker and terminal/SSH

docs.title: 🔑 Step 1: Get an Anthropic API Key
docs.text:
1. Go to the Anthropic Console and sign in.
  2. Create an API key.
  3. Save it securely — you will need it later.

docs.title: 🐳 Step 2: Install Docker (Container Manager)
docs.text:
1. Open Package Center.
  2. Install Container Manager (or Docker on older DSM versions).
  3. Launch it.

docs.title: 📁 Step 3: Prepare a Project Folder
docs.text:
Create a shared folder for the app, for example:

/docker/claude-app/

Inside it, create three files:

app.py
requirements.txt
Dockerfile

docs.title: app.py
docs.text:
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import requests
import os

app = Flask(__name__)

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")

@app.route("/chat", methods=["POST"])
def chat():
    user_input = request.json.get("message")

    response = requests.post(
        "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages",
        headers={
            "x-api-key": ANTHROPIC_API_KEY,
            "anthropic-version": "2023-06-01",
            "content-type": "application/json"
        },
        json={
            "model": "claude-sonnet-4-6",
            "max_tokens": 500,
            "messages": [
                {"role": "user", "content": user_input}
            ]
        }
    )

    return jsonify(response.json())

@app.route("/")
def home():
    return "Claude API is running!"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)

docs.title: requirements.txt
docs.text:
flask
requests

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text:
FROM python:3.11-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY app.py .

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

docs.title: ⚙️ Step 5: Build the Docker Image
docs.text:
SSH into your Synology and run:

cd /volume1/docker/claude-app
docker build -t claude-app .

docs.title: ▶️ Step 6: Run the Container
docs.text:
docker run -d \
  -p 5000:5000 \
  -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<YOUR-API-KEY> \
  --name claude-container \
  claude-app

docs.title: 🌐 Step 7: Test the API
docs.text:
Use curl to send a test message:

curl -X POST http://192.168.x.x:5000/chat \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"message": "Hello Claude"}'

You should receive a JSON response from Claude.

docs.title: 1. Add a Web UI
docs.text:
• Use a simple frontend (React, plain HTML, or Gradio).
  • Connect it to the /chat endpoint.

docs.title: 2. File Processing
docs.text:
Mount a volume when starting the container:

-v /volume1/data:/data

Let Claude process files such as logs or notes.

docs.title: 3. Automation
docs.text:
Combine the container with:

  • Cron jobs
  • Webhooks
  • Home automation tools

docs.title: 4. Reverse Proxy (Recommended)
docs.text:
• Use Synology's Application Portal.
  • Expose your app securely via HTTPS.

docs.title: ⚠️ Tips
docs.text:
• Low-power NAS models struggle with heavy workloads — keep apps lightweight.
  • Monitor your Anthropic API usage to control costs.
  • Use a smaller model (e.g., claude-haiku-4-5-20251001) for high-volume or latency-sensitive tasks.
  • Never hardcode your API key in source files; always pass it as an environment variable.

docs.title: 🧠 Example Use Cases
docs.text:
• Personal AI assistant dashboard
  • Log and file summarization
  • Smart home automation logic
  • Internal chatbot for your documents

docs.title: Setting Up Active Backup for Business for D: Drive Backup
Setting Up Active Backup for Business for D: Drive Backup
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Active Backup for Business (ABB) is Synology's enterprise-grade agent-based backup solution. It enables you to back up your entire Windows PC — or selected volumes — directly to your NAS, with incremental transfers, global deduplication, and flexible restore options.

This guide covers:

  • Installing and configuring ABB on your NAS
  • Installing the agent on your Windows 11 machine
  • Creating a backup task targeting D:\ only
  • Setting schedule, deduplication, and retention
  • Configuring folder exclusions to save NAS space

Note: Your final setup will be professional-grade — Synology Drive handles real-time Obsidian vault sync, while ABB covers full D:\ drive backup and recovery.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Active Backup for Business on the NAS
docs.text:
1. Log into DSM (your NAS web interface).
  2. Open Package Center.
  3. Search for Active Backup for Business and click Install.
  4. Wait for installation to complete.

docs.title: Step 2: Open ABB and Enable PC Backup
docs.text:
1. Open Active Backup for Business from the DSM app menu.
  2. Navigate to the PC section in the left sidebar.
  3. Click Add Device — this will prompt you to download the Windows agent.

Note: Keep this browser window open — you will return to it after installing the agent on your PC.

docs.title: Step 3: Install the ABB Agent on Windows 11
docs.text:
1. Download the Active Backup for Business Agent installer from the ABB interface or from Synology's download center.
  2. Run the installer on your Windows 11 machine.
  3. Accept defaults and complete the installation.
  4. Launch the agent — it will open in the system tray.

docs.title: Step 4: Connect Your PC to the NAS
docs.text:
In the agent application on your Windows PC:

  1. Enter your NAS IP address (e.g. 192.168.1.x).
  2. Enter your DSM username and password.
  3. Click Connect.

Note: Your PC will now appear as a device in Active Backup for Business on the NAS. Return to the NAS browser tab to continue.

docs.title: Step 5: Create a Backup Task
docs.text:
In the ABB interface on your NAS:

  1. Select your PC from the device list.
  2. Click Create Task.

docs.title: Step 6: Select Customized Volume
docs.text:
When prompted to choose what to back up, you will see these options:

  • Entire device
  • System volume
  • Customized volume

Select Customized Volume, then tick D: drive only.

Note: This option backs up only D:\, avoiding wasted space on the C: system drive.

docs.title: Step 7: Set the Backup Schedule
docs.text: Option Description Recommended Daily — scheduled at night (e.g. 2:00 AM) while your PC is on Advanced Event-based: on startup, shutdown, or USB connect

docs.title: Step 8: Enable Deduplication and Compression
docs.text:
Both options are typically enabled by default. Verify they are on:

  • Global deduplication — eliminates duplicate data blocks across backups, saving significant NAS space
  • Compression — reduces backup size further

Note: Leave both enabled. These are among the most valuable features of ABB and cost little in performance.

docs.title: Step 9: Configure the Retention Policy
docs.text:
The retention policy determines how many recovery points are kept before old ones are deleted. It protects against accidental deletions and file corruption.

Recommended options:

  • Keep last 30 versions — simple and predictable
  • Smart Recycle — intelligent thinning that keeps more recent versions and gradually reduces older ones

Note: Smart Recycle is generally the best choice. It maximises recovery options while automatically managing space over time.

docs.title: Step 10: Apply and Run the First Backup
docs.text:
1. Review all settings and click Apply.
  2. The first backup will begin immediately (or at the next scheduled time).

Warning: The first backup will take a long time — it must scan and transfer the entire D:\ drive. All subsequent backups will be incremental (only changed data), which are much faster.

docs.title: Part 3: Folder Exclusions
docs.text: ABB supports file and folder exclusions to reduce backup size. Exclusions are applied as filters — not precise file selection — but they are effective for removing large, unimportant data.

docs.title: How to Access Exclusion Settings
docs.text:
1. Go to Active Backup for Business on your NAS.
  2. Select your PC backup task.
  3. Click Edit.
  4. Look for File Filter or Exclusion Settings.

docs.title: What You Can Exclude
docs.text:
By folder path — exclude entire folders using their full path:

D:\Games\
D:\Downloads\
D:\Temp\

By file type — exclude files by extension across the entire drive:

  • *.iso — disc images
  • *.tmp — temporary files
  • *.log — log files

docs.title: Recommended Exclusions
docs.text: Folder / Pattern Reason D:\Games\ Large game installs — easily re-downloadable D:\Downloads\ Ephemeral files with no long-term value D:\Temp\ Temporary files — not worth backing up *.iso Disc images — very large, easily re-sourced *.tmp Temporary files generated by apps *.log Log files — verbose, low value

docs.title: Exclusion Limitations
docs.text:
• ABB is fundamentally image-based — exclusions are filters, not precise file selection.
  • Path syntax must be exact — a typo means the folder is still backed up.
  • No auto-suggestions — you must know the exact paths.
  • Some system data may still be included even with exclusions.

Note: If your goal is to back up only a few specific folders (not exclude a few), use Synology Drive instead. ABB is best suited for "back up everything except X" scenarios.

docs.title: Do This
docs.text:
• Keep the NAS powered on during scheduled backup windows.
  • Verify sufficient free storage space on the NAS before the first run.
  • Use a wired LAN connection for the initial backup — significantly faster than Wi-Fi.
  • Enable Smart Recycle for automatic retention management.
  • Test a restore of a single file after setup to confirm everything works.

docs.title: Avoid This
docs.text:
• Do not run multiple backup tools on the same folder — this wastes space and causes conflicts.
  • Do not skip retention settings — unlimited versions will eventually fill your NAS.
  • Do not interrupt the first backup once started — let it complete fully.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Tool Coverage and Purpose Synology Drive Obsidian Vault — real-time, versioned sync Active Backup for Business Entire D:\ drive — full incremental backup with restore

docs.title: Syncing a Folder to a Second Synology Volume
Syncing a Folder to a Second Synology Volume
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide covers syncing a folder on a Windows PC to a shared folder that lives on a second, independent storage pool/volume on a Synology NAS (e.g. a second SSD added to a DS720+), using Synology Drive.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
• NAS: Synology DS720+.
  • A second SSD was added and set up as its own independent storage pool and volume — not part of the existing RAID/volume.
  • A shared folder named office-2 was created on that new volume.
  • Goal: two-way sync a folder on a Windows 11 PC with office-2 on the NAS, using the Synology Drive Client.

docs.title: Why "office-2" Doesn't Show Up in Synology Drive Client Right Away
docs.text: Synology Drive Client can only sync to My Drive or a Team Folder — not to an arbitrary shared folder. A shared folder created directly in Control Panel → Shared Folder (or when a new volume is set up) isn't automatically a Team Folder. That's why a plain shared folder like office-2 is visible over the network (\\<YOUR-NAS-IP>\office-2) but doesn't appear as an option when creating a sync task in Synology Drive Client — it first needs to be enabled as a Team Folder.

docs.title: Step 1: Open Synology Drive Admin Console
docs.text: On the NAS desktop (DSM), open Synology Drive Admin Console — the server-side admin app, not the Drive Client app used on your PC.

docs.title: Step 2: Go to Team Folder
docs.text: In the left-hand menu, click Team Folder. You'll see a list of shared folders and their Drive status. Existing shared folders that haven't been enabled for Drive show as Not enabled — in this case, office-2 sits alongside web and backup as not enabled, while office is already Enabled.

docs.title: Step 3: Enable "office-2" as a Team Folder
docs.text: Select the office-2 row, then click Enable.

docs.title: Step 4: Configure Versioning Settings
docs.text:
Enabling a folder for Drive prompts a Settings dialog on the Versioning tab. This controls how many historical file versions are kept and how long they're retained before automatic cleanup. The defaults — version control on, up to 8 versions, rotating out anything older than 30 days — are a sensible starting point. A Security tab sits alongside it for restricting access at the Team Folder level if needed.

Click OK to accept.

docs.title: Step 5: Acknowledge the Enable Notice
docs.text:
A confirmation dialog appears with two notes:

  1. Users with read-only privileges on the Team Folder can only sync files from the server to their devices — changes made locally won't sync back. Privileges are managed in Control Panel → Shared Folder.
  2. Don't mount remote folders or virtual drives inside Team Folders that are already enabled.

Click OK to finish enabling the folder.

docs.title: Step 6: Confirm "office-2" Is Enabled
docs.text:
Back in the Team Folder list, office-2 should now show Enabled, matching office.

Note: If office-2 still doesn't show up as a sync option afterward, check Control Panel → Shared Folder → office-2 → Permissions to confirm your user account has Read/Write access, and Control Panel → User & Group → your account → Applications to confirm Synology Drive isn't blocked for that account.

docs.title: Step 7: Create the Sync Task in Synology Drive Client
docs.text:
On the Windows PC, open Synology Drive Client and create a new sync task:

  • Synology NAS side: /office-2 (or a subfolder of it, if you only want to sync part of it).
  • Your computer side: the local folder to sync, e.g. D:\<YOUR-FOLDER>.
  • Sync direction: Two-way sync (the default) — changes on either side propagate to the other. One-way (download-only or upload-only) is also available under Advanced if you just want a mirror/backup.

Click Done.

docs.title: Step 8: Confirm the Sync Task Is Running
docs.text: The new task appears in Sync Tasks, listed as office-2 (Two-way sync) paired with the local path. A blue circular-arrows icon means the initial sync pass is still running; it changes to a green checkmark once the task catches up and settles into steady-state syncing.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Because this is a two-way sync, deleting a file on either side deletes it on the other. The Team Folder's version history (configured in Step 4) and the shared folder's Recycle Bin (if enabled) are the safety nets for recovering an accidentally deleted or overwritten file.
  • Sync progress and recent transfer logs are available by clicking the sync task, or from the Synology Drive Client icon in the Windows system tray.
  • Sync exclusions (file types, subfolders) and bandwidth limits can be set per task under Sync Rules / Advanced in the task creation dialog.

docs.title: Syncing Google Drive to Synology NAS
Syncing Google Drive to Synology NAS
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Cloud Sync is a Synology package that downloads files from Google Drive to a folder on your NAS automatically. This guide walks you through the full setup.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Cloud Sync
docs.text:
1. Log into DSM.
  2. Open Package Center.
  3. Search for Cloud Sync.
  4. Click Install.

docs.title: Step 2: Open Cloud Sync and Choose Google Drive
docs.text:
1. Launch Cloud Sync from the main menu.
  2. Select Google Drive from the list of cloud providers.
  3. Click Next.

docs.title: Step 3: Authorize Your Google Account
docs.text:
1. On the permissions screen, check the box to grant access to your Google Drive files.
  2. Click Continue.
  3. Sign in to your Google account and allow the requested permissions.

Note: The permission says "see, edit, create, and delete" — this is the standard Google OAuth scope. Cloud Sync will only delete files if you configure it to do so.

docs.title: Step 4: Configure Sync Settings
docs.text:
Set the following options on the configuration screen:

Setting Recommended value Local path A folder on your NAS (e.g., /volume1/GoogleDrive) Remote path / to sync all of Drive, or a specific folder (e.g., /My Folder) Sync direction Download remote changes only

Then enable these two checkboxes:

  • Don't remove files in the destination folder when they are removed in the source folder — prevents accidental deletions on your NAS if you delete something in Drive.
  • Convert Google online documents to Microsoft Office or jpeg formats — downloads Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides as .docx, .xlsx, and .pptx files you can open locally.

Leave Data encryption unchecked unless you need it.

docs.title: Step 5: Start the Sync
docs.text:
Click Next to save your settings. Cloud Sync begins the initial download automatically.

You can monitor progress from the Cloud Sync main window. After the initial sync, any new or updated files in the selected Google Drive folder will download to your NAS automatically.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Sync direction matters. "Download remote changes only" is the safest option. Two-way sync can cause deletions on either side if misconfigured.
  • Sync a subfolder, not all of Drive. If you only need specific content, set the remote path to that folder to avoid downloading everything.
  • Add more tasks later. You can create additional sync tasks for other Google Drive folders from the Cloud Sync main window.

docs.title: Understanding DSM
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) is the operating system built for Synology NAS devices.

It has a browser-based interface, which can make it feel like you are accessing a remote web service — but the OS itself is installed directly on the NAS hardware (the DiskStation).

docs.title: Understanding Personal Space and Folder Structure in Synology Photos
Understanding Personal Space and Folder Structure in Synology Photos
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: The home and homes Folders
docs.text:
In Synology NAS, home and homes are two views of the same data — no files are duplicated.

  • homes folder: The parent folder for all user home directories on the NAS (visible to admins only by default).
  • home folder: A shortcut to the currently logged-in user's personal folder.

When you back up to Personal Space, photos are saved to:

  • Actual path: /homes/<username>/Photos/MobileBackup/...
  • Your shortcut: /home/Photos/MobileBackup/...

Both paths point to the same files.

docs.title: Recommended Settings for a Single-User NAS
docs.text:
If you are running the NAS as a private personal environment:

  1. Enable User Home — this is required.
  2. Set the backup destination in Synology Photos to Personal Space.
  3. Check permissions — if other users are registered on the NAS, confirm they cannot access the homes folder (the default setting) to keep your photos private.

docs.title: Storage Usage
docs.text: If storage usage appears to spike in Storage Manager, this is not caused by duplicate data. It reflects background processing such as index creation, thumbnail generation, and metadata management — all of which run quickly on a DS720+ with WD Red SA500 SSDs.

docs.title: Using Synology NAS as a Claude Workflow Hub
Using Synology NAS as a Claude Workflow Hub
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This guide documents the complete workflow for using Synology NAS as a central file hub between Windows PC (Claude Code) and Google Pixel (Claude mobile app). The setup uses only official tools — no third-party MCP connectors required.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Windows PC (<YOUR-PC>)
└── Claude Code
    └── <YOUR-FOLDER>\          ← local working folder
                │
                │  Synology Drive (Two-way sync)
                ▼
Synology DS720 NAS
└── <NAS-FOLDER>\               ← NAS mirror
                │
                │  Synology Drive app (read/write)
                ▼
Google Pixel
└── Claude app
    └── + button → upload file from Synology Drive app

docs.title: On Windows PC
docs.text:
1. Use Claude Code to create and edit files in your local working folder.
  2. Synology Drive automatically syncs all changes to the NAS in the background.
  3. No manual steps needed — files are always up to date on NAS.

docs.title: On Google Pixel
docs.text:
1. Open the Claude app.
  2. Tap the + button at the bottom of the chat window.
  3. Select the file from the Synology Drive app (e.g. a prompt or MD file created on PC).
  4. Ask Claude to generate a video script, SRT file, or any other output.
  5. Save the output back to NAS via the Synology Drive app if needed.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
Tool Platform Purpose Official Claude Code Windows PC File creation and editing ✅ Anthropic Synology Drive Client Windows PC Auto-sync local folder to NAS ✅ Synology Synology Drive app Google Pixel Access NAS files on mobile ✅ Synology Claude app Google Pixel AI generation using uploaded files ✅ Anthropic

Success

This workflow uses only official tools from Anthropic and Synology. No third-party MCP connectors are required.

docs.title: Why No MCP Connector?
docs.text:
During setup, a community-built MCP server (mcp-server-synology) was considered to allow Claude on Pixel to autonomously access NAS files. It was decided not to use it because:

  • It is not an official tool from Synology or Anthropic.
  • It requires storing NAS credentials in a config file.
  • The simpler alternative — uploading files via the + button in Claude app — achieves the same result safely.

When an official MCP connector becomes available from Synology or Anthropic, this workflow can be upgraded at that point.

docs.title: Sync Configuration

docs.title: Adding a New File Format to the Windows 11 New Menu
Adding a New File Format to the Windows 11 New Menu
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Windows 11's right-click New menu only offers a fixed set of file types out of the box, and there's no built-in UI to add your own (like .md). This guide uses PowerToys' New+ utility to add custom file types.

Note: Requires PowerToys installed (free, from Microsoft Store or GitHub).

docs.title: Step 1: Open PowerToys Settings
docs.text: Launch PowerToys Settings. You land on the Home page.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable New+
docs.text: In the left sidebar, expand File Management and select New+. Turn the New+ toggle on.

docs.title: Step 3: Note the Templates Location
docs.text:
The New+ page shows where your template files live — by default:

C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\PowerToys\NewPlus\Templates

Any file or folder you place here becomes a selectable template in the New+ context menu. You can also toggle display options here, such as hiding file extensions in template names.

docs.title: Step 4: Add a Template File
docs.text: Open the Templates folder and create an empty file with the extension you want — for example, markdown-document.md. Create it directly, or save one from a text editor into that folder.

docs.title: Step 5: Confirm the Template Is Blank
docs.text:
Right-click in a folder → New → your template. If the file it creates isn't empty — it already contains PowerToys' own sample text:

Learn more about New+ by visiting https://aka.ms/PowerToysOverview_NewPlus

...the source template still has that boilerplate baked in, rather than being truly empty. If your file is already blank, skip ahead to Step 10: Use the Template.

The text isn't coming from the folder you're working in — it's baked into the template file itself, in New+'s templates folder. Edit that file once and the boilerplate is gone for good.

docs.title: Step 6: Open the Templates Folder Again
docs.text: You can jump straight back to it via right-click → New+ → Open templates, instead of navigating there manually.

docs.title: Step 7: Find Your Template File
docs.text: Locate the template that matches the one you use from the New menu.

docs.title: Step 8: Clear Its Contents
docs.text: Open the file in a text editor, select all the text, delete it, and save.

docs.title: Step 9: Confirm the File Is Empty
docs.text:
Back in the templates folder, check the file's size — it should now show 0 KB.

Note: If you have more than one New+ template (e.g. one per file type), repeat Steps 7–9 for each one that still contains the default boilerplate.

docs.title: Step 10: Use the Template
docs.text: Right-click in any folder in File Explorer, choose New+, and your template appears in the submenu alongside the example folder. Select it to create a new file with that extension instantly — no typing required, and now genuinely blank.

docs.title: Setting Default View to Extra Large Icons in File Explorer
Setting Default View to Extra Large Icons in File Explorer
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Windows does not offer a single global switch to set Extra large icons for all folders. However, you can configure a folder template so that image folders consistently open with a large icon view.

docs.title: Step 1: Apply the Pictures Template
docs.text:
1. Right-click the folder you want to use for images and select Properties.
  2. Open the Customize tab.
  3. Under Optimize this folder for, select Pictures.
  4. Check Also apply this template to all subfolders.
  5. Click Apply, then OK.

Windows will automatically apply a thumbnail-friendly layout to the folder and its subfolders.

docs.title: Step 2: Save the Icon Size (Optional)
docs.text:
To push the view closer to Extra large icons rather than Large icons:

  1. Open the folder configured in Step 1.
  2. Switch the view to Extra large icons (or press Ctrl+Shift+1).
  3. Click ... → Options.
  4. Open the View tab and click Apply to Folders.
  5. Confirm Yes.

This combines the Pictures template with Explorer's saved view preference and improves the chances that subfolders inherit Extra large icons.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Windows may default to Large icons instead of Extra large icons even after applying these settings. Large icons is a practical compromise as it behaves more reliably.
  • Explorer's folder-view memory can reset after major Windows updates or if its view cache becomes corrupted.
  • Different folder types (Pictures, Documents, Music, General items) store their view settings separately.
  • Network drives and some special folders may ignore these settings entirely.

docs.title: Batch Renaming Photos in XnView MP
Batch Renaming Photos in XnView MP
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

XnView MP's Batch Rename feature lets you rename multiple image files at once using a name template with an auto-incrementing counter. This guide shows how to rename a folder of JPG photos to a sequential series such as photo-series-01.jpg, photo-series-02.jpg, and so on.

docs.title: Step 1: Select Your Files
docs.text:
1. Open XnView MP and navigate to the folder containing your photos.
  2. Press Ctrl+A to select all files, or hold Ctrl and click individual files to select a subset.

Note: The Batch Rename command is only available when at least one file is selected.

docs.title: Step 2: Open Batch Rename
docs.text:
Go to Tools → Batch rename....

The Batch Rename dialog opens and shows a preview table with Old name and New name columns.

docs.title: Step 3: Configure the Name Template
docs.text:
1. Check the Name template checkbox at the top of the dialog.

  2. In the template field, type your base name followed by ## for a two-digit counter:

    photo-series-##

    The ## token is replaced by 01, 02, 03, and so on. Use ### if you need three digits (001, 002, 003).

  3. Set Start to 1 and Step to 1.

docs.title: Step 4: Fix the File Extension Case (Optional)
docs.text:
If your files have uppercase extensions (.JPG) and you want lowercase (.jpg):

  1. Check the Replace checkbox.
  2. Set Replace to JPG and With to jpg.
  3. Check Case sensitive to avoid unintended replacements.

docs.title: Step 5: Preview and Confirm
docs.text:
Check the New name column in the preview table to verify the output looks correct before applying. The files are numbered in the order they are sorted in the browser.

Note: To control the numbering order, close the dialog, sort your files in the desired order in the browser, and then re-open Batch Rename.

docs.title: Step 6: Apply the Rename
docs.text:
Click OK to rename all selected files.

Warning: Renaming cannot be undone from within XnView MP. Back up your files before applying bulk renames.
