docs.title: Adjusting MToon Shading for a Hard Cel-Shaded Look
Adjusting MToon Shading for a Hard Cel-Shaded Look
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A VRM or VRoid model's soft, watercolor-like shading comes from its MToon material settings, not its texture. Adjusting a few Lighting properties can push it toward a harder, anime cel-shaded look before you touch the texture at all.

docs.title: Step 1: Reload the Texture and Preview Shading
docs.text:
After repainting the texture and re-exporting it, reload it in Blender to see the change:

  1. In the Image Editor, with the texture image (for example Image_9) shown, open the Image menu and select Reload (Alt+R).
  2. Switch the 3D viewport's shading mode to Material Preview (Z, then choose Material Preview from the pie menu) to see the model rendered with MToon shading instead of flat Solid shading.

docs.title: Step 2: Adjust the Lighting Settings
docs.text:
In the material's Properties panel, under VRM Material → Lighting:

  • Shading Toony — raise to about 0.9–1.0 for a clean, sharp shadow edge instead of a soft, blurry transition.
  • Shading Shift — moves where the shadow boundary falls. At 1.0, the entire face counts as lit and no shadow appears at all — a useful flat, fully-lit reference point. To bring back anime-style shadows (under the hair, along the jaw, on the neck), lower it gradually toward 0–0.3 until shadow shapes appear.
  • Shade Color — set it to a clearly darker, more saturated tone (for skin, a warm pinkish-orange) rather than plain gray. Gray shadows on skin tend to look dirty rather than anime-like.
  • GI Equalization — raise toward 1.0 for flatter, more even lighting from all directions.

With a flat, repainted texture and Shading Toony, Shading Shift, and GI Equalization all raised to 1.0, the face renders fully lit with no shadow at all — a clean cel look, and a good starting point before dialing shadows back in.

Note: At high Shading Shift values, Blender shows a "The lit area includes non-lit area" warning under Lighting. This is informational, not an error — it's just describing the fully-lit state above.

Note: Repeat this for the hair, clothes, and body materials, not just the face, so the neck and hands match.

docs.title: Applying a Mirror Modifier
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A Mirror modifier duplicates one half of a mesh across an axis, so both halves stay symmetric while you edit only one side — non-destructively until you apply it.

docs.title: Step 1: Identify the Side to Keep
docs.text: Before adding the modifier, decide which half of the mesh to keep — the other half will be replaced by its mirror image.

docs.title: Step 2: Add a Mirror Modifier
docs.text: Select Generate → Mirror.

docs.title: Step 3: Enable Clipping
docs.text: With the modifier added, check Clipping to keep vertices near the center from crossing to the other side, so the seam between the two halves stays welded as you edit.

docs.title: Step 4: Apply the Modifier
docs.text: Click the modifier's dropdown menu, then select Apply to bake the mirrored geometry into the mesh permanently.

docs.title: Applying a Subdivision Surface Modifier
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A Subdivision Surface modifier splits an object's faces into smaller parts, rounding its shape into a smoother surface — non-destructively until you apply it.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Modifier Properties Tab
docs.text: Select the object, click the wrench icon (Modifier Properties), then click Add Modifier.

docs.title: Step 2: Add a Subdivision Surface Modifier
docs.text: Select Generate → Subdivision Surface.

docs.title: Step 3: Review the Default Smoothing
docs.text: With the modifier's default settings, the cube's edges are already noticeably smoother.

docs.title: Step 4: Increase the Subdivision Level
docs.text: Raise Levels Viewport for a smoother result — here, from 1 to 6, turning the cube into a near-perfect sphere.

docs.title: Step 5: Apply the Modifier
docs.text:
Click the modifier's dropdown menu, then select Apply to bake the smoothed shape into the mesh permanently.

The modifier stack is now empty, and the smoothed shape is the object's actual geometry.

Note: A high subdivision level multiplies the mesh's vertex count. Applying it adds all those vertices to the object permanently, which can slow down further edits — consider whether you need it applied, or can leave it non-destructive in the modifier stack instead.

docs.title: Changing the Unit from Meters to Millimeters
Changing the Unit from Meters to Millimeters
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Blender measures scenes in meters by default. For precision work such as product design or 3D printing, switch the scene unit to millimeters.

Note: See this video for a demonstration.

docs.title: Step 1: Open Scene Properties
docs.text: In the Properties editor, click the Scene Properties tab.

docs.title: Step 2: Set the Unit System to Millimeters
docs.text:
Under Units:

  1. Set Unit System to Metric, with Unit Scale at 0.001.
  2. Set Length to Millimeters.

Note: Setting Unit Scale to 0.001 keeps 1 Blender unit equal to 1 millimeter instead of 1 meter, so existing objects keep their size — only the displayed measurements change.

docs.title: Step 3: Match the Viewport Grid Scale
docs.text:
Open Viewport Overlays from the header, then under Guides set Scale to 0.001.

This keeps the viewport grid spacing consistent with the new millimeter unit.

docs.title: Checking Whether Two Shapes Are One Object
Checking Whether Two Shapes Are One Object
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Two shapes can look separate in the viewport while actually being one mesh — a single object with two disconnected "islands" of geometry. In that case, Join won't do anything new, since they're already joined.

docs.title: Check Whether They're Separate
docs.text:
In Object Mode, hover over one shape and press L (or click it).

  • If only that shape highlights, the shapes are separate objects.
  • If both highlight together, they're already part of the same object.

docs.title: Split and Rejoin Properly
docs.text:
If they turn out to be the same object and you want to treat them as separate again:

  1. Press Tab to enter Edit Mode.
  2. Hover over just the piece you want to separate and press L to select its linked vertices and faces only.
  3. Press P → Selection to separate it into its own object.
  4. Back in Object Mode, select the new object, then Shift+click the main shape, then press Ctrl+J to join them (see Joining Multiple Objects).

This gives the two pieces independent origins and transforms again, so operations like Join behave the way you'd expect.

docs.title: Checking an Object's Origin for Mirroring
Checking an Object's Origin for Mirroring
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

For a Mirror modifier to work correctly, the object's origin — and the seam vertices along the cut edge — need to sit exactly on the mirror axis, usually X = 0.

docs.title: Check the Origin's Location Numerically
docs.text: Press N to open the sidebar, then go to the Item tab. With the object selected in Object Mode, check its Location X/Y/Z values. If you're mirroring across X, you want X = 0 — check Y or Z instead if that's your mirror axis.

docs.title: Check the Origin Visually
docs.text: Switch to Front or Top Orthographic view (Numpad 1 / Numpad 7), and enable X-Ray (Alt+Z) if needed. Look at where the object's orange origin dot sits relative to the center gridline running through the world origin.

docs.title: Snap the Origin to World Center
docs.text:
If Location isn't 0 and your model should be centered at world origin:

  1. In Object Mode, press Shift+C (or Shift+S → Cursor to World Origin) to reset the 3D cursor to (0, 0, 0).
  2. Select the object, then Object → Set Origin → Origin to 3D Cursor.

This moves the origin to world center without moving the mesh itself.

Warning: The origin needs to sit on the mirror plane, but that isn't necessarily world origin — it depends on where you want the mirror axis to be. If your model isn't centered at world origin, snapping the origin there would be wrong.

docs.title: Check the Seam Vertices Separately
docs.text: Even with a correct origin, the seam edge itself can be off-axis. In Edit Mode, select the vertices along the cut or seam edge and check their location in the N-panel — they should all match your intended center value exactly, not just be close to it.

docs.title: Checking the Polygon Count
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Show the Statistics Overlay
docs.text: Click the Overlays dropdown (the two overlapping circles icon in the viewport header), then check Statistics. This shows a live text overlay in the top-left of the viewport with Verts, Edges, Faces, Tris, and Objects counts, updating as you select things.

docs.title: Show Scene Statistics in the Status Bar
docs.text:
Right-click the status bar at the bottom of the window and enable Scene Statistics for the same breakdown, always visible for the whole scene.

Note: With modifiers like Mirror or Subdivision Surface applied, the Faces count in Edit Mode reflects the base, unmodified mesh — not the final result. Switch to Object Mode to see the modifier-evaluated count; Blender's Statistics overlay typically shows both the base mesh and evaluated mesh counts when modifiers are active.

docs.title: Cutting a Hole with a Boolean Modifier
Cutting a Hole with a Boolean Modifier
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A Boolean modifier set to Difference cuts one object's shape out of another, non-destructively until you apply it. This follows on from Adding and Naming a Cylinder, Duplicating and Positioning an Object, and Joining Multiple Objects, which prepare the Hole Cutter object used here.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the Object to Cut
docs.text: Select the object the hole will be cut into — here, Bracket.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Modifier Properties Tab
docs.text: In the Properties panel, click the wrench icon (Modifier Properties), then click Add Modifier.

docs.title: Step 3: Add a Boolean Modifier
docs.text: Select Generate → Boolean.

docs.title: Step 4: Set the Operand Object
docs.text: The modifier defaults to Difference, which subtracts the other object's shape. Set its Object field to Hole Cutter — the object that will be subtracted.

docs.title: Step 5: Apply the Modifier
docs.text:
Click the modifier's dropdown menu, then select Apply to bake the cut into the Bracket's mesh.

The three holes now appear where each Hole Cutter cylinder intersected the bracket.

docs.title: Step 6: Delete the Hole Cutter Object
docs.text:
The Hole Cutter object is no longer needed once the modifier is applied.

Right-click it, then select Delete.

docs.title: Duplicating and Positioning an Object
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Duplicating an object in Blender immediately starts moving the copy with your mouse. Confirming that move carelessly can drop the duplicate far from where you wanted it — typing an exact value into Location afterward is the precise way to place it.

docs.title: Step 1: Duplicate the Object
docs.text:
Right-click the object in the viewport, then select Duplicate Objects (or press Shift+D).

Warning: After duplicating, the copy follows your mouse until you confirm the move. Clicking anywhere before positioning it — for example, to check the Outliner — drops the duplicate wherever the mouse happened to be, as shown below: the new Hole Cutter.001 landed hundreds of millimeters from the original.

docs.title: Step 2: Cancel the Move to Keep the Duplicate in Place
docs.text: Duplicate the object again. This time, right-click (or press Esc) immediately after — while the move is still at a zero offset — to cancel it and drop the copy exactly on top of the original instead of following the mouse.

docs.title: Step 3: Position the Duplicate Precisely
docs.text:
In the Properties panel's Transform section (or the viewport sidebar's N-panel), type an exact value into Location — for example, Y = 42 mm — to move the duplicate to a specific spot rather than dragging it by eye.

You can reposition the original object the same way. Here, the original Hole Cutter was moved to Y = -45 mm, giving the bracket three distinct hole positions.

docs.title: Using Number Keys as a Numpad
Using Number Keys as a Numpad
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Laptops often lack a dedicated numpad, which Blender uses for several view shortcuts (like Numpad 7 for Top view). Emulate Numpad lets the number row at the top of the keyboard act as the numpad instead.

docs.title: Enable Emulate Numpad
docs.text:
Go to Edit → Preferences → Input, then check Emulate Numpad under Keyboard.

Note: With this enabled, pressing 1 acts as Numpad 1 (Front view), 7 as Numpad 7 (Top view), and so on — see Switching to Top View.

docs.title: Enabling Auto Navigation Settings
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Blender's Navigation preferences include three Auto options that make orbiting and zooming adapt to what's on screen, instead of always pivoting around the same fixed point.

docs.title: Step 1: Open Navigation Preferences
docs.text: Go to Edit → Preferences, then click Navigation in the sidebar.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable the Auto Settings
docs.text:
Under Orbit & Pan → Auto, check:

  • Orbit Around Selection — orbiting pivots around the selected object instead of the view center.
  • Perspective — automatically switches to Orthographic when you snap to an axis-aligned view (like Top or Front), and back to Perspective otherwise.
  • Depth — scroll-wheel zoom moves toward the point under your cursor instead of always toward the view center.

docs.title: Exporting a UV Layout as an Image
Exporting a UV Layout as an Image
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Export a mesh's UV layout as a flat image, to use as a guide when repainting its texture in another program.

docs.title: Export the UV Layout
docs.text:
1. Go to the UV Editing workspace, with the mesh you want to export selected.
  2. In Edit Mode, press A to select all.
  3. In the UV Editor, select UV → Export UV Layout, and save it as a PNG.

Note: Open the exported PNG as a layer above the texture in an image editor and set its opacity low, so you can see where features like the eyes, mouth, and face edges fall — see Repainting a Texture with Flat Anime Colors.

docs.title: Extruding a Face
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Extrude adds new geometry by pushing a copy of the selected face outward (or inward) along its normal, connecting it to the original with new side faces.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the Face
docs.text: With the Select tool active, switch to Face Select mode and click the face you want to extrude.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose the Extrude Region Tool
docs.text:
Click Extrude Region in the toolbar (or press E).

A gizmo appears on the selected face.

docs.title: Step 3: Set an Exact Distance
docs.text: Type a number to extrude a precise distance along the face's normal, then press Enter (or click) to confirm.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: Once confirmed, the extruded face becomes permanent new geometry — here, the top of the bracket after extruding it 10 mm.

docs.title: Hiding Viewport Overlays
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Vertices, edges, bones, and collider shapes can clutter the viewport when you just want to see how a model actually looks. Each viewport keeps its own overlay settings, so hiding them in one workspace doesn't hide them everywhere.

docs.title: Hide Vertices and Edges
docs.text: Hover over the 3D viewport and press Tab to switch from Edit Mode to Object Mode. The orange vertices and edges disappear.

docs.title: Hide Bones and Colliders
docs.text:
1. In the 3D viewport header, click the small arrow next to the Overlays icon (the two overlapping circles).
  2. Uncheck Bones. Uncheck Extras too if collider circles are still showing.

docs.title: Hide Everything at Once
docs.text:
Click the Overlays icon itself, or press Shift+Alt+Z, to toggle every overlay — bones, vertices, edges, the grid, and everything else — off in one go. Press it again to bring them all back.

Note: The Image Editor panel has its own separate Overlays icon. Faint gray lines still visible there are a UV wireframe display overlay, not part of the actual texture — check whether the model itself looks clean before assuming the texture has a problem. See Reducing the UV Wireframe in the Image Editor for how to hide or dim them.

docs.title: Installing Blender with Automatic Updates
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Blender updates frequently. To avoid manual reinstalls, use one of the following installation methods that support automatic updates.

Method Auto-Update Update Speed Notes Steam Yes Relatively fast Requires a free Steam account Microsoft Store Yes May lag slightly Works immediately with a Microsoft account Blender Launcher Semi-automatic (notified) Fast Best for managing multiple versions Official site No (manual) Fastest Traditional method

Note: If you only need Blender, Microsoft Store is the simplest option — no additional account required. Steam requires a free account but updates automatically. Blender Launcher (GitHub: Victor-IX/blender-launcher-v2) is suited for advanced users who need multiple versions.

docs.title: Installing the MPFB Add-on
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

MPFB (MakeHuman ProceduralFace/Body) is a human character generator and editor add-on for Blender, developed by the MakeHuman Community. It one-click creates a humanoid mesh with parametric body modeling, automatic rigging (including Rigify, with both IK and FK modes), and procedural skin and eye materials.

docs.title: Step 1: Find MPFB on Blender Extensions
docs.text: Go to extensions.blender.org and search for character.

docs.title: Step 2: Get the Add-on
docs.text: Open the MPFB listing, then drag the Get Add-on button from the browser and drop it onto the Blender editor window.

docs.title: Step 3: Enable Online Access
docs.text:
Blender shows an Install Extension dialog reading "Please enable Online Access from the System settings." Click Allow Online Access.

This opens Preferences → System, where Allow Online Access is unchecked by default.

Check Allow Online Access, then close the Preferences window.

docs.title: Step 4: Install the Add-on
docs.text:
Back on the MPFB page, the button now reads Drag and Drop into Blender instead of Get Add-on. Drag it onto the Blender editor window again the same way.

Blender shows a confirmation dialog naming the add-on, its repository, and its size, with Enable Add-on checked. Click OK.

docs.title: Step 5: Confirm the Add-on Is Installed
docs.text:
In the 3D viewport, press N to open the sidebar.

The sidebar opens, showing the Transform panel.

An MPFB tab appears among the sidebar's vertical tabs, confirming the add-on installed successfully.

docs.title: Joining Multiple Objects
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Note: See this video for a demonstration.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the Objects
docs.text: Click one object, then hold Shift and click each additional object to add it to the selection. The last object you click becomes the active object, shown with a lighter outline.

docs.title: Step 2: Join Them
docs.text: Right-click in the viewport, then select Join (or press Ctrl+J).

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm the Result
docs.text: The selected objects merge into a single object, keeping the active object's name. Here, three separate Hole Cutter cylinders became one Hole Cutter object, now spanning all three positions.

docs.title: Lifting the Outer Corners of the Eyes
Lifting the Outer Corners of the Eyes
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Slightly raising the outer corners of the eyes makes a face look sharper and stronger. In Edit Mode, Proportional Editing moves the selected vertex together with a soft-falloff area around it, so the change blends into the surrounding mesh instead of leaving a sharp point.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the Basis Shape Key
docs.text: Open the Object Data tab (green triangle) → Shape Keys, and select Basis. This makes your edits go into the base shape rather than into a blink or expression shape key.

docs.title: Step 2: Enter Edit Mode Close to the Eyes
docs.text:
Switch to the Layout workspace, press Tab to enter Edit Mode, then press Numpad 1 for Front Orthographic view (see Using Number Keys as a Numpad if you have no numpad) and zoom in on the eyes.

Optionally, press Z and choose Material Preview to judge the result with the model's real shading.

docs.title: Step 3: Turn On Mirror Editing
docs.text: In the viewport header, enable the X mirror toggle. Then open Options and check Topology Mirror, so the other eye moves symmetrically when both sides of the mesh have matching topology.

docs.title: Step 4: Turn On Proportional Editing
docs.text: Click the Proportional Editing icon in the header, or press O.

docs.title: Step 5: Select the Outer Corner Vertex
docs.text: Click the vertex at the outer corner of the eye. With mirror editing on, the opposite eye follows.

docs.title: Step 6: Move the Vertex Up
docs.text:
Press G, then Z, move up a little, and click to confirm.

Warning: Proportional Size defaults to 1 m. A head is only about 20 cm wide, so the influence circle covers the whole face and everything moves. Before you move much, change the size while watching the value in the header: scroll the mouse wheel, or press Page Up / Page Down. Bring it down to about 0.015 m — you should then see a small circle around the eye corner. If the number goes the wrong way, use the other direction.

Page Up / Page Down are the easier option, because scrolling the wheel can shift the face before you've started dragging.

docs.title: Fine-Tune the Result
docs.text:
Type a distance instead of dragging. Select the vertex, press G, Z, type 0.003, and press Enter. The vertex moves exactly 3 mm up, with no accidental movement from the mouse or pen.

Use the Move panel. After a move, open the small > Move panel at the bottom-left of the viewport and edit the values there, seeing the result instantly:

  • Proportional Size — try 0.01–0.02.
  • Move Z — the lift amount. Try small values like 0.002–0.005 m.

To open the panel without moving anything, press G, then Enter. Blender remembers the proportional size, so the next move starts at your last value instead of 1 m.

docs.title: Check the Result and Save
docs.text:
1. Press Numpad 1 and zoom out to judge the overall face. A glance from a slight angle helps too.

  2. Press Tab to return to Object Mode and open Object Data → Shape Keys.

  3. Select a blink key (such as Fcl_EYE_Close_L) and drag its Value slider up, first partway and then to 1.0, along with a couple of expressions. Make sure the eyelids still close cleanly, then set every value back to 0.

  4. Save with Ctrl+S, or save a new version of the file so you can compare with the original.

docs.title: Alternative: Sculpt Mode
docs.text: Sculpt Mode can feel more natural than Edit Mode with a pen tablet — see Using a Pen Tablet in Blender. Switch to Sculpt Mode, choose the Grab brush, set a small radius, turn on X symmetry, and drag the outer corner upward like pushing clay. It works on the Basis shape key the same way, so save a copy first and check the blink shape keys afterward.

docs.title: Measuring a Distance with MeasureIt
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

MeasureIt is a free Blender add-on that displays distance, angle, and area measurements directly in the viewport.

docs.title: Step 1: Open Preferences
docs.text: Go to Edit → Preferences.

docs.title: Step 2: Search for MeasureIt
docs.text: In Preferences, click Get Extensions, then search for measureit.

docs.title: Step 3: Install and Enable It
docs.text:
Click Install.

Click the Add-ons tab to confirm it's enabled.

docs.title: Step 4: Save Preferences
docs.text: Open the menu in the lower-left corner, then click Save Preferences so MeasureIt stays enabled the next time you open Blender.

docs.title: Step 5: Open MeasureIt Tools
docs.text: In Edit Mode, open the viewport sidebar's View tab (press N if it's closed), then expand MeasureIt Tools.

docs.title: Step 6: Measure Between Two Vertices
docs.text: Select 2 vertices, then click Segment.

docs.title: Step 7: Show the Measurement
docs.text: Click Show to display the measurement in the viewport.

docs.title: Step 8: Change the Measurement Unit
docs.text: Under Units, choose Millimeters (or another unit) for a more readable value at this scale.

docs.title: Orbiting and Panning the View
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Note: See this video for a demonstration.

Use the middle mouse button to move around the 3D viewport without moving any objects.

docs.title: Orbit the View
docs.text: Hold the middle mouse button and drag.

docs.title: Pan the View
docs.text: Hold Shift and the middle mouse button, then drag.

docs.title: Use the Navigation Gizmo Instead
docs.text:
The viewport also has an on-screen gizmo for orbiting and panning without a middle mouse button.

  1. Click the Show Gizmo icon in the header (or press Ctrl+`) to show or hide it.

  2. The gizmo appears in the top-right corner of the viewport: drag the colored axis ball to orbit the view, and use the icons below it to zoom, pan, and toggle between perspective and orthographic.

  3. Click and drag the hand icon to pan the view — the same result as Shift + middle mouse button drag.

docs.title: Painting Flat Anime Skin with a Stencil Mask
Painting Flat Anime Skin with a Stencil Mask
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This replaces soft, watercolor-style shading on a face texture with a single flat skin color, while keeping the eye, eyelid, nose, and mouth lines. The method uses Texture Paint with a stencil mask — a separate black-and-white image that protects the lines while you paint over everything else.

Note: Three rules matter most:

  1. Do all mask painting and color painting in the 3D Viewport. The stencil has no effect in the 2D Image Editor.
  2. The Mask brush needs Mask Value = 0, so it paints black onto the white stencil.
  3. In this Blender version, a black-on-white mask only protects the lines when Invert is ticked in the Masking popover.

docs.title: Step 1: Back Up the Original Texture
docs.text: Before painting anything, keep an untouched copy of the face texture — for example, Image_9_original.png. Painted textures aren't saved with the .blend file, and changes can't be undone once saved.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable the Stencil Mask
docs.text:
1. Select the Face object and switch to Texture Paint mode.
  2. Pick the Mask tool in the toolbar (Shift+Space → 6).
  3. In the 3D Viewport header, open the Masking popover — the small dropdown right of the Image_9 texture-slot dropdown.
  4. Tick Stencil Mask.

docs.title: Step 3: Create the Stencil Image
docs.text:
1. Expand Stencil Mask with the small arrow and click New.

  2. Find the face texture's size first: in the left Image Editor, press N → Image tab.

  3. In the Create a New Image dialog, use:

    Field Value Name FaceStencil Width / Height Same as the face texture (512 × 512) Generated Type Blank Color White (#FFFFFF) Alpha Off

  4. Click New Image.

  5. Set UV Layer to the face's UV map.

docs.title: Step 4: Isolate the Face with Local View
docs.text:
This hides the hair and body so you can paint on a clean face.

  1. Click Face in the Outliner.

  2. In the 3D Viewport: View → Local View → Toggle Local View (Numpad /).

  3. Press Numpad 1 for the front orthographic view.

docs.title: Step 5: Set Up the Mask Brush
docs.text:
With the Mask tool active, check these in the right-hand Tool properties:

Setting Value Why Strength 1.0 At 0.5 the lines are only half protected. Advanced → Mask Value 0 At 1 the brush paints white onto a white stencil, so nothing happens. Falloff Constant A soft falloff leaves grey edges, which give only partial protection. Falloff → Normal Falloff Off Otherwise angled surfaces like the sides of the nose get weaker strokes. Size About 5–15 px for the lines The texture is only 512 px, so the lines are thin. Zoom in for control.

Warning: Brush settings can reset after reopening Blender or switching brushes. Check them again before each session.

docs.title: Step 6: Make the Mask Visible in the 3D View
docs.text:
1. Switch the viewport to Solid shading — the second sphere. Material Preview (MToon) doesn't draw the stencil overlay.
  2. Open the Texture Paint Overlays popover, the small dropdown right of the general Overlays dropdown, and set Stencil Mask Opacity to about 0.45.
  3. Optionally, set Display Color in the Masking popover to something vivid (blue or green) for better contrast.

You can also keep FaceStencil open in the left Image Editor. It shows exactly what's masked: black means masked.

docs.title: Step 7: Paint Only on the Skin
docs.text:
The grey, semi-transparent flaps around the eyes are separate parts of the Face mesh that hold the eyebrows and eyeliner. They aren't on the skin area of the texture, so they don't need masking — but they can get in the way.

  1. In Options, untick Occlude so strokes reach the skin under the flaps.

  2. Turn on Paint Mask, the square icon right after the Texture Paint mode dropdown.

  3. Press Alt+A to deselect all. Then hover over the skin and press L to select only the skin. With Paint Mask on, only selected faces receive paint.

docs.title: Step 8: Mask the Lines
docs.text:
With the Mask tool in the 3D view, paint over every line you want to keep: eye outlines, eyelid creases, the nose line, and the mouth. Zoom in, and change the brush size with F.

To erase a mistake, set Mask Value to 1 temporarily, paint over it, and then set it back to 0.

docs.title: Step 9: Turn On Invert
docs.text:
In the Masking popover, click the Invert button next to Display Color.

Note: Without Invert, Blender protects the white area and paints over the black lines. With Invert on, the black strokes are protected and everything else is paintable.

Test first: paint one stroke across the mouth with a bright color. If the mouth line stays clean, it's working. Undo the test with Ctrl+Z.

docs.title: Step 10: Paint the Flat Skin Color
docs.text:
1. Switch to the Paint Hard brush, with Blend Mix, Strength 1.0, Falloff Constant, and Normal Falloff off.

  2. Pick the skin color. Show your face texture in the left editor, click the color swatch, use the eyedropper, and click a clean skin area such as the forehead or cheek. Don't sample from the 3D view, since the overlay tints it.

  3. Use a large size (80–150 px or more) and paint over the whole face in the 3D view only. Rotate to cover the sides, jaw, and under the chin.

  4. Switch to Material Preview — the third sphere — to check the real result.

docs.title: Step 11: Save the Images
docs.text:
1. With your face texture in the left editor: Image → Save As…, and save under a new name.

  2. Switch the left editor to FaceStencil and save it too. It's a generated image, and it may come back blank when you reopen the file if it isn't saved.

Warning: Save As changes which file Blender uses. After Save As, the image datablock still shows its old name in Blender, but it now points to the new file on disk — the name in Blender is only a label, not the original filename.

docs.title: Step 12: Return to Normal View and Save
docs.text:
1. View → Local View → Toggle Local View (Numpad /) brings back the hair, ears, and body.
  2. Turn off Paint Mask.
  3. Switch the mode dropdown to Object Mode.
  4. Save the .blend with Ctrl+S.

Note: Other parts of the model, such as the ears or neck, may use their own separate textures and keep the original shading. The same method works there if needed — remember to tick Invert from the start.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The Mask brush paints nothing. Mask Value was probably 1.0, so it painted white onto the white stencil — set Advanced → Mask Value to 0. Also check that Stencil Image actually shows your stencil (FaceStencil); after some undos it can go empty, and you'll need to re-select it from the image dropdown.

  • Strokes show in the stencil image but not on the 3D model. The overlay isn't drawn in Material Preview. Switch to Solid shading. If the face turns completely black, lower Stencil Mask Opacity to about 0.45 (Step 6).

  • The lines got painted over anyway. Invert was probably off — tick Invert in the Masking popover (Step 9). Also make sure you paint in the 3D view, not the 2D Image Editor, and don't use the Smear tool on the texture.

  • The saved file looks different from what Blender shows. After Save As, Blender's image datablock points to the new file, so the original filename on disk is unchanged and no longer used. To load a different file into the same image slot instead, use Image → Replace….

  • Finding the settings. Texture Slots and Masking are popovers in the 3D Viewport header, not in the Tool tab. Stencil Mask Opacity is in its own Texture Paint Overlays popover, just right of the general Overlays dropdown. The shading spheres, from left to right, are Wireframe, Solid, Material Preview, and Rendered. The Paint Mask toggle sits right after the Texture Paint mode dropdown.

docs.title: File Reference
docs.text:
Files produced by this method, all kept alongside the .blend project:

File What It Is Flat-skin texture (for example, image_9_soild.png) The final flat-skin face texture, now used by the model FaceStencil.png The line mask (black = lines). Reusable for other textures. Original texture (for example, Image_9.png) The texture as Blender's image datablock still names it — no longer the file actually in use, once you've saved a new one over it Backup copy (for example, Image_9_original.png) Untouched backup of the original texture, made in Step 1

docs.title: Reducing the Polygon Count
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Several approaches convert a high-poly model into a low-poly one, depending on how much control you need over the result.

docs.title: Method 1: Decimate Modifier
docs.text:
The fastest, fully automated option. Click the wrench icon (Modifier Properties), then Add Modifier → Generate → Decimate. It has three modes:

Mode Best For Collapse Reduces the poly count by a ratio (for example, 0.5 = 50% fewer faces). Works uniformly across the whole mesh. Un-Subdivide Reverses even, regular subdivision cleanly. Planar Merges nearly flat, coplanar faces — good for hard-surface objects, less useful for organic shapes.

Warning: Decimate doesn't respect edge loops, so UVs, rig deformation, and topology flow can degrade — especially around areas like eyes and mouth that need clean loops for expressions.

docs.title: Method 2: Remesh Modifier
docs.text: Add Modifier → Generate → Remesh, using Voxel mode, rebuilds the mesh at a target resolution. This is good for simplifying dense sculpts, but it replaces the existing topology and UVs entirely with a uniform grid.

docs.title: Method 3: Manual Retopology
docs.text:
Manually draw new, clean low-poly topology over the high-poly model, using tools like Poly Build, a Shrinkwrap modifier, or add-ons like RetopoFlow. This is the standard for game-ready or animation-ready characters, since it preserves proper edge loops for deformation — but it takes much more time than the other methods.

Note: If the model already has a Subdivision Surface modifier, its lower-resolution base mesh may already serve as a low-poly cage — check the modifier stack before decimating. If you do need to reduce the base mesh and plan to animate facial expressions, enable Symmetry in Decimate to respect an existing Mirror modifier, rather than decimating blindly.

docs.title: Reducing the UV Wireframe in the Image Editor
Reducing the UV Wireframe in the Image Editor
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

In Texture Paint mode, a dense mesh fills the Image Editor with lines. These are the UV wireframe overlay, drawn on top of the image — they aren't painted into the texture. Methods 1 and 2 only change what's drawn, and Method 3 also limits where you can paint. Switch the overlay back on whenever you need to check where something maps on the texture.

docs.title: Method 1: Hide the Overlays Completely
docs.text: In the left Image Editor header, click the Overlays toggle (the two overlapping circles), or hover over the Image Editor and press Shift+Alt+Z. All overlays, including the UV lines, disappear.

docs.title: Method 2: Dim the Wireframe Instead
docs.text:
1. Click the small arrow next to the Overlays icon.

  2. Under Geometry, lower the Edges value. It defaults to 1.000; a value like 0.190 leaves a faint guide. You can also uncheck the Geometry checkbox to hide the UV lines while keeping the other overlays.

docs.title: Method 3: Show Only the Wires of One Area
docs.text:
A face mesh has many polygons, so every UV edge adds a line. To see only the wires that belong to one part, such as the face skin, use your Edit Mode selection together with Paint Mask (face selection masking). The mask also limits painting to those faces, so you won't accidentally paint the eyes or mouth.

  1. Switch the 3D viewport to Edit Mode.

  2. Select only the face-skin faces. Hover over the skin and press L to select a whole connected part. The Image Editor now shows just those wires.

  3. Switch back to Texture Paint mode. The Image Editor shows every wire again until you turn on the mask.

  4. In the 3D viewport header, click the Paint Mask icon (the small square with a face on it, next to the mode dropdown). The Image Editor now shows only the wires of the selected faces, and the unselected areas are dimmed in the viewport.

To paint elsewhere later, turn the mask off or change the selection in Edit Mode.

docs.title: Method 4: Hide Everything Else
docs.text:
In Edit Mode, invert the selection with Ctrl+I, then press H to hide everything else. Hidden faces are also hidden in Texture Paint, so both the 3D view and the UV overlay show only the face. Press Alt+H in Edit Mode to bring everything back.

Note: The 3D viewport has its own separate overlays, for bones, vertices, and edges — see Hiding Viewport Overlays.

docs.title: Rendering a Slideshow
docs.text:
1. Open Video Editing.

  2. Select the scene.

    Tip

    Select the same scene in both the timeline and the Properties panel.

  3. Open Format.

  4. Select 1920 × 1080.

    Note

    1920 × 1080 means Full HD.

  5. Select 30 fps for the slideshow.

  6. Set the frame range by selecting the start frame and end frame.

  7. Select the output folder.

  8. Select Video, then choose the color mode.

    Note

    BW means black and white.

  9. Select MPEG-4.

  10. Select H.264.

    Note

    H.264 produces an MP4 video.

  11. Select Render Animation.

  12. The MP4 video is generated.

docs.title: Resizing an Object Using Dimensions
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Blender lets you set an object's exact size by typing values directly into the Dimensions fields, instead of dragging or typing a scale factor.

Note: See this video for a demonstration.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Dimensions Panel
docs.text: Press N to open the viewport sidebar's Transform panel, then locate Dimensions.

docs.title: Step 2: Change the Dimensions
docs.text:
Type new values into the Dimensions fields for X, Y, and Z.

Note: Changing dimensions unevenly (not by the same ratio on every axis) gives the object a non-uniform Scale, shown in the status bar as "Active object has non-uniform scale." Some tools and modifiers behave unexpectedly with non-uniform scale — apply the scale (Object → Apply → Scale) if this causes issues.

docs.title: Sculpting with Clay Strips, Smooth, and Grab
Sculpting with Clay Strips, Smooth, and Grab
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Sculpt Mode reshapes a mesh by pushing and pulling its surface with brushes, similar to digital clay. A dense mesh — such as a sphere with a high Subdivision Surface level applied — gives brushes enough detail to work with.

docs.title: Step 1: Switch to the Sculpting Workspace
docs.text: Click the Sculpting tab at the top of the window.

docs.title: Clay Strips: Build Up Volume
docs.text:
Select Clay Strips from the brush shelf at the bottom of the viewport — a more aggressive version of the Clay brush, useful for building up rough volumes.

Adjust Size in the Brush Settings panel to control how wide each stroke is.

Drag across the surface to add raised material.

docs.title: Smooth: Reduce Irregularities
docs.text:
Select Smooth to average nearby vertices' positions, smoothing out rough or jagged areas.

Drag over the area you want to soften.

Increase Size for a broader smoothing effect.

docs.title: Grab: Reposition Volume
docs.text:
Select Grab to move a whole area of vertices with the mouse, useful for adjusting overall shapes and proportions.

Drag to pull the surface into a new shape.

docs.title: Sculpting with a Mask
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A Mask protects part of the mesh from other sculpt brushes, so you can edit one area — like the eyes and mouth of this face — without disturbing the rest.

docs.title: Step 1: Paint a Mask
docs.text:
Select Mask from the brush shelf (or press 3).

Drag over the areas you want to protect.

docs.title: Step 2: Invert the Mask
docs.text: Press Ctrl+I to invert the mask, so the areas you just painted become editable and everything else becomes protected instead.

docs.title: Step 3: Sculpt Within the Unmasked Area
docs.text:
Select Clay Strips again.

Hold Ctrl while dragging to carve inward instead of building up material. The mask keeps the surrounding face untouched.

docs.title: Step 4: Remesh for Clean Topology
docs.text: Open the Remesh panel and set Voxel Size, then click Remesh to rebuild the mesh with clean, evenly distributed geometry.

docs.title: Step 5: Smooth the Result
docs.text: Select Smooth, increase its Size, then drag over any remaining rough areas.

docs.title: Selecting All Objects
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Select everything in the scene at once, rather than clicking each object individually.

docs.title: Select All
docs.text:
With the cursor over the viewport, press A.

Note: To deselect everything instead, press Alt+A.

docs.title: Selecting Vertices, Edges, and Faces
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Blender's Edit Mode lets you select an object's individual vertices, edges, or faces to modify its mesh directly, instead of moving the whole object.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the Object
docs.text: In Object Mode, select the object you want to edit.

docs.title: Step 2: Enter Edit Mode
docs.text:
Click the mode dropdown in the header (or press Tab), then select Edit Mode.

Edit Mode opens in Vertex Select by default, with the mesh's vertices, edges, and faces all selected.

docs.title: Step 3: Switch Select Modes
docs.text:
Use the three icons next to the mode dropdown (or press 1, 2, or 3) to switch between selecting vertices, edges, or faces.

Edge Select — selects a line between two vertices.

Face Select — selects a flat surface, shown with a dot at its center.

docs.title: Step 4: Select Multiple Elements at Once
docs.text: Drag a selection box over several elements to select them all together, instead of clicking each one individually.

docs.title: Switching to Top View
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Clicking an axis on the navigation gizmo snaps the viewport to a straight-on orthographic view from that direction, instead of the free-rotating perspective view.

docs.title: Click the Z Axis on the Navigation Gizmo
docs.text:
Click the blue Z dot at the top of the gizmo in the viewport's top-right corner (or press Numpad 7).

The view switches to Top Orthographic, looking straight down the Z axis.

Note: The gizmo's other dots work the same way — for example, Numpad 1 for Front and Numpad 3 for Right.

docs.title: Using a Pen Tablet in Blender
Using a Pen Tablet in Blender
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Blender works well with pen tablets. The pen tip acts as a left click, and these tips cover the rest of what a mouse normally does.

docs.title: Move Things with the Gizmo
docs.text: Click the Move tool in the left toolbar (the cross-shaped arrows icon). Arrows appear on your selection, and you can drag an arrow with the pen — for example, the blue (Z) arrow to move straight up. Nothing moves until you drag, and you can fine-tune afterward in the Move panel at the bottom-left of the viewport.

docs.title: Navigate Without a Mouse
docs.text: At the top-right of the viewport, drag the colored axis ball to orbit, the hand icon to pan, and the magnifier to zoom. See Orbiting and Panning the View.

docs.title: Orbit with Alt
docs.text: Go to Edit → Preferences → Input and turn on Emulate 3 Button Mouse. Then Alt + pen drag orbits the view.

docs.title: Map the Pen's Side Buttons
docs.text: Your tablet driver can map the pen's side buttons to middle click (orbit) or right click.

docs.title: Try Sculpt Mode for Shaping
docs.text: For organic reshaping, Sculpt Mode can feel more natural with a pen than Edit Mode. Switch from Edit Mode to Sculpt Mode using the top-left dropdown, choose the Grab brush, set a small radius in the header, and turn on X symmetry (the butterfly icon). Then drag as if pushing clay — see Sculpting with Clay Strips, Smooth, and Grab.

docs.title: Using the Scale Tool
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Scale tool resizes the current selection — a whole object in Object Mode, or selected vertices, edges, or faces in Edit Mode — by dragging an on-screen gizmo, instead of typing exact numbers.

docs.title: Step 1: Select What to Scale
docs.text: Select the object, or the vertices, edges, or faces you want to resize.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose the Scale Tool
docs.text:
Click the Scale tool in the toolbar (or press S).

Drag the gizmo's outer circle to scale evenly in all directions, or drag one of its colored axis handles to scale along just that axis.

docs.title: Step 3: Scale Evenly in All Directions
docs.text:
Grab the small white square on the gizmo's outer circle, then drag it.

The object scales up or down evenly on all axes at once, rather than stretching along a single direction.

docs.title: Using X-Ray Mode
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

X-Ray mode makes the mesh semi-transparent, so you can see and select vertices, edges, or faces on the far side of the object — geometry that would otherwise be hidden behind the near side.

docs.title: Toggle X-Ray Mode
docs.text:
Click the Toggle X-Ray icon in the header (or press Alt+Z).

Before — with X-Ray off, only the near side of the hole's geometry is visible and selectable.

After — with X-Ray on, the mesh becomes semi-transparent, revealing and allowing selection of the far side of the hole too.

Note: X-Ray mode also works in Object Mode, where it lets you box-select through overlapping objects instead of only the ones on top.

docs.title: Zooming In on the Face in Texture Paint Mode
Zooming In on the Face in Texture Paint Mode
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

In Texture Paint mode, the View menu is trimmed down and has no Frame Selected option, so a small character can be hard to zoom in on. Several navigation shortcuts still work — hover the mouse over the 3D viewport before using any of them.

docs.title: Method 1: Zoom Region
docs.text: The fastest option. Press Shift+B, then drag a box around the character's head. The view zooms straight into that rectangle. You can also find it under View → Navigation → Zoom Region.

docs.title: Method 2: Center on the Face, Then Scroll
docs.text:
1. Press Alt and middle-click on the face. The view orbits around and centers on that point.
  2. Scroll the mouse wheel to zoom in, or drag with Ctrl and the middle mouse button.

docs.title: Zoom Toward the Mouse (Optional)
docs.text:
To make scrolling zoom toward wherever the cursor is — helpful for painting — turn on Zoom to Mouse Position:

  1. Go to Edit → Preferences.

  2. Click Navigation, then check Zoom to Mouse Position under Zoom.

Now you can point at the face and scroll.

docs.title: Method 3: Frame Selected from Another Mode
docs.text:
1. Switch to Edit Mode (Tab, or the mode dropdown in the viewport header).

  2. Select a few vertices on the face, then press Numpad . (View Selected). If your keyboard has no numpad, see Using Number Keys as a Numpad.

  3. Switch back to Texture Paint mode. The view stays where you put it.

docs.title: Building an Image-to-Image Workflow for Anima
Building an Image-to-Image Workflow for Anima
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Text-to-image starts from a blank Empty Latent Image (pure noise). Image-to-image starts from your own reference image instead. This adds a Load Image → Upscale Image → VAE Encode chain inside the Anima template, feeding the reference into the KSampler in place of the empty latent. The KSampler's denoise value then decides how much of the reference gets repainted.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Subgraph
docs.text: The Text to Image (Anima) node is a subgraph — a node with a small workflow inside it. Click the small icon at the top-right corner of the node (tooltip: "Subgraph node for Text to Image (Anima)") to open it.

docs.title: Step 2: Add a Load Image Node
docs.text: Double-click an empty part of the canvas to open the node search, then click Load Image in the list (or press Enter). The panel on the right is only a preview until you click.

docs.title: Step 3: Load Your Reference Image
docs.text:
Drop the file directly onto the Load Image node, or click choose file to upload. Dropping it onto empty canvas may load it as a workflow instead.

Note: Crop the reference first. A first attempt here used a full screenshot with the source app's interface still around the character — the model copies whatever is in the picture, interface included.

docs.title: Step 4: Add Upscale Image and Set the Size
docs.text: Search Upscale Image and add it. Connect Load Image's IMAGE output to Upscale Image's image input, then set width and height to 1024 (it defaults to 512).

docs.title: Step 5: Add VAE Encode and Connect It
docs.text:
Search VAE Encode — the plain one, not VAE Encode (for Inpainting).

Connect:

  • Upscale Image's IMAGE → VAE Encode's pixels
  • Load VAE's VAE (in the Model group) → VAE Encode's vae

docs.title: Step 6: Feed the Encoded Image into the KSampler
docs.text: Drag VAE Encode's LATENT output to the KSampler's latent_image input. This replaces the link from Empty Latent Image, which can stay where it is, unused. From here on, the subgraph's width/height fields have no effect.

docs.title: Step 7: Lower Denoise to 0.60
docs.text: At 1.00, the reference is ignored completely. 0.60 is a good starting point.

docs.title: Step 8: Fine-Tune Upscale Image
docs.text:
• crop → center. The reference isn't square, so disabled would squash it into 1024 × 1024 and stretch the face. center trims the sides instead.
  • upscale_method → lanczos. nearest-exact gives a blocky enlargement that the model may copy.

docs.title: Step 9: Run It
docs.text: Run works from inside the subgraph too. A message appears near the Run button once the job finishes.

docs.title: Step 10: Return to the Main View and Check the Result
docs.text:
The path at the top — for example, image_anima_base_v1 / Text to Image (Anima) — is the breadcrumb. Click the first part to leave the subgraph. This is not the same as the tab at the very top of the window, which is the open workflow file.

Note: The prompt still influences details even at a moderate denoise. In this test, the prompt still described the reference's original character — "amber eyes" — and the result kept the reference's pose, hair shape, and dark top, but the eyes came out amber rather than matching the reference's blue eyes. At denoise 0.60, the reference controls layout and color while the prompt still wins on fine details. Update the prompt to match your reference for a closer result.

docs.title: Choosing a Denoise Value
docs.text:
Denoise What Happens 0.30 – 0.50 Stays close to the reference; mostly changes style and fine detail. 0.55 – 0.70 Keeps pose, layout, and colors but redraws a lot. Usually the sweet spot. 0.80+ Only loosely follows the reference. 1.00 Ignores the reference — the same as text-to-image.

If the result looks too much like the reference image, raise denoise. If the face or pose drifts, lower it.

docs.title: Backing Up a Prompt
docs.text:
Every PNG that ComfyUI saves also stores the full workflow inside it, including the prompt, seed, and settings. Drag an output PNG onto the canvas to restore everything that made it. You can also keep prompts in a Note or Markdown Note node, or save separate workflows — see Saving and Finding ComfyUI Workflows.

Warning: Image-to-image copies a picture, not a character. Keeping the same character consistent across new poses and scenes needs other methods, such as IPAdapter or ControlNet.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Image to Image Workflow — official docs.
  • Anima Base v1 ComfyUI Workflow Example — official docs.
  • image_anima_base_v1.json — the template's source file.

docs.title: Enlarging the Prompt Text in ComfyUI
Enlarging the Prompt Text in ComfyUI
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The prompt text inside a node's textarea is small by default. These are three ways to make it more readable, from quickest to most persistent.

docs.title: Method 1: Edit in the Parameters Panel
docs.text: Select the node. Its prompt appears in the right-hand Parameters panel at a normal, readable size, and you can edit it there directly — no settings change needed.

docs.title: Method 2: Raise the Textarea Widget Font Size
docs.text:
This changes the font size in every text node's textarea, not just one.

  1. Click Settings (gear icon, bottom-left).

  2. Click Appearance, then find Node Widget → Textarea widget font size. It defaults to 10.

  3. Raise the value — for example, to 20.

You can also type "font size" into the settings search box to jump straight to it. The search also surfaces a related Lite Graph → Canvas → Zoom Node Level of Detail - font size threshold setting, which controls how far you can zoom out before node text stops rendering in detail.

Note: A GitHub issue reports that this setting has no effect when "Nodes 2.0" is enabled. If raising the value doesn't change anything, check whether Nodes 2.0 is turned on.

docs.title: Method 3: Zoom the Canvas
docs.text:
The prompt text scales with the graph's zoom level, so zooming in on the node makes it more readable without changing any setting.

Note: Ctrl++ / Ctrl+- should zoom the entire ComfyUI Desktop window, similar to a browser. This comes from the app's Electron base, not from a ComfyUI setting.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: • Customizing ComfyUI Appearance — official docs, covers the font size setting and a custom user.css for further control.

docs.title: Installing ComfyUI with the Desktop Installer
Installing ComfyUI with the Desktop Installer
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The official ComfyUI desktop installer is available from the official site. Follow the on-screen instructions to complete the installation.

https://www.comfy.org/

Note: If the installer fails with an error, check whether your NVIDIA GPU driver is up to date. Install the NVIDIA App to manage driver updates: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/software/nvidia-app/

docs.title: Running Anima Locally with ComfyUI
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Anima is a text-to-image model with a ready-made workflow template bundled in ComfyUI Desktop, so no manual node setup is needed.

docs.title: Step 1: Open Your ComfyUI Instance
docs.text: From the ComfyUI Desktop launcher, open your local ComfyUI instance (not Comfy Cloud).

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Anima Template
docs.text:
Open the Text to Image (Anima) template. It loads as a small graph with a text prompt node connected to a Text to Image (Anima) node and a Save Image node.

Note: The Markdown Note node on the template lists where its models are stored and links to download them if they're missing.

docs.title: Step 3: Enter a Prompt and Run
docs.text: Type your prompt into the text box, then click Run.

docs.title: Step 4: View the Result
docs.text:
The generated image appears in the Save Image node once the job finishes.

Note: The prompt box in the node is small and hard to read. See Enlarging the Prompt Text in ComfyUI for ways to fix that.

docs.title: Running FLUX Locally with ComfyUI
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Run FLUX by Black Forest Labs locally using ComfyUI on Windows.

docs.title: GPU requirements
docs.text:
Tier GPU VRAM Minimum RTX 3060 12 GB Recommended RTX 4070 Ti / 4080 / 4090 16 GB+

NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support is required.

docs.title: Check your GPU
docs.text:
Open Task Manager → Performance → GPU, or run:

Win + R → dxdiag

In the DirectX Diagnostic Tool, click the Display 1 tab to see your Chip Type and Display Memory (VRAM).

docs.title: Download the portable version
docs.text:
1. Go to the ComfyUI GitHub releases page.
  2. Download ComfyUI_windows_portable.
  3. Extract it to a simple path, e.g.:
C:\AI\ComfyUI

docs.title: Launch ComfyUI
docs.text:
Double-click run_nvidia_gpu.bat.

ComfyUI will open in your browser at:

http://127.0.0.1:8188

If the UI loads — you are ready to continue.

docs.title: Step 2: Download the FLUX Model
docs.text:
1. Go to Hugging Face and download one of:

    • FLUX.1-dev — most popular, higher quality
    • FLUX.1-schnell — lighter and faster

  2. Place the .safetensors file in:

ComfyUI\models\checkpoints\

docs.title: Step 3: Install Required Nodes
docs.text:
FLUX is not standard Stable Diffusion and requires additional custom nodes.

  1. Open ComfyUI Manager.
  2. Click Install Custom Nodes.

  3. Search for and install:

    • Flux nodes
    • T5 loader
    • Updated sampler nodes (if prompted)

  4. Restart ComfyUI after installing.

docs.title: Step 4: Set Up the FLUX Workflow
docs.text:
Build the following node graph in ComfyUI:

Load Checkpoint (Flux)
       ↓
CLIP / T5 Text Encode
       ↓
KSampler
       ↓
VAE Decode
       ↓
Save Image

Note: FLUX uses a T5 text encoder instead of the classic CLIP encoder used in standard Stable Diffusion workflows.

docs.title: Low VRAM (under 16 GB)
docs.text:
Open run_nvidia_gpu.bat and append the following flags after python main.py:

--force-fp16 --lowvram

docs.title: High VRAM (16 GB+)
docs.text: --force-fp16

docs.title: Enable xFormers (optional)
docs.text:
If xFormers is not enabled automatically, install it manually:

pip install xformers

This can significantly speed up image generation.

docs.title: Test Your Setup
docs.text:
Try this prompt to verify everything is working:

cinematic portrait of a cyberpunk samurai, neon lighting, ultra detailed, 35mm photography

Recommended settings:

Setting Value Resolution 1024 × 1024 Steps 20–30 CFG scale 3–5

docs.title: Saving and Finding ComfyUI Workflows
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Workflows sidebar only lists workflows you've saved. It has no save button of its own, so a new, unsaved workflow shows "No workflows found" until you save it.

docs.title: Step 1: Save As
docs.text: Right-click the workflow tab, then choose Save As. Other ways: the C logo (top-left) → File → Save As, or Ctrl+S.

docs.title: Step 2: Name It and Confirm
docs.text: Enter a filename — for example, anima_img2img — then click Confirm. The tab takes the new name, and the dot marking unsaved changes disappears.

docs.title: Step 3: Find It Again Later
docs.text: It now appears in the Workflows sidebar. Click it to open it.

docs.title: Templates vs. Workflows
docs.text:
Saving a workflow doesn't change the template it was based on. Templates are the read-only starting points bundled with ComfyUI; Workflows are your own saved files.

Open Templates in the left sidebar, and search for the original template's name to open it fresh again.

An unsaved workflow tab and a saved one are separate: the "Unsaved Workflow" tab is a workflow that has never been saved, distinct from a saved workflow like anima_img2img open in another tab.

docs.title: References

docs.title: Understanding Spectrum in ComfyUI
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Spectrum is an inference acceleration technique for diffusion models. Instead of running the full UNet/DiT every step, it skips some steps by using predictions — achieving roughly 1.5–2× speed-up depending on settings.

docs.title: Recommended Nodes
docs.text:
Node Notes ComfyUI Spectrum SDXL Node (ruwwww) Best for general use — supports SDXL and Anima (DiT), easy to tune Spectrum SDXL Proper Closer to the paper; SDXL only; less customisable Anima-Enhancer Anima-specific; focused on image quality; not general-purpose

Start with ComfyUI Spectrum SDXL Node.

docs.title: window (most important)
docs.text:
• Small → stable but slower
  • Large → faster but prone to artifacts
  • Recommended starting value: 2–3

docs.title: Late-step behaviour
docs.text: Spectrum tends to produce artifacts in the final steps. Turn it off for the last 20% of steps to avoid this.

docs.title: Colour desaturation
docs.text: Prediction errors can reduce colour saturation. Enable the calibration feature or turn Spectrum off for the later steps.

docs.title: Recommended Starting Settings
docs.text: Setting Value window 2–3 m 2–3 lam 0.1–0.3 Last 20% of steps Spectrum off

docs.title: Installing GIMP on Windows
docs.text: Download and install GIMP using the official installer.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Go to the official GIMP download page: https://www.gimp.org/downloads/

  2. Click Download GIMP 3.x.x directly under GIMP for Windows. Do not select GIMP on Microsoft Store.

  3. Double-click the downloaded installer file.

  4. In Select install mode, click Install for me only (recommended).

  5. Follow the setup wizard instructions.

docs.title: Repainting a Texture with Flat Anime Colors
Repainting a Texture with Flat Anime Colors
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Flat, solid colors are a defining trait of anime-style art. This repaints a soft, gradient-shaded texture — such as a VRM or VRoid model's skin — into flat color regions in GIMP.

Note: This assumes the shader itself has already been set up for hard-edged shadows — see Adjusting MToon Shading for a Hard Cel-Shaded Look. Repainting the texture alone won't produce a cel-shaded look if the shader is still set to a soft transition.

docs.title: Set Up a Reference Layer
docs.text: Open a backup copy of the original texture, then use File → Open as Layers to add the exported UV layout (see Exporting a UV Layout as an Image) as a layer on top. Lower that layer's opacity to around 40% (right-click it → Edit Layer Attributes) so it acts as a faint guide rather than obscuring the texture underneath — enough to see where the eyes, mouth, and face edges are.

docs.title: Paint in Flat Layers
docs.text:
• Base skin layer — fill the face area with one flat skin color using the Bucket Fill tool (Fill whole selection). Anime skin reads as flat because the shader itself draws the shadow.
  • Blush layer — paint the cheeks with the Pencil tool, or the Paintbrush with Hardness at 100, for hard edges. A few diagonal hatch lines on the cheeks is a classic anime touch.
  • Detail layer — crisp nose and mouth lines, if needed.

docs.title: Useful GIMP Tools
docs.text:
• Colors → Posterize quickly reduces a soft gradient to a few flat color steps — useful as a quick test, though hand-painting usually looks cleaner.
  • The Color Picker (O) samples a skin tone from the original, so the new colors stay related to it.

docs.title: Export Back to the 3D Application
docs.text:
1. Hide the reference layer — click its visibility (eye) icon in the Layers panel — so the UV wireframe isn't included in the exported image.

  2. Open File → Export (Ctrl+E) to re-export using the same filename and settings as your last export.

  3. Confirm the filename and click Export.

  4. If the file already exists, confirm Replace to overwrite it.

Keep the image the same size as the original. GIMP's Save only creates an .xcf project file — keep saving that too, so your layers and masks are still there for later tweaks, but it isn't what the 3D application reads.

Once exported, reload the texture in Blender — see Adjusting MToon Shading for a Hard Cel-Shaded Look.

Note: VRoid Studio (free) also has built-in texture editing with layers, letting you paint directly on the 3D model and export a new VRM. This is worth considering instead of GIMP if you haven't made any Blender-side edits yet, since those wouldn't carry over to a re-exported VRM — see Editing Face Texture.

docs.title: Updating GIMP to the Latest Version
Updating GIMP to the Latest Version
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Uninstall the older version before installing the latest version to avoid having multiple installations.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open Settings → Apps → Installed apps.

  2. Locate the older version of GIMP.

  3. Click Uninstall and complete the removal process.

  4. Restart your PC.

    Warning: Installing the new version without restarting first can cause an error during setup.

  5. Go to the official GIMP download page and click Download GIMP x.x.x directly under GIMP for Windows.

  6. Run the installer. In Select install mode, click Install for me only (recommended).

  7. Follow the remaining setup wizard steps to complete the installation.

docs.title: Note
docs.text:
• Your custom brushes, plugins, and preferences are stored in your user profile and are not removed when uninstalling the application.
  • If both versions were installed using different methods (for example, Microsoft Store and standalone installer), uninstall the version you do not intend to use.

docs.title: Adding a Cinematic Camera to a Level Sequence
Adding a Cinematic Camera to a Level Sequence
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • A Level Sequence created and open in the Sequencer panel. See Create a Level Sequence.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. In the Sequencer panel, click + Track.

  2. Select Actor to Sequencer.

  3. Choose the character Blueprint (e.g., bp_AnimeCharacter) to add it as a track.

  4. Click the camera icon in the Sequencer toolbar.

  5. Select Create Camera.

Unreal Engine adds a Cinematic Camera Actor and switches the Viewport to the camera's point of view, showing a framed movie-style shot.

docs.title: Adding a Fab Asset to a Project
Adding a Fab Asset to a Project
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Animating a Control Rig in Sequencer
Animating a Control Rig in Sequencer
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Once a Control Rig asset has custom bone controls wired up and tested, it can drive a real animation in Sequencer — Unreal's cinematic/level-sequence timeline — by keyframing the controls directly, instead of editing curves inside a single Animation Sequence asset. This example animates both of silber's eye controls (J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl and J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl) from a neutral pose at the start of the sequence to a rotated pose at the end.

Note: This page assumes the Control Rig already exists and its controls are wired to drive the matching bones. See Creating a Control Rig for that prerequisite workflow.

docs.title: Adding the Control Rig to the Level
Step 1: Drag the Control Rig Into the Level
docs.text: In the Content Browser, drag the SK_silber_Ctrl Rig (Control Rig asset) into the level viewport.

docs.title: Step 2: Confirm the Actor and Sequencer
docs.text: Dropping the Control Rig into the level adds the character actor and opens a Sequencer panel for it. In the Anim Outliner, the tree shows SK_silber_CtrlRig containing J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl and J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl. Sequencer's own track list, below, is still collapsed at this point.

docs.title: Step 1: Expand the Track Hierarchy
docs.text: In the Sequencer panel, expand the SK_silber_CtrlRig track and its child track to reveal J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl and J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl as separate, keyable sub-tracks, alongside a Transform track for the actor as a whole.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the Left Eye Control Track
docs.text: Click the J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl track to select it. Its Details panel shows the control's own Location, Rotation, and Scale, separate from the actor's.

docs.title: Step 2: Key the Start Frame
docs.text: With the playhead at the start of the sequence (frame 0000) and J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl still selected, press S to add a keyframe at the current playhead position. A diamond keyframe marker appears on the track at the start.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the Right Eye Control Track and Key the Start Frame
docs.text: Select J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl and press S at the same start frame. Both tracks now show a keyframe marker at frame 0000.

docs.title: Step 1: Move the Playhead to the End and Key the Left Eye
docs.text: Click the transport bar's To End button to jump the playhead to the end of the sequence (frame 0149). Select J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl, change its Rotator Z value (here, to -10.00), and press S to add a second keyframe.

docs.title: Step 2: Key the Right Eye at the End
docs.text: Select J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl, change its Rotator Z value (here, to -5.00), and press S to key it at the same end frame. Both tracks now hold two keyframes each — one at the start, one at the end.

docs.title: Step 1: Play the Sequence
docs.text: Move the playhead back into the middle of the timeline and click Play in the transport bar. The SK_silber_CtrlRig track shows both J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl and J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl sub-tracks with two keyframes each, visible at the start and end of the timeline. The viewport shows the character's face in close-up with the eyes visibly shifted mid-playback, confirming the keyframed animation plays correctly.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: To use this animation outside Sequencer — for example, feeding it into a Pose Asset — see Baking a Control Rig Animation.

docs.title: Applying an Animation to a Chaos Cloth Simulation
Applying an Animation to a Chaos Cloth Simulation
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

By default, a Chaos Cloth Asset simulates against a static reference pose. To preview how a garment behaves during actual movement, export a retargeted animation from your character's IK Retargeter and assign it to the cloth asset's Animation Asset property.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
This guide assumes you already have:

  • A character retargeted into the project through ABP_GenericRetarget's Retargeter Maps, with its own IK Retargeter asset (for example RTG_UEFN_VroidBoyBlue001) — see Retargeting a VRM Character to Game Animation Sample.
  • A Chaos Cloth Asset built for that character (for example CA_VroidBoyShirt) — see Creating a Chaos Cloth Asset and Applying Chaos Cloth Simulation.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the IK Retargeter Behind Your Character's Retarget Tag
docs.text:
1. In the Content Browser, navigate to Content → Blueprints → RetargetedCharacters and select ABP_GenericRetarget.

  2. Open it, and in its Class Defaults, find the Retargeter Maps entry for your character's tag. Note the IK Retargeter asset in the Value column — for example, the entry mapped to RTG_UEFN_VroidBoyBlue001.

    Note: Setting up this array entry is covered in Retargeting a VRM Character to Game Animation Sample. This step just locates the IK Retargeter asset it already points to.

  3. Locate that asset in the Content Browser (in this project, under Vroid → Rigs) and open it.

docs.title: Step 2: Preview and Export a Retargeted Animation
docs.text:
1. In the IK Retargeter editor, open the Asset Browser tab. It lists the source animation sequences available to preview through the retarget.

  2. Select an animation to preview it on both the source skeleton and your retargeted character in the viewport. Once you've found the one you want, click Export Selected Animations.

  3. In the Export Animations dialog, select a destination folder (for example Animations), set a Prefix under Rename New Assets (for example Vroid), then click Export.

docs.title: Step 3: Assign the Exported Animation to the Cloth Asset
docs.text:
1. Open your Chaos Cloth Asset (for example CA_VroidBoyShirt).
  2. In its Asset Details panel, under Blueprint Variables, set Animation Asset to the animation you just exported.

The Simulation Viewport now plays that animation instead of a static reference pose, so you can see how the cloth reacts to actual movement.

docs.title: Troubleshooting: Lower Body Sinks Into the Ground
docs.text: If the character's legs appear to sink below the floor while the animation plays in the Cloth Asset Editor's preview, work through these checks in order.

docs.title: Checking the Retarget Chain Assignments
docs.text:
Back in the IK Retargeter editor's Target tab, filter the hierarchy for leg and check the Retarget Chain column for the leg bones — each should map to LeftLeg or RightLeg as expected.

Select any of these entries to highlight the actual rig chain on the target character in the viewport, confirming it lines up with the source.

If the leg chains are mapped correctly, move to the next check.

docs.title: Checking the Default Target IK Rig
docs.text:
1. Still on the Target tab, note the asset under Default Target IK Rig (for example IK_UEFN_VroidBoyBlue001_Mannequin).

  2. Locate and open that IK Rig asset.

  3. In the viewport, confirm there's an IK goal at both wrists and both ankles. In the Solver Stack panel, confirm a Full Body IK solver is present (1 - Full Body IK).

If the goals and solver are both present and correct, move to the next check.

docs.title: Setting Root Behavior to Free and Re-Exporting
docs.text:
1. With the Full Body IK solver selected in the Solver Stack, find Root Behavior under Full Body IK Settings and set it to Free.

  2. Go back to the IK Retargeter's Asset Browser and export the animation again (same process as Step 2), using a different prefix so you don't overwrite the original export — for example, a second export in this workflow used the prefix Vroid2.

  3. Assign the newly exported animation to the Cloth Asset's Animation Asset property, as in Step 3.

docs.title: Ruling Out a Floor-Clipping Illusion
docs.text:
If the character still appears low or sunk after re-exporting with Root Behavior set to Free, the retargeting settings are most likely fine — this can be a rendering or preview quirk rather than an actual retargeting problem.

To check, open the Cloth Asset Editor's Preview Scene settings and disable Show Floor to hide the floor mesh.

Note: If the legs read correctly once the floor mesh is out of the way, the floor was visually clipping into the character rather than the animation actually sinking below it. Re-enable Show Floor once you've confirmed this — the walk cycle below plays with the shirt simulating naturally and the legs clearly on the ground.

docs.title: Applying Chaos Cloth Simulation
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.
