This guide covers the weight-painting and physical-parameter-tuning phase of Chaos Cloth simulation in Unreal Engine 5 — painting the Max Distance weight map, tuning the Dataflow graph's simulation nodes, wiring up collision, and testing the result in Play mode.

Reference Video: How to Create Cloth Simulation Easily with Chaos Cloth in Unreal Engine 5 by Dream Recompile

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
This guide assumes you already have:

  • A Chaos Cloth data asset created from your garment's mesh section (for example CA_VroidBoyShirt), with its Dataflow graph extracting that section from the base skeletal mesh — see Creating a Chaos Cloth Asset.
  • A physics asset for your character, used later for cloth collision.
  • Any bone adjustments the garment needs already made.

docs.title: Step 1: Enable the Chaos Cloth Plugins
docs.text:
1. Open Edit → Plugins.
  2. Search for chaos and enable Chaos Cloth and Chaos Cloth Asset.
  3. Restart the editor if prompted.

Note: Leave Cloth Asset Editor (Deprecated) unchecked — it belongs to the older, pre-Dataflow clothing tool and is not needed for this workflow.

docs.title: Step 2: Paint the Max Distance Weight Map
docs.text:
Proper weight painting keeps the fabric anchored where it should stay rigid and lets it move freely everywhere else.

  1. In the Cloth Asset Editor, switch to the Cloth tab and select the WeightMap_MaxDistance node in the Dataflow graph.
  2. Click Paint We... (Paint Weight Maps) in the toolbar. The garment's flattened front and back pattern appears in the 2D preview, fully unpainted.
  3. In the brush panel, set Radius and Value (0.0–1.0), and adjust Falloff for a softer edge.
  4. Paint anchor points — the collar, shoulder seams, and hem — down toward 0.0 so they stay pinned to the body. Leave the rest of the garment near 1.0 so it simulates freely.
  5. Click Accept to commit the weight map.

Note: The paint tool's default Mesh Display mode shows weight as grayscale — 0.0 (black) is fully fixed, 1.0 (white) is fully simulated. Switching the display to Ramp shows the same values as a color gradient instead.

docs.title: Step 3: Set the Max Distance and Attachment Range
docs.text:
1. Select the SimulationMaxDistanceConfig node. Its Hi value (in centimeters) scales the weight map you just painted into an actual distance the cloth can move away from the base mesh — lower it to keep the fabric close to the body, raise it to allow more drape.
  2. Select the SimulationLongRangeAttachmentConfig node. Tether Stiffness and Tether Scale govern how far the simulated vertices can stretch away from their pinned anchors before the tether pulls them back.

Warning: If the cloth stretches away from the body indefinitely during simulation, raise Tether Stiffness first before touching anything else — see Troubleshooting below.

docs.title: Step 4: Tune Bending, Mass, and Aerodynamics
docs.text:
Select each of the following nodes in the Dataflow graph and adjust their values on the Node Details panel:

  • SimulationBendingConfig — Bending Stiffness (split into Warp, Weft, and Bias, matching the fabric's weave axes) controls how easily the cloth folds and creases. Buckling Stiffness controls how sharply it creases once bending exceeds a threshold, instead of folding smoothly.
  • SimulationMassConfig — with Mass Mode set to Density, the Density range controls the fabric's overall weight. Heavier density moves more slowly; lighter density moves quickly and floats.
  • SimulationAerodynamicsConfig — Drag and Lift control air resistance and the aerodynamic lift pushing up under the fabric. Wind Velocity and Fluid Density simulate ambient wind.

Note: A SimulationDampingConfig node also sits in the graph between Aerodynamics and Self-Collision. Increasing its value suppresses jitter at the cost of energetic, fluttering motion — see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Step 5: Assign Collision
docs.text:
1. Select the SetPhysicsAsset node and assign your character's physics asset (from Before You Start) — this is what the simulated cloth collides against.
  2. Select the SimulationCollisionConfig node and set Friction Coefficient and Collision Thickness for how the cloth slides against the body.
  3. SimulationSelfCollisionSpheresConfig, earlier in the graph, controls collision between different parts of the cloth itself (for example, a sleeve against the torso).

docs.title: Step 6: Evaluate and Preview the Simulation
docs.text:
1. Click Evaluate Dataflow Graph (or press F5) to rebuild the cloth with your new settings.
  2. Switch to the Simulation Viewport tab and click Play to run a live simulation preview.
  3. Watch the overlay stats — Active Cloths, Dynamic Particles, Iterations, Substeps, and Simulation Time — and check that the garment settles naturally instead of exploding or jittering.

Note: To see the collision bodies the cloth is colliding against, drawn directly on the mesh, see Displaying Collisions in the Skeletal Mesh Editor.

Note: This preview plays a static reference pose by default. To see the cloth react to actual movement, see Applying an Animation to a Chaos Cloth Simulation.

docs.title: Step 7: Fix Clipping by Refining Collision
docs.text:
If part of the body pokes through the simulated cloth, the physics asset's collision shapes usually need adjusting rather than the cloth parameters themselves.

  1. Open your character's physics asset, right-click the bone where clipping occurs, and choose Add Primitive → Add Capsule (or Add Sphere) to cover the gap.
  2. Back in the Cloth Asset Editor, point the SetPhysicsAsset node at the updated physics asset.
  3. Evaluate the graph again and re-run the simulation preview to confirm the clipping is gone.

Warning: Save a duplicate of the physics asset before adding new collision primitives (as shown above) — new capsules or spheres can affect ragdoll and collision behavior elsewhere if the asset is shared.

docs.title: Step 8: Attach the Cloth to a Test Character
docs.text:
A Chaos Cloth data asset renders as its own actor, separate from the base skeletal mesh, so it needs to be attached and kept in sync through a Blueprint rather than picked from a simple dropdown.

  1. Duplicate an existing Blueprint that already attaches a simulated component to the base mesh — the example here duplicates a template from Content → Blueprints → RetargetedCharacters into a new test Blueprint (BP_Test).
  2. Add your Chaos Cloth data asset as a component under the base mesh component.
  3. Reuse the existing Get Attach Parent → Get Child Component → Add Tick Prerequisite Component logic (copied from another component-attachment Blueprint in the project) so the cloth component follows the base mesh and simulates only after it updates each frame.
  4. Compile and save.

docs.title: Step 9: Hide the Original Garment Section
docs.text:
With the simulated cloth now rendering as its own mesh, the static garment section on the base skeletal mesh would otherwise render underneath it and clip through.

  1. Open the base skeletal mesh editor and expand LOD 0 → Sections.
  2. Find the section matching your garment's material (for example, a _CLOTH material slot) and disable it so only the simulated cloth renders.

docs.title: Step 10: Test in Play Mode
docs.text: Press Play and move the character around the level. Confirm the cloth reacts to motion smoothly, without exploding, clipping through the body, or jittering excessively.

docs.title: Tuning Parameters
docs.text:
Each classic Chaos Cloth parameter lives on a specific node in the Dataflow graph:

Parameter Dataflow Node Effect Max Distance SimulationMaxDistanceConfig (fed by the painted WeightMap_MaxDistance) Scales the weight map into the actual distance, in centimeters, cloth vertices may move from the base mesh. Tether Stiffness / Tether Scale SimulationLongRangeAttachmentConfig How tightly simulated vertices are pulled back toward their pinned anchors. Raise if the cloth stretches too far from the body. Bending Stiffness (Warp / Weft / Bias) SimulationBendingConfig How easily the cloth folds and creases. High values give a stiffer material with fewer wrinkles; low values give a soft, heavily creased material. Buckling Stiffness SimulationBendingConfig How sharply the cloth creases once it bends past a threshold, instead of folding smoothly. Density SimulationMassConfig Overall weight of the fabric. High density moves slowly (leather, heavy wool); low density moves quickly and floats (silk, satin). Drag / Lift SimulationAerodynamicsConfig Air resistance slowing the cloth down, and aerodynamic pressure lifting it. Raise for flowing capes or fluttering fabric. Damping SimulationDampingConfig Resistance to motion that suppresses jitter. High damping gives smooth, viscous movement; low damping gives energetic, chaotic movement. Friction Coefficient / Collision Thickness SimulationCollisionConfig Sliding resistance and collision margin against the character's physics asset. Self-Collision Sphere Radius / Stiffness SimulationSelfCollisionSpheresConfig Collision between different parts of the cloth itself, such as a sleeve against the torso.

docs.title: Fabric Presets by Material Type
docs.text:
Use these as starting points, then adjust the Lo/Hi ranges on each node to taste:

Material Type Density Bending Stiffness Damping / Drag Heavy Leather High (1.5+) High (0.7–0.9) Moderate Cotton / Linen Medium (1.0) Low (0.2–0.4) Low / Moderate Flowing Cape Medium-Low Low (0.1–0.3) High Drag Silk / Satin Low (< 0.5) Very Low (< 0.2) Moderate Lift

docs.title: Mesh Exploding or Infinite Stretching
docs.text:
Warning: This is the most common failure mode and can make the simulation unusable if left unchecked.

  • Raise Tether Stiffness on SimulationLongRangeAttachmentConfig.
  • Check your weight paint: boundary vertices directly against static geometry (collar, waistband) must be fully pinned (0.0).

docs.title: Body Clipping
docs.text:
• Add or adjust collision primitives on the character's physics asset — see Step 7 above for a worked example.
  • Slightly raise Friction Coefficient, or adjust Collision Thickness, on SimulationCollisionConfig.

docs.title: Excessive Jittering
docs.text: • Slightly raise Damping on SimulationDampingConfig to stabilize the motion.

docs.title: Baking a Control Rig Animation
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Once a Control Rig animation is keyframed in Sequencer, bake it into a standalone Animation Sequence asset so it can be used outside that sequence — for example, creating a Pose Asset from it.

Note: This continues from Animating a Control Rig in Sequencer.

docs.title: Step 1: Bake the Animation Sequence
docs.text: In Sequencer, right-click the SK_silber_CtrlRig skeletal mesh track. Under Create Animation Assets, select Bake Animation Sequence.

docs.title: Step 2: Name the Animation Asset
docs.text: A Create a New Animation Asset dialog opens. Select a destination folder and enter a name — for example, SKEL_silber_Anim_LookLeft.

docs.title: Step 3: Export
docs.text: An Animation Sequence Options dialog opens, showing export settings (Export Transforms, Export Morph Targets, Interpolation, and so on). The defaults work for most cases. Click Export.

docs.title: Step 4: Confirm the New Animation Sequence
docs.text: The new Animation Sequence asset appears in the Content Browser alongside the character's other assets.

docs.title: Step 5: Check the Animation
docs.text: Open the new asset and play it back to confirm the baked animation matches what was keyframed in Sequencer.

docs.title: Capturing Unreal Editor Screenshots with Claude Code
Capturing Unreal Editor Screenshots with Claude Code
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

With the Unreal MCP plugin connected, Claude Code can capture screenshots of the Unreal Editor directly — no external screenshot tool or browser automation needed.

docs.title: Available Capture Tools
docs.text:
The plugin's EditorToolset.EditorAppToolset toolset exposes three image-capture tools:

Tool Captures CaptureEditorImage The entire editor application as you see it on your desktop — all panels, viewport, outliner, and so on. Use this for a general screenshot of the editor. CaptureViewport Just the level viewport, with optional annotation overlays (a world-space grid, plus actor name/position labels) — useful for spatial reasoning tasks such as directing actor placement. CaptureAssetImage A thumbnail of a specific asset, such as a static mesh, material, or texture.

All three return a ToolsetImage — base64-encoded PNG data plus its MIME type.

docs.title: Working Around Large Results
docs.text:
The raw tool result can be large enough to exceed the tool-output token limit, in which case it's redirected to a saved file instead of being returned inline. To view it anyway:

  1. Parse the JSON result and extract returnValue.data.

  2. Base64-decode it and write it out as a PNG file — for example, in PowerShell:

    [System.IO.File]::WriteAllBytes(
    "<YOUR-FOLDER>\screenshot.png",
    [System.Convert]::FromBase64String($base64Data)
)

  3. Read the resulting PNG file to view it.

docs.title: Example Call
docs.text:
mcp__unreal-mcp__call_tool(
  tool_name = "CaptureEditorImage",
  toolset_name = "EditorToolset.EditorAppToolset",
  arguments = {}
)

docs.title: Centering the View in the Blueprint Editor
Centering the View in the Blueprint Editor
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

These techniques re-center or zoom the Blueprint graph editor to fit its nodes on screen.

docs.title: Method 1: Fit All Nodes in View
docs.text:
1. Click inside the graph area (the empty gray space) to give the Blueprint editor panel focus.
  2. Press Home.
  3. The view zooms and pans to fit all nodes in the current graph.

Use this when the graph feels scattered or you've lost track of where everything is.

docs.title: Method 2: Fit Selected Nodes in View
docs.text:
1. Select the nodes you want to focus on — click a single node, drag a selection box around several, or hold Ctrl and click each node to add it to the selection.
  2. Press F.
  3. The view zooms and pans to fit only the selected nodes.

Use this to jump to one part of a large graph, such as a specific event chain.

docs.title: Method 3: Pan and Zoom Manually
docs.text:
1. Hold the right mouse button and drag to pan around the graph.
  2. Scroll the mouse wheel to zoom in or out.
  3. Release the right mouse button once you're positioned where you want.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Action Shortcut Fit all nodes in view Home Fit selected node(s) in view F Pan Right-click + drag Zoom Mouse scroll wheel

docs.title: Changing Camera Speed
docs.text: Adjust the viewport camera movement speed.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. In the viewport toolbar, click Camera Speed.

  2. Drag the slider to set the desired speed.

docs.title: Changing Clothing in Anime Character Pack (Legacy)
Changing Clothing in Anime Character Pack (Legacy)
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide explains how to swap the torso clothing on the male anime character in the Anime Character Pack (Legacy) by Studio SyndiCat. The pack uses a Construction Script inside the character Blueprint to apply meshes — so the correct method is through Class Defaults, not by editing mesh components directly.

docs.title: Available Tops for Male Characters
docs.text:
The pack includes three top options, located at: Content > AnimeCharacters > Blueprints > Characters > Male_Average > Tops

Folder Mesh Name Description Starter_TShirt skl_AnimeM_Top_Tshirt Red t-shirt Starter_Tank skl_AnimeM_Top_tank Black tank top Starter_Nak skl_AnimeM_Top_nak No top (naked body mesh)

docs.title: Why Not Edit the Component Directly?
docs.text: The Blueprint's Construction Script sets the character's mesh components programmatically at runtime using variables from the Appearance category. If you change the Skeletal Mesh on the Top component directly — either in the Blueprint editor or as a level instance override — the Construction Script will override it back to the variable value. You must change the variable, not the component.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Character Blueprint
docs.text: In the Outliner, find bp_AnimeCharacter and click the Edit bp_AnimeCharacter link next to it to open the Blueprint editor.

docs.title: Step 2: Open Class Defaults and Find the Appearance Section
docs.text:
In the Blueprint editor toolbar, click Class Defaults. In the Details panel on the right, scroll down to find the Appearance section. You will see four mesh variables:

  • Head Mesh
  • Torso Mesh
  • Bottom Mesh
  • Hair Mesh

docs.title: Step 3: Change the Torso Mesh
docs.text: Click the dropdown next to Torso Mesh (currently skl_AnimeM_Top_nak) and select the clothing mesh you want — for example, skl_AnimeM_Top_Tshirt for the red t-shirt.

docs.title: Step 4: Compile and Save
docs.text: Click Compile then Save in the Blueprint editor toolbar.

docs.title: Step 5: Return to the Main Viewport
docs.text: Close the Blueprint editor. The character in the viewport will now be wearing the selected top.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• This change applies to all instances of bp_AnimeCharacter in the level, because it modifies the Blueprint's class defaults.
  • The same Appearance section contains Bottom Mesh and Hair Mesh — use the same method to change pants or hairstyle.

docs.title: Changing the Timeline's Time Format
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

An Animation Sequence or Anim Montage's timeline can display positions as frame numbers or as seconds.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Timeline Context Menu
docs.text: Right-click the time ruler above the track list. Under Timeline Options, open the Time Format submenu.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose Frames or Seconds
docs.text:
Select Frames to show whole frame numbers (for example, 2), or Seconds to show elapsed time (for example, 2.00).

Note: The same menu has Additional Display options — Percentage and Secondary — for showing extra position info alongside the main format.

Note: This is the same time display shown in the playhead tooltip covered in Moving the Playhead.

docs.title: Checking Available Animation Sets
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Game Animation Sample project ships with a large library of animation sequences, organized by category under the UEFN_Mannequin character, plus a set of motion-matching databases used to search that library at runtime. Use this guide to browse what's already included before retargeting or exporting new animations.

docs.title: Step 1: Browse Animation Sequences by Category
docs.text:
In the Content Browser, navigate to Content → Characters → UEFN_Mannequin → Animations. This folder splits the included animation sequences into category subfolders — for example Jump, alongside others such as Idle, Interactions, and Run.

Open a category folder to see its animation sequences as a thumbnail grid, each with a live preview of the pose. For example, the Jump folder contains sequences like M_Neutral_Jump_B_Land_Run_Heavy, covering different jump heights, landing types, and directions.

docs.title: Step 2: Check the Motion Matching Database
docs.text:
Under the same Animations folder, open MotionMatchingData → Databases. This folder holds subfolders grouping animations by density (Dense, Extreme_Sparse, Relaxed, Sparse) alongside two assets of type Pose Search Database: PSD_Ragdoll and PSD_Traversal.

A Pose Search Database is the asset type that Motion Matching searches against at runtime to pick the best-matching pose from the library. This project's Content Browser view doesn't expose much more detail than the asset type and name — open one directly in its own editor if you need to inspect its contents further.

Note: The source notes for this workflow referred to these as "PDS files," but the asset type shown in the editor is Pose Search Database, abbreviated PSD_ in the asset name.

docs.title: Checking Morph Target and Pose Counts
Checking Morph Target and Pose Counts
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Content Browser's asset info tooltip shows how many morph targets a Skeletal Mesh has, or how many poses a Pose Asset holds, without opening the asset itself.

docs.title: Checking a Skeletal Mesh's Morph Target Count
docs.text:
Select a Skeletal Mesh in the Content Browser. Its info tooltip shows a Morph Targets count — confirming, for example, that a VRM import brought in its blendshapes successfully.

Note: After importing a VRM character, checking this count confirms its face animation blendshapes came through.

docs.title: Checking a Pose Asset's Pose Count
docs.text:
Select a Pose Asset in the Content Browser. Its info tooltip shows a Poses count instead.

Note: A Pose Asset created from an animation gets one pose per sampled frame — a count this high usually means it needs cleanup. See Isolating a Single Pose in a Pose Asset.

docs.title: Clipping an Animation with an Anim Montage
Clipping an Animation with an Anim Montage
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

An Animation Sequence's own length can't be trimmed directly (see Understanding the Number of Sampled Frames Limit). To play back just part of one — for example, isolating the single peak frame of a fast facial expression — wrap it in an Anim Montage and set a start/end range on the segment instead.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Anim Montage
docs.text: In the Content Browser, right-click the Animation Sequence (for example A_face_kento-blue_sorrow). Under Create, select Create AnimMontage.

docs.title: Step 2: Find the Animation Segment's Start and End Time
docs.text: Open the new Montage and select its animation segment. The Details panel's Animation Segment section shows Start Time and End Time, defaulting to the full length of the source animation (0.0 to 75.0 frames in this example).

docs.title: Step 3: Set the Range You Want
docs.text: Change Start Time and End Time to bracket the part you want to isolate. Here, the expression's peak was at frame 3, so Start Time is set to 2.0 and End Time to 4.0. Move the playhead back to the start, and lower the playback speed dropdown — for example to x0.1 — if the clipped range plays too fast to see clearly.

docs.title: Step 4: Scrub Through the Slowed Playback
docs.text: Scrub or play through the slowed-down range to find the exact moment you want.

docs.title: Creating an Animation from a Pose
Creating an Animation from a Pose
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This walkthrough builds a single-expression Animation Sequence from scratch by keyframing one facial curve, starting from an existing pose-holding asset. The example uses A_face_silber, an Animation Sequence belonging to the silber VRM character (folder VroidSilber), and creates a new expression animation named SKEL_silber_anim_surprised around the Fcl_ALL_Surprised curve.

Note: See Creating a Pose Asset from an Animation Sequence for the reverse workflow — turning an animation like the one built here back into a Pose Asset.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Source Animation
docs.text: In the Content Browser, open the VroidSilber folder and double-click A_face_silber (an Animation Sequence) to open it.

docs.title: Step 2: Create an Animation from the Current Pose
docs.text:
With A_face_silber open, click Create Asset → Create Animation, then select Current Pose.

Note: Current Pose captures only the single frame the playhead is currently on, producing a fresh one-frame Animation Sequence. This is the opposite choice from Creating a Pose Asset from an Animation Sequence, which uses Current Animation to capture an entire existing clip.

docs.title: Step 3: Name the New Animation Asset
docs.text:
A Create a New Animation Asset dialog opens. Confirm the destination folder and the animation's name. The screenshot shows the VroidSilber folder selected and the Animation Name field pre-filled as SKEL_silber_anim_surprised.

Click OK to create the file.

docs.title: Step 4: Confirm the Animation Opens Automatically
docs.text: The new animation asset opens in its own editor tab automatically. At this point its Curves section is empty (Curves (0)).

docs.title: Step 5: Open the Add Curve Menu
docs.text: Next to Curves, open the dropdown and select Add Curve.... This opens a Create Curve panel listing every available curve name on the skeleton, in alphabetical order.

docs.title: Step 6: Select the Curve
docs.text:
Type into the Create Curve search box to filter the list. Searching sur narrows the list to the Surprised family of curves — Face.M_F00_Fcl_ALL_Surprised, Fcl_BRW_Surprised, Fcl_EYE_Surprised, and Fcl_MTH_Surprised. Select Fcl_ALL_Surprised.

Note: The narrower BRW (brow), EYE, and MTH (mouth) curves drive only one part of the face each. ALL drives the combined expression across all three at once, which is why it's the one picked for a single-expression animation.

docs.title: Step 7: Open the Curve Editor
docs.text: The Fcl_ALL_Surprised curve now appears under Curves. Open its row's dropdown and select Edit Curve to open the Curve Editor tab.

docs.title: Step 8: Add a Key at the Start
docs.text: In the Curve Editor, right-click the empty graph area and select Add Key. A key is added at the playhead's current position — the animation's starting point, with a value of 0.

docs.title: Step 9: Move the Playhead Toward the End
docs.text:
Drag the playhead across the timeline toward the animation's end point.

Note: See Moving the Playhead for the two ways to position the playhead precisely — dragging the ruler, or typing an exact frame number.

docs.title: Step 10: Add a Key at the End
docs.text: Right-click the graph again and select Add Key. A second key is added at this new playhead position.

docs.title: Step 11: Raise the End Key to 1
docs.text: With the new key selected, edit its value field and set it to 1. The curve now draws as a rising diagonal line from 0 to 1 — the single-expression animation is complete.

docs.title: Step 1: Disable Looping
docs.text: In the transport bar below the preview, click the loop-mode button until its tooltip reads No Looping. This prevents the playback from repeating.

docs.title: Step 2: Return the Playhead to the Start
docs.text: Click the jump-to-start button in the transport bar to move the playhead back to frame 0.

docs.title: Step 3: Slow Down Playback
docs.text: Open the playback speed dropdown and select x0.1. At full speed, a one-second animation plays too fast to evaluate frame by frame.

docs.title: Step 4: Play the Animation
docs.text: Click Play. The silber character's expression rises smoothly into the surprised pose — mouth open, eyes widened — confirming the curve works as expected.

docs.title: Increasing the Play Duration
docs.text: A newly created single-pose animation defaults to a very short play duration (one frame's worth of time). To stretch it out:

docs.title: Step 1: Right-Click the Time Row and Append Frames
docs.text: Right-click the time row (the ruler above the curve graph) and select Append frames at end of sequence.

docs.title: Step 2: Set the Number of Frames to Add
docs.text: A Number of Frames to Add field appears. Enter 1 and confirm.

docs.title: Step 3: Locate the Shifted Key
docs.text: Appending a frame doubles the total sequence length. The key that used to sit at the animation's end (100%) now reads as sitting at the sequence's midpoint.

docs.title: Step 4: Disable Time Snapping
docs.text: Select that key, then click the Toggle Time Snapping icon in the Curve Editor toolbar to turn snapping off. This is required to move the key to an exact time rather than the nearest whole frame.

docs.title: Step 5: Move the Key Back to the Start
docs.text:
With snapping disabled, edit the selected key's time field and set it to 0.

Note: The source memo describes this move as necessary to "play the same animation in 2 seconds," but neither the memo nor the screenshots fully explain the resulting curve shape after the key is relocated — the numeric field changes are confirmed here, but the underlying reasoning isn't independently verified in this session. Treat this step as documented technique rather than a fully explained mechanism.

Note: See Understanding the Number of Sampled Frames Limit for background on Append Frames at End of Sequence and why an Animation Sequence's frame count can't be edited directly in the Details panel.

docs.title: Step 6: Play the Extended Animation
docs.text: Click Play again. The same expression now plays out across the extended, two-frame timeline.

docs.title: Decreasing the Play Duration
docs.text: To shrink the play duration back down — for example, from two seconds back to one:

docs.title: Step 1: Move the Playhead to the New End Point
docs.text: Use the transport bar's step-back button (or drag the ruler) to move the playhead to the frame where you want the animation to end — in this case, the 1 second mark.

docs.title: Step 2: Remove the Frames After That Point
docs.text:
Right-click the time row and select Remove frames in range 2 to 2.

Warning: Removing frames trims the sequence permanently. Undo (Ctrl+Z) recovers it within the same editing session, but there's no separate confirmation step before the frames are cut.

The sequence's total length drops back to 1.

docs.title: Step 3: Select the Key at the End Point
docs.text: Because the sequence's total length was cut in half, the key that used to sit at the very end now evaluates partway through the shortened curve — its value tooltip reads 0.5 instead of 1.

docs.title: Step 4: Set the Value Back to 1
docs.text: Edit the key's value field and set it back to 1, restoring the full expression at the new end point.

docs.title: Step 5: Play the Restored Animation
docs.text: Click Play to confirm the animation now plays the full expression across the shortened, one-second timeline again.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Once a single-expression animation like this one exists, it becomes source material for other tools:

  • Creating a Pose Asset from an Animation Sequence — feed this animation back into Create Asset → Create PoseAsset to extract its poses.
  • Understanding the Number of Sampled Frames Limit — more on the Append Frames at End of Sequence command used above.
  • Moving the Playhead — the two ways to position the playhead precisely while keyframing.

docs.title: Creating a Chaos Cloth Asset
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This covers the modern Dataflow-based Chaos Cloth workflow. It builds a ClothAsset from a garment section that already exists on a skinned character mesh — for example a shirt imported as its own material section through VRM4U — and prepares it for weight painting.

Note: This is not the deprecated "Clothing" panel workflow (right-click a skeletal mesh section → Create Clothing Data from Section). That system is being phased out. Follow this guide instead, and leave Cloth Asset Editor (Deprecated) unchecked wherever it appears.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: You need a skinned character mesh where the garment is already its own material section (not merged with skin or hair). This guide uses SKM_VroidBoyBlue001, whose shirt lives in its own section, as the example.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Cloth Asset
docs.text:
In the Content Browser, right-click inside your character's mesh folder and open the Create menu. Under the Chaos Cloth category, select ClothAsset ("Cloth asset for pattern based simulation").

Name the new asset after the garment, for example CA_VroidBoyShirt. Unreal applies the CA_ prefix automatically as part of its Cloth Asset naming convention.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose the Dataflow Graph Template
docs.text:
Unreal immediately opens the Choose Dataflow Setup dialog, offering four templates: Empty Dataflow, Static Mesh Cloth, Skeletal Mesh Cloth, and USD Cloth.

Select Skeletal Mesh Cloth ("Add a Dataflow graph that builds a Cloth Asset from Skeletal Meshes. Requires the ChaosClothAssetDataflowNodes plug-in.") and click OK.

Note: Clicking No Dataflow instead continues without attaching a graph, leaving you to build the whole node network by hand. The Skeletal Mesh Cloth template pre-wires the nodes this guide uses, so there's no reason to skip it.

docs.title: Step 3: Open the Cloth Asset Editor
docs.text:
The new CA_VroidBoyShirt asset appears in the Content Browser. Double-click it to open the Cloth Asset Editor.

The Construction tab's Dataflow Graph panel already contains a template graph: a SkeletalMesh_SIM → SkeletalMeshImport_SIM chain and a SkeletalMesh_RENDER → SkeletalMeshImport_RENDER chain, both feeding into a MergeClothCollections node, followed by further nodes for weight maps and a physics asset. The template's own comment boxes number these as steps — this guide covers steps 1 through the merge; weight-map painting (step 3 onward) is covered in the next guide.

docs.title: Step 4: Assign the Source Skeletal Mesh
docs.text:
Select the SkeletalMesh_SIM node and set its Skeletal Mesh property to your character's mesh, for example SKM_VroidBoyBlue001.

Repeat for the SkeletalMesh_RENDER node, assigning the same mesh.

Note: SIM drives the simulation mesh — the flattened pattern used for weight painting and cloth physics. RENDER drives the mesh actually drawn on screen. Both need the same source mesh so the section you extract next lines up between them.

docs.title: Step 5: Find the Garment's Section Index
docs.text:
The SkeletalMeshImport nodes extract a single material section from the source mesh by index. Find the right index by opening the source mesh itself: double-click SKM_VroidBoyBlue001 to open it in the Skeletal Mesh Editor, then check its material element list.

Locate the element whose material corresponds to the garment — in this example, Element 11 uses MI_N00_004_0_Tops_01_CLOTH, so the shirt's section index is 11.

docs.title: Step 6: Extract the Section into SIM
docs.text:
Back in the Cloth Asset Editor, select the SkeletalMeshImport_SIM node. In its Node Details, check Import Single Section and set Section Index to the value you found — 11 in this example.

The 2D View tab updates to show the extracted, flattened cloth pattern (front and back panels), which the next guide uses for weight painting.

docs.title: Step 7: Extract the Section into RENDER
docs.text:
Select the SkeletalMeshImport_RENDER node. By default, Import Single Section is unchecked, so the node imports the entire body mesh — visible as the full character outline in the Construction viewport.

Check Import Single Section. With Section Index still at its default of 0, the viewport now shows the wrong, tiny section.

Set Section Index to the same value used for SIM (11).

docs.title: Step 8: Evaluate the Dataflow Graph
docs.text:
Property changes don't refresh the preview automatically. Click Evaluate Dataflow Graph in the toolbar (or press F8) to trigger an evaluation of the graph's terminal nodes.

The Construction viewport now shows the correctly extracted shirt shape for the render mesh. Use the viewport's display-mode dropdown to switch between 3DView and Render to confirm both look correct.

docs.title: Step 9: Confirm the Merge
docs.text:
Select the MergeClothCollections node. It combines the SIM and RENDER collections into a single cloth collection, which downstream nodes consume — including the WeightMap_MaxDistance node, whose tooltip notes that the MaxDistance weight map must be painted before simulating.

Save the asset (Ctrl+S). CA_VroidBoyShirt now has a merged cloth collection ready for weight painting.

Weight-painting this asset and tuning its simulation parameters are covered in Applying Chaos Cloth Simulation.

docs.title: Creating a Control Rig
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Reference: How to Create Control Rigs in Unreal Engine by Epic Games

This walkthrough builds a Control Rig asset from scratch for the silber VRM character's base skeletal mesh, SK_silber. Unlike the Animation Sequence / Curve Editor workflow used for facial expression curves, a Control Rig adds custom bone controls wired through a node graph (the Forwards Solve graph), so the controls can drive bones directly and later be keyframed in Sequencer. This example wires up two controls — one for each eye bone — and tests that moving each control rotates the matching eye.

Note: See Animating a Control Rig in Sequencer for the follow-up workflow that uses the rig built here to keyframe an animation.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the Skeletal Mesh
docs.text: In the Content Browser, open the VroidSilber folder and select SK_silber, the character's Skeletal Mesh.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Control Rig
docs.text: Right-click SK_silber and select Create → Control Rig.

docs.title: Step 3: Open the New Control Rig Asset
docs.text: A new SK_silber_CtrlRig asset (type Control Rig) appears in the Content Browser. Double-click it to open the Control Rig editor.

docs.title: Adding Eye Controls in the Rig Hierarchy
Step 1: Open the Rig Hierarchy Tab
docs.text: The Control Rig editor opens with an empty Forwards Solve graph containing only the Forwards Solve event node and its Execute pin. Open the Rig Hierarchy tab (bottom-left panel) to see the skeleton's bone tree.

docs.title: Step 2: Find the Eye Bones
docs.text: Type eye into the Rig Hierarchy's search box to filter the bone tree down to J_Adj_L_FaceEye and J_Adj_R_FaceEye, the left and right eye adjustment bones.

docs.title: Step 3: Create a Control for the Left Eye
docs.text: Right-click J_Adj_L_FaceEye and select New Element → New Control. A new control, J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl, is added. Its Details panel shows Animation Type: Animation Control and Value Type: Euler Transform.

docs.title: Step 4: Create a Control for the Right Eye
docs.text: Repeat the same right-click → New Element → New Control on J_Adj_R_FaceEye, creating J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl.

docs.title: Step 5: Move Both Controls Under Their Bones
docs.text:
Drag each _ctrl item onto its matching bone in the tree so it becomes nested underneath — J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl under J_Adj_L_FaceEye, and J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl under J_Adj_R_FaceEye. The preview viewport now shows colored gizmo rings around both eyes.

Note: Immediately after creation (Step 3 and Step 4 above), each new control appears at the root of the hierarchy rather than nested under its bone — the drag-to-nest shown here is a separate, deliberate step.

docs.title: Step 1: Drag the Control Into the Graph
docs.text: Drag J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl from the Rig Hierarchy into the Forwards Solve graph and release. From the menu that appears, select Get Control.

docs.title: Step 2: Get Transform Node Added
docs.text: A Get Transform - Control node is added, preconfigured with Type: Control and Name: J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl, exposing a Transform output pin.

docs.title: Step 3: Drag the Bone Into the Graph
docs.text: Drag J_Adj_L_FaceEye (the bone itself, not the control) from the Rig Hierarchy into the graph. From the menu, select Set Bone.

docs.title: Step 4: Set Transform Node Added
docs.text: A Set Transform - Bone node is added, with pins for Execute, Item, Space, Initial, Value, Weight, and Propagate to Children.

docs.title: Step 5: Connect Transform to Value
docs.text: Drag a wire from the Get Transform - Control node's Transform output pin to the Set Transform - Bone node's Value input pin.

docs.title: Step 6: Connect Execute to Execute
docs.text: Drag a wire from the Forwards Solve event node's Execute output pin to the Set Transform - Bone node's Execute input pin, so the bone update actually runs each frame. The screenshot above already shows this connection made, alongside the Transform-to-Value wire from Step 5.

docs.title: Step 7: Test the Left Eye
docs.text: With the wiring in place, select J_Adj_L_FaceEye_ctrl and change its Rotator Z value (for example, to -9.0) in the Details panel. The left eye moves in the preview viewport, confirming the control drives the bone.

docs.title: Step 1: Repeat Get/Set for the Right Eye
docs.text: Repeat Steps 1–4 from the previous section for the right eye: drag J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl into the graph and select Get Control, then drag J_Adj_R_FaceEye and select Set Bone. This adds a second Get Transform - Control node (Name: J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl) and a second Set Transform - Bone node.

docs.title: Step 2: Confirm the Full Graph
docs.text: Wire the right eye's Get Transform - Control → Transform output to its Set Transform - Bone → Value input, the same as for the left eye. Connect its Execute input from the left eye's Set Transform - Bone node's Execute output pin, chaining the two bone updates after the Forwards Solve event. The full graph now shows: Forwards Solve → left eye Set Transform - Bone → right eye Set Transform - Bone, with each Get Transform - Control node feeding its matching Set Transform - Bone node's Value pin.

docs.title: Step 3: Test the Right Eye
docs.text: Select J_Adj_R_FaceEye_ctrl and change its Rotator Z value (for example, to -9.0). The right eye moves independently of the left.

docs.title: Step 4: Confirm Both Eyes Move Correctly
docs.text: With both controls wired, both eyes rotate independently when their respective values change. The Control Rig is complete.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
With the Control Rig wired and tested, it's ready to drive an actual animation:

  • Animating a Control Rig in Sequencer — drag this Control Rig into the level and keyframe its eye controls in Sequencer.

docs.title: Creating a Custom MetaHuman Character
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Build an original character with MetaHuman Creator. Tested with Unreal Engine 5.8.1 — menu wording may differ slightly between engine versions.

Warning: Order matters. Once you create a rig, the Import, Head & Body, and Materials tools lock (Remove Rig unlocks them again). Hair and clothing stay editable. Shape the face, body, and skin before rigging.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Project
docs.text: In the Unreal Project Browser, choose Games → Third Person, set Blueprint, Target Platform to Desktop, Quality Preset to Maximum, name the project, and click Create.

docs.title: Step 2: Install MetaHuman Creator Core Data
docs.text:
In the Epic Games Launcher, go to Unreal Engine → Library, open the dropdown arrow next to Launch on your engine version, and choose Options.

Tick MetaHuman Creator Core Data (about 5.75 GB) and click Apply.

docs.title: Step 3: Enable the MetaHuman Creator Plugin
docs.text: In the editor, open Edit → Plugins, search for meta, tick MetaHuman Creator (marked Beta), and click Restart Now.

docs.title: Step 4: Add a MetaHuman Character Asset
docs.text:
In the Content Browser, create a folder called MetaHuman. Open it, right-click empty space, and choose MetaHuman → MetaHuman Character.

Note: Epic's docs suggest naming these assets with an MHC_ prefix, for example MHC_Sunita. Rename before you build more on top of it.

docs.title: Step 5: Open Creator and Pick a Preset
docs.text:
Double-click the asset to open MetaHuman Creator. The left toolbox has seven tabs: Presets, Import, Head & Body, Materials, Hair & Clothing, Export, Assembly.

Open Presets, click a character, and press Apply Preset.

docs.title: Step 6: Choose Hair and Clothing
docs.text:
Open Hair & Clothing. The Selection sub-tab lists hairstyles, eyebrows, and other grooms — click one to apply it.

The Details sub-tab holds the overrides: hair color, roughness, whiteness, lightness, dye color, and the outfit's primary and secondary colors.

Warning: A red "Video memory has been exhausted … over budget" line in the viewport means the preview is using more VRAM than the GPU has (an 8 GB card can hit this). Try lowering the viewport rendering quality profile, close other GPU-heavy apps, and avoid downloading 8K textures until you need them. If it persists, restart the editor.

docs.title: Creating a Level Sequence
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A Level Sequence is the container for cinematic animations in Unreal Engine. It holds camera tracks, character tracks, and the timeline for rendering video.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. In the main toolbar, click the Cinematics icon (film strip icon, near the Play button).

  2. Select Add Level Sequence.

  3. Enter a name (e.g., Intro_Sequence) and click Save.

  4. The Sequencer panel opens at the bottom of the editor, showing a timeline with frame markers.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: Press Ctrl + Shift + S to save all assets before closing the editor.

docs.title: Creating a Physics Asset
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A Physics Asset builds collision bodies for a skeleton's bones, so simulated Chaos Cloth (and ragdoll physics) can collide with the character's body instead of clipping through it. This guide covers generating a new Physics Asset for a skeletal mesh, reviewing the auto-generated collision bodies, and regenerating an individual body after adjusting a bone.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Physics Asset Field
docs.text: In the Skeletal Mesh editor, open the Asset Details panel and scroll to the Physics section. If no Physics Asset is assigned yet, the Physics Asset field shows None.

docs.title: Step 2: Name and Save the New Asset
docs.text:
Create a new Physics Asset from this field. In the Save Asset As dialog, choose a destination folder and a name for the asset — for example, SKM_VroidBoyBlue001_PhysicsAsset — then click Save.

Note: If a physics asset already exists in the destination folder, give the new one a distinct name so you don't overwrite it.

docs.title: Step 3: Confirm the Source Skeletal Mesh
docs.text: A Pick Skeletal Mesh dialog lists the skeletal meshes in the project. Select the mesh the Physics Asset should be generated from (for example, SKM_VroidBoyBlue001).

docs.title: Step 4: Configure Body Creation and Create the Asset
docs.text:
The New Physics Asset dialog controls how collision bodies are generated:

  • Min Bone Size — 20.0.
  • Primitive Type — Capsule.
  • Vertex Weighting Type — Dominant Weight.
  • Include Child Bones, Auto Orient to Bone, and Walk Past Small Bones — checked.
  • Create Body for All Bones — unchecked (only bones large enough or weighted enough get a body).
  • Disable Collisions by Default — checked, under Constraint Creation.

Click Create Asset.

docs.title: Step 5: Review the Generated Physics Asset
docs.text:
The new Physics Asset opens in its own editor tab, with capsule collision bodies generated for the main skeleton bones. The viewport stats confirm the result — for example, 14 Bodies, 14 Primitives (14 Capsules), and 13 Constraints (6 Cross Constraints).

Note: If you need to regenerate the bodies with different settings, adjust the Body Creation options in the bottom-right panel and click Generate All Bodies.

Note: These capsule bodies are an approximation. For collision that follows the mesh's exact shape instead, see Generating a Skinned Triangle Mesh Collision Primitive.

docs.title: Step 6: Adjust a Bone in the Skeleton Tree
docs.text: If a generated collision body doesn't line up correctly with a limb, go back to the Skeletal Mesh editor and reposition the underlying bone — see Moving a Body Part for the full steps.

docs.title: Step 7: Review and Regenerate the Affected Body
docs.text:
Switch back to the Physics Asset editor tab. Select the same bone in its Skeleton Tree to highlight the corresponding collision body in the viewport, and check its properties in the Details panel — Mass, Linear Damping, Angular Damping, Enable Gravity, and Physics Type.

Use the Center Of Mass Offset gizmo to fine-tune the body's pivot if needed, then click Re-generate Bodies (or Generate All Bodies) to rebuild collision for the adjusted bone.

Note: A Physics Asset created here can be assigned as the collision source when applying Chaos Cloth simulation.

docs.title: Creating a Pose Asset from an Animation Sequence
Creating a Pose Asset from an Animation Sequence
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A Pose Asset can be generated directly from an already-open Animation Sequence using Current Animation, instead of building one from scratch. This example uses SKEL_silber_anim_surprised, the two-keyed animation built in Creating an Animation from a Pose — because that source animation has only two keys (a start key at 0 and an end key at 1), Current Animation produces exactly two poses to clean up here, not one per every sampled frame.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Source Animation
docs.text: In the Content Browser, open the source Animation Sequence — here, SKEL_silber_anim_surprised.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Pose Asset
docs.text: Click Create Asset → Create PoseAsset, then select Current Animation ("Create Animation from current animation") rather than Current Pose, which would only capture whatever single frame the playhead was on.

docs.title: Step 3: Name and Create the Asset
docs.text: A Create a New Animation Asset dialog opens, prompting you to select a destination folder and confirm a name. The screenshot shows the VroidSilber folder selected and the name field pre-filled as SKEL_silber_Pose_surprised. Click OK.

docs.title: Step 4: Check the Generated Poses
docs.text:
The new Pose Asset opens automatically, with one pose per key in the source animation — Pose_0 and Pose_1. Select Pose_0 and check its value in the curve list on the right: it reads 0.000000, matching the animation's start key.

Note: If your source animation has many sampled frames instead of just a couple of hand-placed keys, Current Animation generates one pose per frame instead of two — see Isolating a Single Pose in a Pose Asset for cleaning up that larger case.

docs.title: Step 5: Delete the Unwanted Pose
docs.text: Right-click Pose_0 (the 0.000000 pose) and select Delete.

docs.title: Step 6: Rename the Remaining Pose
docs.text: Only Pose_1 remains, holding the curve's 1.000000 value. Right-click it, select Rename, and give it a meaningful name — for example, Surprised.

docs.title: Step 7: Check the Final Pose
docs.text: Change the pose's Weight slider to confirm it blends correctly — setting it to 0.5 here shows the expression at half strength.

docs.title: Creating a Project
docs.text:
1. Select a project category (for example, Games).

  2. Select a template (for example, Third Person).

  3. Set the Project Defaults:

    • Blueprint or C++
    • Target Platform
    • Quality Preset
    • Starter Content (optional)

  4. Set the Project Location.

  5. Enter the Project Name.

  6. Click Create.

docs.title: Creating a Video Project
docs.text: Create a new Unreal Engine project configured for film and video production.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open Unreal Engine and launch the Unreal Project Browser.

  2. Select Film / Video & Live Events in the left category panel.

  3. Select Blank under project templates.

  4. Configure the project settings:

    • Enable or disable Starter Content as needed.
    • Enable Raytracing if required.
    • Set the project location.
    • Enter a Project Name.

  5. Click Create.

docs.title: Note
docs.text: The Film / Video & Live Events category configures Unreal Engine with tools optimized for cinematic production workflows.

docs.title: Deleting a Project
docs.text:
Follow these steps to delete an Unreal Engine project.

Warning

Deleting the project folder permanently removes the project. Make sure you have a backup if needed.

  1. Launch Unreal Engine.

  2. In the Unreal Project Browser, select the project you want to delete, then click Browse.

  3. In File Explorer, delete the project folder.

    Default location (example):
C:\Users\<username>\Documents\Unreal Projects\

  4. Restart Unreal Engine.

    The project will no longer appear in the Project Browser.

docs.title: Displaying Collisions in the Skeletal Mesh Editor
Displaying Collisions in the Skeletal Mesh Editor
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This shows the collision bodies a Chaos Cloth simulation is currently using, drawn directly on the mesh in the Skeletal Mesh editor's viewport. Use this to check collision fit while previewing the simulation, without switching to the Physics Asset editor.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Character Show-Flags Menu
docs.text: In the Skeletal Mesh editor, click the eye icon in the viewport toolbar to open the Character menu.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Clothing Submenu
docs.text: Hover over Clothing in the Scene Elements list to open its flyout submenu.

docs.title: Step 3: Enable the Collisions Flag
docs.text:
Under Cloth Asset Visualization, check Collisions ("Draws the collision bodies the simulation is currently using"). Collision capsules appear directly on the mesh in the viewport, following the simulated cloth.

Note: The same submenu has other Cloth Asset Visualization flags worth knowing about — Max Distances and Backstops visualize the weight maps painted in Applying Chaos Cloth Simulation, and Physical Mesh Wireframe shows the simulation mesh itself. The Sections Display Mode group above it (Show All Sections, Show Only Cloth Sections, Hide Only Cloth Sections) controls which mesh sections render at all, independent of these visualization flags.

docs.title: Displaying Plugin Content in the Content Browser
Displaying Plugin Content in the Content Browser
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Some plugins, such as VRM4U, ship their own Content folder with assets you may want to browse or reference directly. The Content Browser hides plugin content by default.

docs.title: Step 1: Open View Options
docs.text: In the Content Browser, click the settings icon in the toolbar to open its view options.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable Plugin Content
docs.text: Under Show, check Plugin Content ("Show plugin content in the view?").

docs.title: Result
docs.text: A Plugins entry appears in the Content Browser's folder tree alongside your project's own Content folder, letting you browse assets shipped inside installed plugins.

docs.title: Exploring the LookAtPOI Level's Look-At Demos in Game Animation Sample
Exploring the LookAtPOI Level's Look-At Demos in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Game Animation Sample project includes a standalone LookAtPOI_Level that showcases the look-at head/eye-tracking system across three self-contained demos: Loops, Patrol & Move, and Gestures. This is a different, more in-depth way to explore the look-at system than the simple purple-circle demo built into the hub — see Watching a Target Point for that simpler version. LookAtPOI_Level lives outside the hub as its own level asset and lets you inspect each look-at scenario individually, including live parameter tweaking.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the LookAtPOI_Level Asset
docs.text:
In the Content Browser, navigate to Content → Levels → Level Prototyping, and double-click LookAtPOI_Level to open it.

Note: This folder holds several standalone demo levels you can open directly, separate from the hub's signposted navigation (see Moving to the NPC Level and Moving to the Ragdoll Level for that hub-based approach).

docs.title: Step 2: Press Play to See the Demo Overview
docs.text: Press Play. The level places three characters side by side on the floor, each labeled with the demo it represents: Patrol & Move, Loops, and Gestures.

docs.title: Step 3: Click a Label to Select a Demo
docs.text:
Once you are playing, an on-screen prompt reads "LClick Labels over the characters to control LookAt." Left-click the label above a character to zoom the camera into that character's demo.

All three demos are loaded and running at the same time — clicking a different label just re-frames the camera onto that character, it does not restart the level or reload the demo you were previously viewing.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
The Loops demo cycles a character through different idle animation loops while its head and eyes track a moving target as you orbit the camera.

  • Rotate the camera by moving the mouse; scale (zoom) with the mouse wheel.
  • Select Loop dropdown switches which animation loop plays — Idle, Sprint, Walk, or Crouch.
  • Enable Look At checkbox toggles the tracking on and off.
  • About Loops Sample opens an info panel explaining the demo, including how to live-tweak its solver settings by opening the DA_LookAtPOI_Loops data asset and setting DevMode = True.

docs.title: Patrol & Move
docs.text:
The Patrol & Move demo has an NPC walk a patrol route between points while a nearby character's look-at tracks it as it moves.

  • Patrol Move Type dropdown selects the movement pattern (observed set to Alternating, which walks the NPC back and forth between points).
  • Move button starts the patrol.
  • Reset Location button returns the NPC to its starting position.
  • Enable Look At checkbox toggles the tracking.
  • About Patrol Sample opens an info panel about the demo.

docs.title: Gestures
docs.text:
The Gestures demo plays a selectable gesture animation on a character while a nearby character's look-at tracks it.

  • Select Gesture dropdown picks which gesture to play (observed set to Come On In); a tooltip below it reminds you to select a gesture and hit Play.
  • Enable Additive Pose Fix checkbox toggles an additive pose correction option.
  • Enable Look At checkbox toggles the tracking.
  • About Gestures Sample opens an info panel about the demo.

docs.title: Shared Controls
docs.text:
Every demo shares the same Enable Look At checkbox and an About [Demo] Sample info button. Each demo also has a player-pawn toggle button in its bottom-right corner: it reads Spawn Player while you are spectating, and switches to Spectator Mode once you have spawned a controllable pawn, letting you switch back to a free spectator camera.

Note: No on-screen prompt was captured for navigating back out to the three-character overview after zooming into a demo — if you do not see one, try scrolling the mouse wheel out or pressing Spectator Mode first.

docs.title: Finding an Animation Asset
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A character skeleton like SKEL_kento-blue accumulates many similarly named assets — A_face_kento-blue, POSE_face_kento-blue, POSE_retarget_kento-blue, and so on. Unreal offers more than one way to track down the specific Animation Sequence you need.

docs.title: Step 1: Check a Pose Asset's Source Animation Field
docs.text:
If you already have a Pose Asset open, such as POSE_face_kento-blue, its Asset Details panel has a Source Animation field under the Source category. It names the Animation Sequence the pose asset was built from — for example A_face_kento-blue.

Note: This screenshot only shows the field's value, not the result of clicking the small browse/target icon next to it. If your version of the editor has one, it should jump straight to that asset in the Content Browser — but that click isn't captured here.

docs.title: Step 2: Browse the Content Browser
docs.text:
Open the Content Browser and navigate to the character's asset folder — in this example, Content → VroidKento. Animation Sequences appear as thumbnails alongside related assets (Pose Assets, IK rigs, mannequins).

Note: The screenshot shows the Search VroidKento filter box empty — the asset here was located by browsing the folder's thumbnails, not by typing a name into the filter.

docs.title: Step 3: Use the Asset Browser Panel Inside an Editor
docs.text:
Any already-open Animation Sequence, Skeletal Mesh, or Pose Asset editor docks an Asset Browser panel (bottom-right by default). It lists other assets that share the same skeleton — here, A_face_kento-blue, a preview variant, and two Pose Assets — so you can switch between related assets without leaving the current editor.

Note: As in Step 2, the Search Assets box in this panel is also empty in the screenshot. Filtering by name is available in both panels, but neither screenshot demonstrates it being used.

Note: For more on how a Pose Asset's Source Animation relates to its baked pose values, see Understanding Pose Weights vs. Curve Values.

docs.title: Fixing the Missing Third Person Template
Fixing the Missing Third Person Template
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The New Project dialog shows only Blank, even under the Games tab — Third Person, First Person, Top Down, and the other templates are missing.

docs.title: Cause
docs.text: This isn't a UI issue — the Third Person template itself isn't installed on your machine. In the Epic Games Launcher install, template and starter-content packs are optional components that can get skipped or dropped during install or update. When that happens, the templates disappear from the New Project dialog.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
1. Open the Epic Games Launcher and go to your Library. Find your Unreal Engine version.
  2. Click the dropdown arrow (or gear/options icon) next to Launch and choose Options.
  3. Make sure Templates and Feature Packs is checked (sometimes labeled as additional feature/target packs), then click Verify (or Update) to redownload the missing files.
  4. Once it finishes, relaunch Unreal Engine and open New Project → Games tab again. Third Person, First Person, Top Down, Vehicle, and the other templates should now appear alongside Blank.

docs.title: If That Doesn't Work
docs.text:
If Verify doesn't restore the templates, a full uninstall and reinstall of the engine is the more forceful fallback.

Note: Your projects are safe during this — they're stored separately in your Unreal Projects folder, not inside the engine install.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Missing templates choice when opening UE5 project browser – Epic Developer Community Forums
  • Updated game templates for Unreal Engine 5.6—available now
  • Third Person Template in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.8 Documentation

docs.title: Focusing the Camera on the Face
Focusing the Camera on the Face
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Focusing on an Object works on individual bones too, not just whole actors — useful for framing a close-up of the face while reviewing facial animation curves.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the Head Bone
docs.text: In the Skeleton Tree search box, type head to filter the list down to the head bone, then select J_Bip_C_Head.

docs.title: Step 2: Focus the Camera on It
docs.text: Press F. The camera frames and orbits around the selected bone instead of the whole character.

docs.title: Step 3: Deselect to Hide the Manipulator
docs.text: Click any blank space in the viewport to clear the selection and hide the manipulator gizmo, leaving an unobstructed view of the face.

docs.title: Step 4: Enable Distance Based Camera Speed
docs.text: At this close zoom range, enable Distance Based Camera Speed in the viewport's camera speed dropdown (top toolbar) so mouse-driven camera movement scales sensibly instead of feeling too fast or too slow.

docs.title: Focusing on an Object
docs.text: Move the camera to the selected object.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Select an object in the Viewport or Outliner.
  2. Press F.

docs.title: Focusing the Play Range in the Curve Editor
Focusing the Play Range in the Curve Editor
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Curve Editor has two framing shortcuts for the current play range, depending on whether you want the curve to fill the view or keep some breathing room around it.

docs.title: Before Framing
docs.text: By default, the curve may only fill part of the visible area, or extend past it.

docs.title: Press A to Maximize the Play Range
docs.text: Press A to frame the play range so it fills the entire width of the graph area, with no margin before the start or after the end.

docs.title: Press F to Add Space Around the Play Range
docs.text: Press F to frame the play range with a small margin of space before the start position and after the end position.

docs.title: Generating a Skinned Triangle Mesh Collision Primitive
Generating a Skinned Triangle Mesh Collision Primitive
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A Skinned Triangle Mesh primitive follows the exact shape of the character's skinned mesh, instead of approximating it with capsules. Use it where the simple auto-generated bodies from Creating a Physics Asset are too coarse — for example, tight cloth collision against a detailed silhouette — at the cost of more expensive collision checks than a capsule.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Physics Asset Editor
docs.text: Open the Physics Asset editor for your character, either an existing one or a new empty one — see Creating a Physics Asset for how to create one.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Advanced Primitives Menu
docs.text: Right-click in the viewport to open the context menu.

docs.title: Step 3: Generate the Skinned Triangle Mesh
docs.text:
Under Create Advanced Primitives, select Generate Skinned Triangle Mesh ("Generate a Skinned Triangle Mesh primitive from the current preview skeletal mesh.").

Note: The same menu section has Import ML Levelset Data, another advanced collision primitive type not covered here.

A new triangle-mesh body appears in the asset, matching the mesh's surface. You can keep it alongside or in place of the auto-generated capsule bodies from Creating a Physics Asset, depending on how much collision accuracy the character needs.

docs.title: Getting Back to the Default Character in Game Animation Sample
Getting Back to the Default Character in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide is specific to Epic's Game Animation Sample project. See Swapping the Character for how to switch to a specific character preset instead.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Game Animation Widget
docs.text: Play the game and walk your character onto the Game Animation Widget plate to open the widget, then scroll to the Visual Override (Using child actor component in Pawns) section.

docs.title: Step 2: Double-Click Any Character
docs.text:
Double-click any character thumbnail — regardless of which one — to reset your character back to the default, UEFN Mannequin.

Note: A single click swaps to that character instead (see Swapping the Character); double-clicking any thumbnail always reverts to the default, no matter which one you double-click.

docs.title: Importing a VRM Character
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This requires the VRM4U plugin to already be installed and enabled.

docs.title: Step 1: Create a Folder for the Character
docs.text: In the Content Browser, create a dedicated folder for the character, such as Content/AnimeCharacter.

docs.title: Step 2: Import the VRM File
docs.text: Drag and drop your exported .vrm file into this folder. Keep the default settings in the import window and click Import.

docs.title: Step 3: Review the Generated Assets
docs.text:
VRM4U automatically generates:

  • A Skeletal Mesh
  • Pre-configured Materials & Textures (cell-shading ready)
  • An IK Retargeter asset
  • Blendshape / face animation assets

Select the generated Skeletal Mesh in the Content Browser and check its info tooltip's Morph Targets count to confirm the blendshapes came through — see Checking Morph Target and Pose Counts.

Note: To get the character walking and animating using the default mannequin animations, see Setting Up Animation for a VRM Character. If you're using the Game Animation Sample project specifically, see Retargeting a VRM Character to Game Animation Sample instead.

docs.title: Installing an Older Version of Unreal Engine
Installing an Older Version of Unreal Engine
Steps
docs.text:
1. Click here.

  2. Click here.

  3. Select the desired version.

docs.title: Installing the VRM4U Plugin
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

VRM4U is a third-party plugin that lets Unreal Engine import .vrm character files — such as one exported from VRoid Studio — as a skeletal mesh with materials, an IK retargeter, and blendshapes ready to use.

Warning: Do not drag a .vrm file into Unreal Engine before installing and enabling VRM4U, or the editor will crash.

docs.title: Step 1: Download VRM4U
docs.text: Go to the VRM4U releases page and download the zip archive that matches your Unreal Engine version — the filename encodes it, for example VRM4U_5_8_<date>.zip for UE 5.8. Extract the downloaded zip file.

docs.title: Step 2: Find Your Project's Root Folder
docs.text: In the Content Browser, right-click the Content folder and select Show in Explorer, then navigate up one level to the project's root folder (<YOUR-PROJECT-PATH>\).

docs.title: Step 3: Copy the Plugin into Your Project
docs.text:
Copy the extracted Plugins folder into your project's root folder.

Note: If a Plugins folder already exists in your project, copy just the VRM4U folder into your existing Plugins folder instead of replacing it.

docs.title: Step 4: Restart and Verify
docs.text:
Restart your Unreal Engine project. Go to Edit → Plugins and confirm VRM4U is listed and enabled.

Note: You may see a message reading "Plugin 'VRM4U' failed to load because module 'VRM4UCaptureEditor' could not be loaded." Closing this dialog and continuing is fine — the main VRM4U import functionality still works even if this optional submodule fails to load.

Note: Some workflows also enable Unreal's built-in OSC (Open Sound Control) plugin alongside VRM4U, to send or receive real-time facial tracking data from external tools. This is not required for a basic VRM import — only enable it if your pipeline needs live OSC streaming.

docs.title: Step 1: Search Fab for VRM4U
docs.text: In the Epic Games Launcher, open the Fab tab and search for VRM4U. Select dylo's VRM4U under Tools & Plugins — this is the standard listing for the plugin.

docs.title: Step 2: Check Engine Compatibility
docs.text: On the listing's product page, check the dropdown of supported Unreal Engine versions to confirm it covers your installed version.

docs.title: Step 3: Install the Plugin
docs.text:
Click Add to Library, then open the Epic Games Launcher's Library tab and install VRM4U directly into your project from there.

Note: If you downloaded the plugin manually instead of installing it through the Library tab, enable it the same way as Method 1's Step 4 — via Edit → Plugins.

docs.title: Isolating a Single Pose in a Pose Asset
Isolating a Single Pose in a Pose Asset
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Creating a Pose Asset from an Animation Sequence using Current Animation generates one pose per key in the source animation. A hand-keyed animation with just a start and end key produces two poses, easy to clean up — but a densely-sampled animation produces one pose per frame instead: 76 poses (Pose_0 through Pose_75) for a 75-frame clip, not the single named pose you usually want. Clean this up by deleting the poses you don't need and renaming the one you're keeping.

docs.title: Step 1: Find the Frame with the Curve Value You Want
docs.text: Check which pose corresponds to the frame where your target curve reaches its intended value — here, Pose_3 holds fcl_all_sorrow at 1.000000, matching the source animation's peak frame.

docs.title: Step 2: Select and Delete the Unwanted Poses
docs.text:
Select a range of poses you don't need — for example Pose_0 through Pose_2 — right-click, and choose Delete.

Repeat across the rest of the list — for example Pose_66 through Pose_75 — until only the pose you want to keep remains.

docs.title: Step 3: Rename the Remaining Pose
docs.text:
Right-click the pose you kept and select Rename to give it a meaningful name, such as Sorrow.

Note: The screenshots show multiple poses selected at once before deleting, which is faster than removing them one at a time — the exact selection method (Shift-click, Ctrl-click) isn't captured, but both are standard for multi-selecting list rows in Unreal Engine.

docs.title: Moving an Actor in Third Person
Moving an Actor in Third Person
docs.text: Control the default Third Person character during gameplay.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Click Play to start the game.

  2. Use W, A, S, and D to move.

  3. Press Space Bar to jump.

  4. Press Esc to stop the game.

docs.title: Moving, Rotating, or Resizing a Body Part
Moving, Rotating, or Resizing a Body Part
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide covers repositioning, rotating, or scaling an individual bone on a skinned character mesh, using the Skeleton Tree in the Skeletal Mesh editor. Use this when a bone needs a small manual adjustment — for example, straightening an arm before generating collision, fixing a joint that doesn't match a piece of clothing, or enlarging a hand that's too small.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Skeletal Mesh Editor
docs.text: Open your character's Skeletal Mesh editor and select the Skin tab. Make sure the Skeleton Tree panel is visible on the right.

docs.title: Step 2: Find the Bone
docs.text:
In the Skeleton Tree search box, type part of the bone's name to filter the list — for example, typing ar filters the list down to the arm bones.

Select the bone you want to adjust, such as J_Bip_L_UpperArm. A manipulation gizmo appears on the bone's pivot in the viewport.

docs.title: Step 3: Move or Rotate the Bone
docs.text:
Switch the gizmo mode with the standard Unreal Engine hotkeys — W for Move, E for Rotate, R for Scale — then drag the gizmo to adjust the bone. Every bone below it in the hierarchy transforms along with it.

For example, scaling J_Bip_L_Hand up enlarges the entire hand:

Note: If you make a mistake, press Ctrl+/ to reset the selected bone's transform, or Ctrl+Shift+/ to reset every bone back to the reference pose.

Warning: Moving a bone changes the character's reference pose. Anything generated from that pose — collision bodies on a Physics Asset, Chaos Cloth simulation, or retargeted animations — may need to be regenerated afterward to match.

docs.title: Moving the Playhead
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

An Animation Sequence editor's curve panel has two ways to set the current frame: dragging on the timeline itself, or typing an exact value.

docs.title: Dragging the Time Row
docs.text:
Click and drag anywhere in the ruler row that shows time (the row with the frame ticks, above the curve list) to scrub the playhead. The screenshot below shows the playhead sitting at frame 15, with its position tooltip — 15 (15.00) (20%) — displayed above the ruler.

Note: The screenshot captures the playhead's resting position and tooltip, not the mouse mid-drag. The dragging technique itself comes from this page's source memo rather than being directly visible in the image.

docs.title: Typing an Exact Frame Number
docs.text:
Next to the Filter search box (used to filter the curve list, not the timeline), there's a small numeric field. The same screenshot shows it holding 15, matching the playhead's position on the ruler — confirming this field jumps the playhead to a typed frame number.

Note: Only one screenshot exists for this topic, so it can't show a before/after of typing into this field. Its value simply matches where the playhead ended up.

docs.title: Moving to the NPC Level in Game Animation Sample
Moving to the NPC Level in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Game Animation Sample hub connects to several other levels through signposted portals on the ground — one of them leads to the NPC Level.

docs.title: Step 1: Play the Game and Find the Plates
docs.text: Press Play. You start in the main hub, surrounded by labeled plates and signs on the ground pointing to different areas and features.

docs.title: Step 2: Locate the "To NPCLevel" Sign
docs.text: Look for the blue arrow-shaped sign labeled To NPCLevel near the edge of the hub.

docs.title: Step 3: Walk Onto the Sign
docs.text: Walk your character onto the arrow to load the NPC Level, the same way walking onto the Game Animation Widget plate opens that widget (see Swapping the Character).

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The NPC Level loads with your character standing among several NPCs positioned around the level.

Note: To sit down on one of the benches yourself, see Sitting on a Bench in the NPC Level.

docs.title: Moving to the Ragdoll Level in Game Animation Sample
Moving to the Ragdoll Level in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Game Animation Sample hub connects to several other levels through signposted portals on the ground — one of them leads to the Ragdoll Level.

docs.title: Step 1: Locate the "To RagdollLevel" Sign
docs.text: Press Play. Look for the blue arrow-shaped sign labeled To RagdollLevel on the ground of the main hub.

docs.title: Step 2: Walk Onto the Sign
docs.text: Walk your character onto the arrow to load the Ragdoll Level.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The Ragdoll Level loads with a Controls panel listing the level's actions for keyboard and mouse (KB&M) and controller:

Action KB&M Controller Enter Ragdoll R X Get Up Space A Shove / Tackle E Y Takedown Left Mouse RT Spawn Dummy Aim + E Aim + Y Rotate Dummy Aim + E Aim + Y
