Note: Spawn Dummy and Rotate Dummy share the same input in this panel — aiming and pressing the button spawns a dummy if none is out yet, or rotates the existing one if there already is one.

docs.title: Navigating Viewport
docs.text: The Viewport is the panel where you view and edit your level.

docs.title: Look Around
docs.text:
1. Hold the right mouse button.
  2. Move the mouse.

The camera rotates in the direction you move the mouse.

docs.title: Move the Camera
docs.text:
1. Hold the right mouse button.
  2. Press the following keys:
Key Action W Move forward S Move backward A Move left D Move right Q Move down E Move up

docs.title: Move Faster or Slower
docs.text:
Hold the right mouse button, then use:

  • Mouse wheel up — Move faster
  • Mouse wheel down — Move slower

docs.title: Move While Holding Middle Mouse Button (Optional)
docs.text:
Hold the middle mouse button, then move the mouse.

The camera pans left, right, up, or down.

docs.title: Move and Turn with the Left Mouse Button (Optional)
docs.text:
1. Hold the left mouse button.
  2. Move the mouse forward or back to move the camera forward or backward.
  3. Move the mouse left or right to turn the camera left or right.

docs.title: Pan with Both Mouse Buttons (Optional)
docs.text:
Hold the left and right mouse buttons together, then move the mouse to slide the camera without rotating it. This is the same pan as holding the middle mouse button.

Note: These controls also apply in the Skeletal Mesh Editor (Persona) and Static Mesh Editor's preview viewports, not just the main Level Editor viewport.

docs.title: Opening a Curve in the Curve Editor
Opening a Curve in the Curve Editor
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

An Animation Sequence's compact curve list (in the bottom panel, under Curves) plots every curve at once, at a small scale. To work on one curve in more detail, open it in a dedicated Curve Editor tab.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Curve's Dropdown Menu
docs.text: In the Curves list, click the small ▼ Curve dropdown next to the curve you want — in this example, Fcl_EYE_Close_L. It opens a menu with Edit Curve, Convert To Metadata, Remove Curve, and Add Comment.

docs.title: Step 2: Select Edit Curve
docs.text:
Click Edit Curve. A new Curve Editor tab opens next to the animation's main tab, showing just that curve's keyframes plotted against value and time — here, Fcl_EYE_Close_L rising from 0 to 1 and back down to 0.

Note: These two screenshots capture opening the Curve Editor, not a keyframe or tangent actually being dragged. The Curve Editor's toolbar (Selection, Tangents, Snap, and framing tools) is visible for further editing, but that editing itself isn't shown here. To frame the play range once you're in here, see Focusing the Play Range in the Curve Editor.

Note: If a Post process Animation Blueprint status bar is visible above the curve panel, it's modifying curves on top of whatever you see in the Curve Editor — see Understanding the Post Process Animation Blueprint.

docs.title: Orbiting Around the Selected Object
docs.text: Rotate the camera around the selected object.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Select an object in the Viewport or Outliner.
  2. Press F to focus on the object.
  3. Hold Alt.
  4. Hold the left mouse button and move the mouse to orbit around the object.

docs.title: Optional
docs.text:
• Hold Alt + middle mouse button to pan.
  • Hold Alt + right mouse button to zoom.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Press F on the object first — it centers the orbit pivot on it, so Alt + left mouse button drag spins cleanly around it instead of some far-off point.
  • The Orbit toggle button in the viewport toolbar (near the camera-speed controls) lets you orbit with a plain left mouse button drag once enabled — handy if you don't want to hold Alt.

docs.title: Placing a Character Blueprint in the Scene
Placing a Character Blueprint in the Scene
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the Content Drawer (Ctrl + Space).

  2. Navigate to the asset's Blueprints → Characters folder.

  3. Locate the character Blueprint file (blue icon). For the Anime Character Pack, this is bp_AnimeCharacter.

    Note: Use the Blueprint file, not the raw Skeletal Mesh (SK_...). The Blueprint includes animation support and character logic.

  4. Click and drag the Blueprint into the Viewport and release to place the character.

  5. If the character is facing backward, rotate it 180°:

    1. Select the character in the Viewport.
    2. Press E to activate the Rotate tool.
    3. In the Details panel under Transform → Rotation, set Z to 180 and press Enter.

docs.title: Player Movement Controls in Game Animation Sample
Player Movement Controls in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

These are the default keyboard controls for moving and traversing obstacles in the Game Animation Sample project.

Action Key Move (W A S D) Running is the default movement state — no key is held to run Toggle Walk / Run Left Ctrl (Right Shoulder Button on a controller) Sprint Hold Left Shift while moving forward Crouch C (while stationary or walking) Slide Press C while sprinting forward (W + Left Shift + C) Jump / Vault Space (while moving or on the ground) Ledge Catch Press or hold Space while falling near a ledge

Note: Walking is not a hold-to-walk key. Press Left Ctrl (or the controller's Right Shoulder Button) to toggle between the walk and run movement modes — the character stays in that mode until you toggle it again.

Note: Ledge Catch triggers automatically — press or hold Space as your character falls near a ledge, and it grabs on instead of falling past it.

docs.title: Renaming a Blueprint Project
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Reference Video: UE5 Quick Tip 24: 3 Steps to Correctly Rename Your Projects by WorldofLevelDesign

Renaming a project's folder alone breaks it — Unreal Engine also needs the .uproject file and a few config entries updated to match. This applies to Blueprint projects only; C++ projects need additional code references updated too.

docs.title: Step 1: Rename the Outer Project Folder
docs.text:
In the Epic Games Launcher, go to Library, right-click the project, and select Show in Folder. Go up one directory level and rename the project folder itself.

Note: Keep project names under 20 characters, and use underscores instead of dashes.

docs.title: Step 2: Rename the .uproject File
docs.text: Open the renamed project folder. Locate the .uproject file (for example, OldName.uproject) and rename it to match the folder's new name exactly.

docs.title: Step 3: Update DefaultEngine.ini
docs.text:
Open Config/DefaultEngine.ini inside the project folder and update three entries to the new name:

  • Under [URL], update GameName=YourNewName.
  • Under [/Script/Engine.Engine], update both references to the old project name.

Save and close the file.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: Double-click the .uproject file to launch the renamed project. The Epic Games Launcher automatically updates to show the new name.

docs.title: Resetting Viewport View
docs.text: Use these methods to restore the Viewport to a normal view.

docs.title: Return to Perspective view
docs.text:
1. Click the view mode selector in the top-left corner of the Viewport.
  2. Select Perspective.

This restores the standard 3D view.

docs.title: Reposition the camera
docs.text:
1. Hold the right mouse button.
  2. Press W, A, S, D, Q, or E to move the camera.
  3. Move the mouse to adjust the viewing angle.

This lets you manually return to the desired view.

docs.title: Restore focus to an Actor (optional)
docs.text:
1. Select an Actor.
  2. Press F.

The Viewport centers on the selected Actor.

Note: This focuses the camera on an Actor. It does not restore a default Viewport position.

docs.title: Restore default editor layout (if Viewport is missing)
docs.text:
1. Click Window → Load Layout → Default Editor Layout.

This restores the default Viewport and panel layout.

docs.title: Retargeting a VRM Character to Game Animation Sample
Retargeting a VRM Character to Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide binds an imported VRM character to the Game Animation Sample project's animation system, using its tag-based retargeting setup rather than copying an Animation Blueprint by hand.

Reference Video: Anime Character to Game Animation Sample in Unreal Engine 5 by Code With Ro

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
Complete these first:

  1. Exporting a Character as VRM
  2. Installing the VRM4U Plugin
  3. Importing a VRM Character

docs.title: Step 1: Duplicate the Sandbox Character Blueprint
docs.text:
1. Open World Settings (Window → World Settings).
  2. Under GameMode Override, find Default Pawn Class (CBP_SandboxCharacter). Click the magnifying glass icon next to it to locate it in the Content Browser, under Content → RetargetedCharacters.
  3. Select one of the existing character Blueprints, such as CBP_SandboxCharacter_Quinn, press Ctrl+D to duplicate it, and rename the copy — for example, BP_Test.

docs.title: Step 2: Assign Your Mesh and a Custom Tag
docs.text:
1. Double-click your new Blueprint to open it.

  2. Select the Mesh component in the Components panel, then in the Details panel under Mesh → Skeletal Mesh Asset, select your imported character mesh.

  3. Scroll to Tags → Component Tags and replace the existing tag with a custom one, such as RTG_UEFN_to_Test.

    Warning: Component tags are case-sensitive. Use the exact same tag in the next step.

  4. Click Compile and Save.

docs.title: Step 3: Add a Retargeter Map Entry
docs.text:
1. With Mesh still selected, click the magnifying glass icon next to Anim Class (ABP_GenericRetarget) to locate it in the Content Browser, then double-click to open it.
  2. In the Details panel, find the Retargeter Maps array and click + (Add Element):
    • Key — your custom tag from Step 2, such as RTG_UEFN_to_Test.
    • Value — the IK Retargeter asset that VRM4U generated during import, such as RTG_UEFN_YourCharacter.
  3. Click Compile and Save.

docs.title: Step 4: Test Play
docs.text:
1. Return to the main level viewport, open World Settings → GameMode Override, and change Default Pawn Class to your new character Blueprint.
  2. Press Play to test locomotion, vaulting, and directional animations on your character.

docs.title: Sculpting a Custom Morph Target
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Sculpt Morph Target lets you reshape a Skeletal Mesh directly in the viewport by painting a new morph target with a brush — useful for deformations a bone can't produce alone, like pulling on a character's cheek.

docs.title: Step 1: Enable the Sculpting Plugin
docs.text: Sculpting requires the experimental Skeletal Mesh Morph Target Editing Tools plugin. Go to Edit → Plugins, search for morph, and enable it. Restart the editor when prompted.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Skeletal Mesh
docs.text: In the Content Browser, open the Skeletal Mesh you want to sculpt.

docs.title: Step 3: Create a New Morph Target
docs.text: Select the Morph tab, then click + in the Morph Targets panel and choose New Morph Target.

docs.title: Step 4: Name and Preview the Morph Target
docs.text: Name the new morph target, then set its Weight to 1.0 so the sculpt previews at full strength while you work.

docs.title: Step 5: Sculpt the Shape
docs.text:
Click Sculpt Morph Target.

Adjust the Brush Size, select a sculpting mode such as Move, then drag on the mesh to reshape it — for example, dragging on the cheek pulls it outward.

docs.title: Step 6: Undo Part of the Sculpt
docs.text:
If part of a sculpt looks wrong, switch the brush type to EraseSculptLayer and brush back over that area to remove the change.

Note: Click Apply to Asset when you're done to save the sculpt to the morph target.

docs.title: Setting Up Animation for a VRM Character
Setting Up Animation for a VRM Character
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

After importing a VRM character with VRM4U, retarget the default mannequin animations onto it, wire up an Animation Blueprint, and assign both to a playable character Blueprint.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Retarget Menu
docs.text: Navigate to the default mannequin animation folder, such as Characters/Mannequins/Animations/. Right-click ABP_Manny (or ABP_Quinn) and select Retarget Animation Assets.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure the Retarget Target
docs.text: In the retarget window, uncheck Auto-generate Retargeter. Set Target Skeletal Mesh to your imported VRM character mesh, and Retarget Asset to the IK Retargeter that VRM4U generated — it automatically matches A-pose alignment.

docs.title: Step 3: Select and Export Animations
docs.text:
Select the animations and blendspaces to transfer, such as:

  • Idle (MF_Idle or MM_Idle)
  • Walk/Run blendspace (BS_MM_WalkRun)
  • Jump start (MM_Jump)
  • Fall loop (MM_FallLoop)

Click Export Animations, choose a destination folder, such as Content/AnimeCharacter/Animations, and confirm the export.

docs.title: Step 4: Create the Blueprint
docs.text: In your character folder, right-click and select Animation → Animation Blueprint. Select your VRM character's skeleton and name the Blueprint, such as ABP_AnimeCharacter.

docs.title: Step 5: Copy the Event Graph
docs.text: Open your new Animation Blueprint alongside ABP_Manny. Copy the Event Graph nodes from ABP_Manny into your Blueprint's Event Graph, then right-click any missing variable warnings (Velocity, ShouldMove, IsFalling, and so on) and select Create Variable.

docs.title: Step 6: Copy the Anim Graph and Update References
docs.text:
Copy the Anim Graph state machine nodes from ABP_Manny. Open each state and update the animation references:

  • Locomotion / Idle — replace the default mannequin idle with your retargeted idle animation, and make sure Loop Animation is checked.
  • Walk/Run — replace with the retargeted BS_MM_WalkRun blendspace and wire it to Ground Speed.
  • Jump / Fall — replace with the retargeted jump and fall animations.

Note: If mesh distortion occurs during land transitions, try unlinking or removing the landing additive animation.

Compile and save the Blueprint.

docs.title: Step 7: Set the Mesh and Animation Class
docs.text: Open your playable character Blueprint, such as BP_ThirdPersonCharacter. Select the Mesh component and set Skeletal Mesh to your imported VRM character mesh, and Anim Class to your new Animation Blueprint.

docs.title: Step 8: Adjust the Capsule Component
docs.text: Select the Capsule Component and adjust its height and radius to match the smaller anime character scale — for example, lower Capsule Half Height to around 85–87. Adjust the mesh's vertical position slightly down so the character's feet sit precisely on the base of the capsule.

docs.title: Step 9: Test
docs.text: Compile, save, and press Play to test movement, jumping, and the cell-shaded visuals.

docs.title: Setting Up the MCP Plugin for Claude Code
Setting Up the MCP Plugin for Claude Code
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Unreal MCP plugin lets an AI coding agent, such as Claude Code, connect directly to the Unreal Editor over the Model Context Protocol — giving it awareness and control over Blueprints, PCG graphs, materials, actors, and levels.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Unreal Engine 5.8 or newer
  • Git for Windows or PowerShell
  • Claude Code installed and authenticated — see Installing Claude Code on Windows 11

docs.title: Step 1: Enable the Required Plugins
docs.text:
Open your project and go to Edit → Plugins. Search for and enable these three plugins:

  • Unreal MCP — enables Model Context Protocol communication.
  • Terminal — enables built-in terminal support for communicating with AI agents inside Unreal Engine.
  • Editor Tool Set — bridges the editor and the AI agent, granting it context and control over Blueprints, PCG graphs, materials, actors, and levels.

Click Restart Now when prompted to restart the Unreal Editor.

docs.title: Step 2: Turn On Auto Start Server
docs.text: Open Edit → Editor Preferences, then scroll to Model Context Protocol in the left sidebar. Check Auto Start Server so the MCP server starts automatically whenever the project opens.

docs.title: Step 3: Add a Terminal Startup Sequence
docs.text:
In Editor Preferences, scroll to the Terminal settings and add a startup sequence, replacing the path with your own project's:

set TERM=xterm-256color
cd "<YOUR-PROJECT-PATH>"
claude

Note: To find your project's local path, open the Content Drawer, right-click the Content folder, and select Show in Explorer. Copy the path up to the root project folder.

docs.title: Step 4: Generate the Client Configuration
docs.text:
Back in the Unreal Editor, open the console command bar (~ key) and run:

mcp.GenerateClientConfig claude

Note: If you're using Cursor, VS Code, or ChatGPT instead, replace claude with that client's identifier.

Verify that mcp.json was created in your project's root folder, then restart Unreal Engine once more.

docs.title: Step 5: Connect and Test the AI Agent
docs.text:
Open Tools → Terminal. If prompted to trust the directory, accept it. Confirm that Claude Code initializes and detects the local MCP server (port 8080 by default). Open or create a test level, then enter a prompt such as:

"Create 5 different colored cubes stacked on top of each other in my level."

Claude Code generates the static meshes, material instances, and actor positions directly in your viewport.

docs.title: What You Can Do Next
docs.text:
Once connected, an AI agent can help with:

  • Level design and asset placement — procedural generation, lighting setups, actor transforms.
  • Blueprint and C++ logic — generating nodes, debugging Blueprint logic, or writing C++ source code.
  • PCG (Procedural Content Generation) — constructing complex PCG graphs, such as city or terrain generators.
  • Material creation — setting up master materials, parameter groups, and material instances programmatically.

docs.title: Sitting on a Bench in the NPC Level in Game Animation Sample
Sitting on a Bench in the NPC Level in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

NPCLevel is a standalone demo level, opened directly from the Content Browser the same way as LookAtPOI_Level, that shows the Smart Object system driving NPC behavior — including NPCs automatically sitting on benches. This is different from reaching the NPC area through the hub's To NPCLevel sign (see Moving to the NPC Level); opening NPCLevel directly drops you straight into the standalone demo scene without going through the hub.

docs.title: Step 1: Open NPCLevel and Press Play
docs.text:
In the Content Browser, navigate to Content → Levels → Level Prototyping, double-click NPCLevel, and press Play. NPCs in the level are already using its BP_SmartBench actors — you will see some already seated on benches as soon as the level loads.

Note: These NPCs sit down on their own through Smart Object components (AIC_NPC_SmartObject) — this is AI-driven behavior, not the result of any player input.

docs.title: Step 2: Approach an Open Bench
docs.text:
Press W to walk close to the bench.

Note: The available screenshots only capture NPCs that are already seated through their own AI behavior — none of them show the player character in the act of sitting down. The step below is based on the author's own notes rather than an on-screen prompt.

docs.title: Step 3: Sit Down
docs.text: Press E to sit down on the bench.

docs.title: Spawning the Locomotor Robot in Game Animation Sample
Spawning the Locomotor Robot in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

By default, the level uses the Sandbox game mode and its usual playable character. Switching the level's GameMode Override to GM_Locomotor instead spawns a quadruped "locomotor" robot.

docs.title: Step 1: Note the Default State
docs.text: By default, GameMode Override is set to GM_Sandbox with Default Pawn Class SandboxCharacter, and the level spawns your usual character.

docs.title: Step 2: Change the GameMode Override
docs.text: Open World Settings (Window → World Settings) and set GameMode Override to GM_Locomotor. This game mode's Default Pawn Class is BP_Walker — the quadruped locomotor robot.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: The level now spawns the locomotor robot instead of the usual character.

docs.title: Swapping the Character in Game Animation Sample
Swapping the Character in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide is specific to Epic's Game Animation Sample project, which includes a set of swappable character presets and an in-game Game Animation Widget for testing them.

docs.title: Step 1: Play the Game and Find the Plates
docs.text: Press Play. In the sandbox level, look for the labeled plates on the ground, including one marked Game Animation Widget.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Game Animation Widget
docs.text: Walk your character onto the Game Animation Widget plate. A prompt appears, and the widget opens.

docs.title: Step 3: Scroll to Visual Override
docs.text: In the widget, scroll down to the Visual Override (Using child actor component in Pawns) section. This row lists the selectable character presets as thumbnails.

docs.title: Step 4: Select a Character
docs.text:
Hover over a thumbnail to see its asset name in a tooltip, then click it to swap your character to that preset.

Note: To reset back to the default character instead of picking a specific one, see Getting Back to the Default Character.

docs.title: Available Characters
docs.text:
• UEFN Mannequin — the default character.
  • Echo — a female character.
  • Twinblast — a male character.
  • Kellan — a MetaHuman character.
  • Manny — the UE Mannequin (male).
  • Quinn — the UE default mannequin (female).
  • UE4 Mannequin

docs.title: Understanding Pose Weights vs. Curve Values
Understanding Pose Weights vs. Curve Values
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A Pose Asset (such as POSE_face_kento-blue) lists each pose on the left and the curve values it drives on the right. It's easy to assume the two panels stay in sync — they don't.

docs.title: Selecting a Pose Shows Its Baked Curve Value
docs.text: Selecting a pose row, such as surprised, shows that pose's baked curve value on the right — for example, Fcl_ALL_Surprised at 1.000000.

docs.title: Changing a Pose's Weight Does Not Change Its Curve Value
docs.text:
The Weight field next to a pose only controls how strongly that pose blends into the viewport preview. Setting surprised's weight to 0.5 changes the preview, but Fcl_ALL_Surprised in the curve list on the right still reads 1.000000 — the pose's actual baked value hasn't changed.

Note: To actually change what a pose does, edit its source animation's curves and re-derive the pose from that — editing the Weight field only previews a blend, it doesn't author the pose.

docs.title: Understanding the Post Process Animation Blueprint
Understanding the Post Process Animation Blueprint
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

A skeletal mesh can have a Post Process Animation Blueprint assigned to it — a second Anim Blueprint layered on top of whatever animation is already playing, used here to drive facial expression curves (Fcl_ALL_*, Fcl_MTH_*) on top of the base animation.

docs.title: Recognizing It
docs.text: Opening an animation asset for a mesh with one assigned shows a status bar reading "Post process Animation Blueprint 'ABP_Post_<character>' is running. Post process modifies curves."

docs.title: Disabling and Editing It
docs.text:
• Click Disable to preview the animation without the post-process layer applied — this shows the plain baked animation, without whatever curve-driven modifications the Post Process Animation Blueprint adds.
  • Click Edit to open the Post Process Animation Blueprint itself.

Note: Assigning a Post Process Animation Blueprint to a skeletal mesh in the first place is done through the mesh's own asset settings, not from this status bar — that step isn't covered here.

docs.title: Understanding the Number of Sampled Frames Limit
Understanding the Number of Sampled Frames Limit
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

An Animation Sequence's Number of Sampled Frames and Playback Range Stop Time fields resist editing directly in the Details panel.

docs.title: Why It's Read-Only
docs.text: Number of Sampled Frames reflects the total frame count the animation was originally imported or created with — it's a read-out of the source data, not an editable setting. If it's stuck at 1 and grayed out, the sequence effectively contains only a single frame, usually from an import issue or how the source was keyed.

docs.title: Trimming or Extending Instead
docs.text:
• To play back only part of the sequence: wrap it in an Anim Montage and set a Start/End range on the segment — see Clipping an Animation with an Anim Montage.
  • To add more frames to the sequence itself: find the frame number control at the bottom-right of the graph editor, right-click it, and choose Append Frames at End of Sequence.

Note: The Append Frames option above wasn't tested directly in this session — it's included as documented Unreal Engine behavior, not something confirmed on screen here.

docs.title: Viewing the Read-Me and Its Release Notes in Game Animation Sample
Viewing the Read-Me and Its Release Notes in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The hub's Read-Me sign opens an in-game popup with a link to Epic's blog post covering what's new in the current release.

docs.title: Step 1: Find the Read-Me Sign
docs.text: In the hub, look for the green Read-Me sign among the other labeled plates.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Read-Me
docs.text: Walk your character onto the sign to open the Read Me window, which shows a welcome message and a link to the release's blog post.

docs.title: Step 3: Open the Blog Post in a Browser
docs.text: Open the URL shown in the Read Me window in a browser to read Epic's tech blog post about the release.

docs.title: Two Featured Functions in the Release
docs.text:
The blog post highlights new tech added in this update, including:

  • Physics Control Component & Physics Control Asset — the Physics Control Component drives a physics asset through linear and angular motors and can modify the state of physics bodies. The Physics Control Asset stores and edits reusable profiles for it, making it easier to build robust, physically animated characters.

  • Multi-Character Motion Matching & Pose Search Interaction Assets — new tools for performing pose searches across multiple Skeletal Meshes, plus Pose Search Interaction Assets for setting up multi-character animations with motion warp handling, searchable via Motion Match Multi functions.

docs.title: Watching a Target Point in Game Animation Sample
Watching a Target Point in Game Animation Sample
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Some areas of the sandbox include a look-at target — a white pole with a sphere head planted in the ground. Standing inside the purple circle around one of these targets makes your character continuously look toward it.

docs.title: Step 1: Enter the Purple Circle
docs.text: Walk your character into the purple circular area on the ground near a target point.

docs.title: Step 2: Watch the Character Track the Target
docs.text:
As you move around inside the circle, the character's head and eyes turn to keep looking at the target point instead of facing your movement direction.

Note: For a more in-depth look at this same look-at system, with live parameter tweaking across several scenarios, see Exploring the LookAtPOI Level's Look-At Demos.

docs.title: Zooming In and Out
docs.text: Zoom the viewport camera in or out.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Scroll the mouse wheel up to zoom in.
  2. Scroll the mouse wheel down to zoom out.

docs.title: Adding a Sticker to a Texture
Adding a Sticker to a Texture
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Sticker tool lets you drop a flat image — such as a logo — onto a clothing texture directly, without hand-painting it.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Texture Editor
docs.text: Click Edit Texture under Customize in the right panel for the item you want to edit.

docs.title: Step 2: Select the Layer
docs.text: In the left panel, select the texture layer you want to add the sticker to.

docs.title: Step 3: Place the Sticker
docs.text:
Select the Sticker tool from the toolbar, then choose the image file to use as a sticker. Drag it into position on the 3D preview.

Note: Sticker Mode offers 3D (drag directly on the model) and 2D (position on the flat UV canvas) placement, along with Sticker Opacity and Layer Opacity controls.

docs.title: Step 4: Apply the Sticker
docs.text: Click the sticker image while it is still selected to bake it into the texture layer.

docs.title: Step 5: Confirm the Result
docs.text: The sticker is now part of the texture and shows on the model. The updated item is also saved as a new entry under Custom Items.

docs.title: Applying the Manga-Style Comics Effect
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Comics post-processing effect in Photo Booth posterizes colors into flat bands and adds halftone-style dot shading, turning a captured photo into a print-style manga panel. It only applies to Photo Booth captures, not to the live viewport.

docs.title: Step 1: Open Post-Processing and Enable Comics
docs.text:
1. Open Photo Booth (camera icon, top right).
  2. In the left sidebar, select Post-processing.
  3. Check Comics.

docs.title: Step 2: Adjust Color Ratio and Thresholds
docs.text:
The Comics panel exposes Color Ratio, Min Threshold, Max Threshold, Tone Density, Tone Size, Oil Painting, and color pickers for Color, Inner Color, and Outer Color.

  • Color Ratio 0.5 — a light two-tone posterize that keeps most of the model's original color and shading.

  • Color Ratio 1.0 — a near-monochrome posterize with visible halftone dot shading in the hoodie's shadow.

  • Color Ratio 5.0 (version 1) — with Min Threshold 0.358 and Max Threshold 0.176, colors invert into high-contrast bands with hard white highlight streaks in the hair.

  • Color Ratio 5.0 (version 2) — raising Min Threshold to 0.833 crushes the face and body to a near-black silhouette, leaving only the eyes and hair highlights visible.

Note: Small changes to Min Threshold and Max Threshold make a large visual difference at high Color Ratio values — adjust in small increments.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: A lower Color Ratio (0.5–1.0) gives a print-manga panel look, while pushing Color Ratio to 5.0 and tuning the thresholds produces a high-contrast, ink-heavy panel style.

docs.title: Manga-Style Look Settings
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Look tab controls how VRoid Studio renders your model in real time. Combining these four settings — Outline, Rim Light, Shading, and Eye Alignment — pushes the default render toward a flat, print-style manga look instead of the smoother default anime shading.

docs.title: Set the Outline Width
docs.text:
Location: Look tab → Outline.

A width of 0.150 works as a solid starting point for Hair, Face, Body, and Accessory outlines — thick enough to read as a manga-style line without overwhelming the model.

docs.title: Set the Rim Light
docs.text:
Location: Look tab → Rim Light.

For a flat manga look, set Intensity and Concentration to 0 for Hair, Face, and Body. This removes the lit rim glow along backlit edges, which reads as a 3D render cue rather than a manga one.

Rim Light can also be tuned per part if you want a partial glow instead of removing it entirely:

docs.title: Set the Shading
docs.text:
Location: Look tab → Shading.

For a hard-edged, two-tone manga shadow, use a low Shading Area and high Shading Hardness — a negative Shading Area shrinks the shaded region, and a Shading Hardness near 1.000 gives it a crisp edge instead of a soft gradient. Shading Area and Shading Hardness can be tuned separately for Hair, Face, and Body.

For comparison, lowering Shading Hardness and raising Shading Area and Shade Softness on the Face produces a softer, more painterly shadow — closer to standard anime shading than the manga look:

docs.title: Align the Eyes
docs.text:
Location: Look tab → Eye Alignment.

Set Inner, Outer, Upper, and Lower all to 0 to keep the eyes in their neutral, unadjusted position.

docs.title: Changing Iris Color
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide explains how to change the iris color of a character in VRoid Studio.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Go to the Face tab → Irises panel.
  2. In the Color section on the right panel, select the scope: Both Eyes, R Eye, or L Eye.
  3. Click the color swatch to open the color picker and choose a new color.

Note: To set different colors for each eye, switch between the R Eye and L Eye tabs and pick a color for each.

docs.title: Checking a VRM Model Online
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

After exporting a character as VRM, you can check how it looks without opening Unreal Engine. Pick a method based on how much detail you need.

docs.title: Method 1: Check the Look Only
docs.text:
If you just want a quick look at the model with no detailed checks, drag and drop the VRM file onto the three-vrm viewer — this is the simplest option.

Note: For more detail, see the three-vrm examples list or pixiv's press release.

docs.title: Method 2: Check Expressions and Other Details
docs.text: To check details like facial expressions, use the VTubeMe VRM Viewer. It shows model info such as author, license, format, triangle count, and material count, plus Expressions sliders (blink, happy, angry, sad, relaxed, surprised, aa, ih, and more) for testing each expression individually. You can also drop a .vrma file to play an animation on the model, or try the built-in Idle and Walk presets.

docs.title: Method 3: Make Changes to the Model
docs.text: To actually modify the model, use Unreal Engine — see Importing a VRM Character.

docs.title: Creating Custom Glasses
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide walks through adding a pair of glasses from a built-in template, then adjusting its shape and color.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Accessories Tab
docs.text: Select the Accessories tab. If the model has no accessories yet, click Create New under Add Accessories.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose a Glasses Template
docs.text:
In the template picker, select the Glasses category icon, then pick a template, such as Glasses (Thick) or Glasses (Thin).

Note: The icons on the left of the picker switch between accessory categories — glasses are one of several, alongside categories such as hats. See Creating a Custom Hat for the same workflow applied to a hat.

docs.title: Step 3: Customize the Glasses
docs.text: The glasses are added to the Accessories list. Use Color to change their color, and the Parameters panel to adjust the frame, bridge, and temple shape — Frame (Thinner/Larger), Bridge (Thinner/Thicker), and Temple (Thinner/Thicker/Looser/Tighter), among others. Click Edit Texture to paint the texture directly instead.

docs.title: Creating a Custom Hat
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide walks through adding a hat from a built-in template, then adjusting its shape and color.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Accessories Tab
docs.text: Select the Accessories tab. If the model has no accessories yet, click Create New under Add Accessories.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose a Hat Template
docs.text:
In the template picker, select the Hats category icon, then pick a template, such as Cap, Top Hat, Hat, Witch Hat, or Army Cap.

Note: The icons on the left of the picker switch between accessory categories — hats are one of several, alongside categories such as glasses. See Creating Custom Glasses for the same workflow applied to glasses.

docs.title: Step 3: Customize the Hat
docs.text: The hat is added to the Accessories list. Use Color to change its color, and the Parameters panel to adjust its shape — for a top hat this includes Brim Position (Z), Brim Thickness, Brim Size, Brim Width (X/Z), and several Bend Brim and Wavy Brim sliders. Click Edit Texture to paint the texture directly instead.

docs.title: Creating a Custom T-Shirt
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide walks through creating a new T-shirt from a built-in template, then recoloring it in the Texture Editor.

docs.title: Step 1: Start a New Custom Top
docs.text: Select the Outfit tab, then Tops, then the Custom sub-tab. Click Create New under Custom Items.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose a T-Shirt Template
docs.text: In the Choose Template window, select the Tops category, then pick a T-shirt template, such as Extra Short Sleeved T-Shirt.

docs.title: Step 3: Open the Texture Editor
docs.text: A plain white T-shirt is created from the template. Click Edit Texture under Customize in the right panel.

docs.title: Step 4: Lock the Layer and Change the Color
docs.text: In the left panel, select the layer and lock it. Then pick a new Brush Color and paint over the shirt to change its color.

docs.title: Step 5: Save the New Item
docs.text:
The recolored T-shirt appears on the model. Save it as a new entry under Custom Items to keep it alongside the original.

Note: See Using Custom Templates for Tops for more on browsing template categories, and Adding a Sticker to a Texture to place a logo instead of a flat color.

docs.title: Deleting Hair Curve Control Points
docs.text:
In the Edit Preset screen, the curve editor under Hair Parameters → Curve lets you adjust the curve shape using control points.

  • Add: Click on the curve line to add a control point.
  • Delete: Left-click on a control point to delete it.

In the image below, the control point is highlighted with a red square.

docs.title: Editing Face Texture
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Skin Texture Editor
docs.text:
1. Click Face in the top menu bar.
  2. In the left sidebar, click the Skin icon.
  3. Under Custom Items, select the Skin item.
  4. Click the Edit Texture button in the right panel.

docs.title: Step 2: Edit the Texture
docs.text:
The Texture Editor opens. It has three main areas:

  • Left panel — Color Calibration settings: Skin Color, Shin Color, Shadow Color, and Blush Color.
  • Center left — A live 3D preview of the character's face.
  • Center right — The texture canvas displaying the face UV map, where you paint directly.

Use the brush settings on the right to adjust Brush Color, Brush Type, Brush Width, Brush Opacity, Pen Pressure Sensitivity, Drawing Style, Layer Opacity, and Drawing Mode. Paint on the texture canvas to customize the face texture.

docs.title: Editing Hair Texture
docs.text: Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Hairstyle Editor
docs.text:
1. Click Hairstyle in the top menu bar.
  2. In the left panel, select the hair part you want to edit (e.g., Front).
  3. Under Custom Items, select the desired hair item.
  4. Click the Edit Hairstyle button on the right panel.

docs.title: Step 2: Select a Hair Group or Part and Open the Material
docs.text:
1. In the Edit Preset screen, the left panel lists all hair groups and hair parts. Select the one you want to edit.
  2. On the right panel, find the Materials section.
  3. Click the arrow icon (▶) to the left of the Material label to open the material dropdown.

docs.title: Step 3: Open the Texture Editor
docs.text: 1. With the material expanded, click the Edit Texture button.

docs.title: Step 4: Edit the Texture
docs.text:
The Material Texture Editor opens. It has three main areas:

  • Left panel — Texture layers (Base, Highlights), Hair Group Bumpmap, and Color Calibration settings.
  • Center — A live 3D preview of the character alongside the texture canvas where you paint.
  • Right panel — Brush settings: Brush Color, Brush Type, Brush Width, Brush Opacity, Pen Pressure Sensitivity, Editing Mode, Layer Opacity, and Drawing Mode.

Paint directly on the texture canvas to customize the hair texture.

docs.title: Exporting a Character as VRM
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Exporting to VRM produces a single portable file that other applications — such as Unreal Engine via the VRM4U plugin — can import as a fully rigged character.

docs.title: Step 1: Prepare Your Character
docs.text: Adjust hair, body proportions, face shape, and clothing as desired.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Export Menu
docs.text: Click Export / Share in the top-right corner.

docs.title: Step 3: Choose Export as VRM
docs.text: Select Export as VRM.

docs.title: Step 4: Fill in the Metadata
docs.text: Fill in the required metadata fields, such as Title and Author.

docs.title: Step 5: Save the File
docs.text:
Click Export, then save the .vrm file to a location you can find later.

Note: To bring this character into Unreal Engine, see Installing the VRM4U Plugin and Importing a VRM Character.

docs.title: Recoloring Hair Using Shader Color
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This method lets you change the overall hair color while keeping the highlight patterns in the texture intact.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the Material Texture Editor for the hair part you want to recolor (see Edit Hair Texture).
  2. In the left panel, scroll down to Color Calibration.
  3. Expand Shader Color.
  4. Check the Base Color checkbox and click its color swatch to choose your desired hair color.
  5. Optionally, also check Shade Color to control the shadow/shading tone separately.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Shader Color → Base Color applies the color at the rendering level, so the painted texture patterns (highlight blobs, hair flow details) are preserved.
  • This is different from Color Calibration → Main Color, which tints on top of the existing texture color — causing unwanted color blending (e.g. brown over purple → reddish).
  • For simple recoloring, Shader Color is the recommended approach. Use an external image editor only if you need fine-grained control over the texture itself.

docs.title: Removing a Skin Mask
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Skin Mask hides the character's skin underneath clothing so it doesn't show through gaps in the mesh. Painting over the mask reveals skin in areas it currently hides.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Texture Editor
docs.text: Click Edit Texture under Customize in the right panel for the item you want to edit.

docs.title: Step 2: Switch to the Skin Mask Tab
docs.text: At the top of the Texture Editor, select Skin Mask, then select the layer in the left panel.

docs.title: Step 3: Sample the White Area
docs.text: Using the eyedropper tool, pick up the color from a white area of the texture.

docs.title: Step 4: Paint Over the Black Area
docs.text:
Paint over the black area with the sampled white color to remove the mask there.

Note: White areas of the Skin Mask show skin normally; black areas hide it. Painting a black area white removes the mask in that spot.

docs.title: Resizing Hair
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide explains how to shorten hair in VRoid Studio using the Resize tool.

docs.title: Step 1: Check the Current Hair Length
docs.text: Open your model in the Edit Preset screen. Identify the hair that needs resizing.

docs.title: Step 2: Select the Hair Group
docs.text: In the left panel, select the hair group you want to resize. The selected group is highlighted.

docs.title: Step 3: Select the Resize Tool
docs.text: Click the Resize tool in the toolbar. The selection outline and manipulator handles appear around the hair.

docs.title: Step 4: Pull Up the Green Manipulator
docs.text: Drag the green (Y-axis) manipulator upward to shorten the hair.

docs.title: Step 5: Confirm the Result
docs.text: The hair is now shorter. Verify the new length looks natural on the model.

docs.title: Resizing Pupil
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

This guide explains how to resize the pupil of a character in VRoid Studio.

The Iris Size (X) and Iris Size (Y) sliders in the Parameters section control the size of the iris, not the pupil. There is no slider to resize the pupil directly.

To make the pupil bigger or smaller, select a different preset from the left panel in the Face tab → Irises panel. Each preset has a different pupil size.

docs.title: Using Custom Templates for Tops
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Custom Items let you start a new clothing piece from one of VRoid Studio's built-in templates instead of building a mesh from scratch.

docs.title: Step 1: Start a New Custom Item
docs.text: Select the Outfit tab, then Tops, then the Custom sub-tab. Click Create New under Custom Items.

docs.title: Step 2: Choose a Template
docs.text:
In the Choose Template window, select the Tops category to browse the available base shapes, such as T-shirts, uniform vests, and hoodies.

Note: The left side of the Choose Template window also lists other categories — Dresses, Bottoms, Neck Accessories, Arm Accessories, and more — for starting custom items in those slots.

Note: See Creating a Custom T-Shirt for a full walkthrough that continues from this point through editing and recoloring the texture.

docs.title: Using a Guide to Draw a Texture
Using a Guide to Draw a Texture
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Exporting a UV guide lets you bring the model's wireframe into the Texture Editor as a semi-transparent reference layer, so you can draw a new design without losing track of where seams and panels line up.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Texture Editor
docs.text: Click Edit Texture under Customize in the right panel for the item you want to edit.

docs.title: Step 2: Select the Layer
docs.text: In the left panel, select the texture layer you want to export a guide from.

docs.title: Step 3: Export the Guide
docs.text: Right-click the layer and select Export Guide from the context menu.

docs.title: Step 4: Save the Guide Image
docs.text: In the save dialog, choose a location and save the guide image.

docs.title: Step 5: Import the Guide as a New Layer
docs.text:
• Use the layer list's import option and select the guide image you just saved.
  • The image is added to the layer list as a new layer, and its wireframe becomes visible on the model.

docs.title: Step 6: Rename the Layer and Lower Its Opacity
docs.text: Rename the new layer to something like "Guide", then reduce its Layer Opacity — for example, to around 30 — so it becomes a faint, semi-transparent overlay instead of covering the texture completely.

docs.title: Step 7: Create a Draft Layer
docs.text: Add a new layer above the guide layer to hold your artwork.

docs.title: Step 8: Move the Draft Layer Below the Guide
docs.text:
• Right-click the draft layer and select Move Down.
  • The draft layer now sits beneath the guide layer, so the guide's wireframe overlays your artwork as a semi-transparent reference while you draw.

docs.title: Step 9: Export the Layers for External Editing
docs.text: If you want to edit the texture in an external image editor, export each layer individually — the guide, the draft, and the base layer.

docs.title: Adding CoeiroInk Voices to YMM4
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

CoeiroInk (COEIROINK) is a free local AI text-to-speech engine that integrates directly with YMM4. It runs on your PC and connects via a local API, similar to VOICEVOX.

docs.title: What is CoeiroInk?
docs.text:
• Free TTS engine developed by Shirowani
  • Includes downloadable voice characters
  • Default port: 50032 (can run simultaneously with VOICEVOX on port 50021)
  • Available at https://coeiroink.com

docs.title: Step 1: Install CoeiroInk
docs.text:
1. Go to https://coeiroink.com and download the appropriate version:
    • Windows / CPU — recommended for most users
    • Windows / GPU — faster synthesis if you have an NVIDIA GPU
  2. Extract the downloaded ZIP file
  3. Run the .exe self-extractor inside to get the final folder
  4. Launch COEIROINKv2.exe

Note: The download is a ZIP containing a self-extracting EXE. You need to extract twice to get the final application folder.

Warning: engine.exe inside the CoeiroInk folder may be flagged as a virus by security software. If CoeiroInk fails to launch, check your security software's quarantine and manually restore engine.exe.

docs.title: Step 2: Set the Executable Path in YMM4
docs.text:
1. In YMM4, go to File → Settings
  2. Navigate to Voice synthesis → COEIROINK v2
  3. Click the folder icon and select COEIROINKv2.exe from your CoeiroInk folder
  4. Optionally enable "Run in background" — this launches CoeiroInk silently without opening its UI every time YMM4 generates a voice

docs.title: Step 3: Register a Character in YMM4
docs.text:
1. Go to File → Edit character
  2. Click the + button to create a new character
  3. Set the following:
    • Name: your preferred character name (e.g. Tsukuyomi)
    • Group: COEIROINK
    • Voice: select COEIROINK v2 / [character name] from the dropdown
    • Style: choose a style (e.g. れいせい = calm)
  4. Close the Character settings window

Note: If a newly installed CoeiroInk character doesn't appear in the voice dropdown, look for a refresh button in the voice list to reload available voices.

docs.title: Step 4: Launch CoeiroInk Before Using YMM4
docs.text: Before generating voices in YMM4, launch COEIROINKv2.exe first — unless you enabled "Run in background" in Step 2.

docs.title: Use the Voice in YMM4
docs.text:
Once registered, the character works like any other YMM4 character:

  • Select the character from the bottom bar and type dialogue to add voice items
  • Or use a scenario CSV file with the character name in Column A

docs.title: Terms of Use
docs.text:
When publishing videos that use CoeiroInk voices, you must include a credit in the video content or description. The required format is:

COEIROINK合成音声名

For example: COEIROINK つくよみちゃん

Check the individual voice character's terms for any additional requirements.

docs.title: Default Voice: Tsukuyomi-chan (つくよみちゃん)
docs.text:
CoeiroInk includes Tsukuyomi-chan as the built-in starter character with the following styles:

Style (JP) Meaning れいせい Calm おちゃめ Playful びっくり Surprised こわい Scary

Additional voices can be downloaded from https://coeiroink.com.

docs.title: Importing Voice Lines via Scenario File in YMM4
Importing Voice Lines via Scenario File in YMM4
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

YukkuriMovieMaker4 (YMM4) supports bulk voice generation by importing a scenario file (CSV or TXT). This lets you write all your dialogue in a spreadsheet and import it in one go, instead of typing lines one by one.

docs.title: CSV Format
docs.text:
The scenario file uses a simple two-column structure:

CharacterName,Dialogue text here
CharacterName,Another line of dialogue
Column Content A Character name (must exactly match the name registered in YMM4) B Dialogue / セリフ

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Yukkuri Reimu,Hello! Welcome to my channel.
YukkuriMarisa,Hey everyone, good to see you!
Yukkuri Reimu,Today we are going to talk about something interesting.
YukkuriMarisa,That sounds exciting! Let's get started.

Warning: The name in Column A must be identical to the registered character name in YMM4, including spaces (or lack thereof). For example: Yukkuri Reimu (with space) vs YukkuriMarisa (no space).

docs.title: Step 1: Create the CSV in Excel
docs.text:
1. Open Excel and enter character names in Column A, dialogue in Column B
  2. No headers — start data from row 1
  3. Save as: File → Save As → CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited)

Note: Save your scenario files to a dedicated folder, e.g. D:\<YOUR-FOLDER>\projects\creator\ymm

docs.title: Step 2: Import into YMM4
docs.text:
1. In YMM4, go to File → Open scenario file
  2. Navigate to your CSV file and select it
  3. If a character name is unrecognized, a dropdown will appear — assign the correct character manually
  4. Review the lines in the scenario editor
  5. Click Add to timeline to generate all voice items at once

docs.title: Result
docs.text: YMM4 will automatically generate voice clips and place them sequentially on the timeline. Each line becomes its own voice item assigned to the correct character.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• Supports .csv and .txt formats (shown in file dialog as Scenario file (*.csv;*.txt))
  • Long lines may affect timing — keep dialogue concise per line
  • Voice speed, pitch, and other settings are applied from each character's existing YMM4 configuration
  • Scenario files can be edited and re-imported to regenerate voice lines in bulk

docs.title: Installing YukkuriMovieMaker4
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

YukkuriMovieMaker4 (YMM4) is a free, portable video editing tool developed by 饅頭遣い, popular for creating Yukkuri commentary videos. It is not available on Steam — download it directly from the official site.

Requirements:

  • Windows 10 or 11
  • .NET Framework 4.7.2 or later
  • DirectX 11 compatible GPU

docs.title: Step 1: Download
docs.text:
1. Go to the official site and download the app:

    https://manjubox.net/ymm4/

  2. Click one of the following:

docs.title: Accessing Flashcard Deluxe Local Exports on Google Pixel
Accessing Flashcard Deluxe Local Exports on Google Pixel
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

On modern Android versions, the operating system restricts access to the /Android/data/ folder for security. Because Flashcard Deluxe exports to its own private directory, the files will not appear in the standard Files by Google app.

To find your files, you must use the hidden system "Files" tool instead of the standard app.

docs.title: ⚠️ Important: "Files" vs. "Files by Google"
docs.text:
While the icons look similar, they have different permission levels:

  • Files by Google (Colorful icon): Cannot access the /Android/data/ folder. Use this for general cleanup only.
  • Files (Blue folder icon): The only native way to access restricted app data folders on your Pixel.

docs.title: The Storage Path
docs.text: Flashcard Deluxe saves local exports to: Internal Storage → Android → data → com.orangeorapple.flashcards → files → Import Export

docs.title: Step-by-Step Guide
docs.text:
1. Open Settings: Navigate to Settings → Storage.
  2. Access the System Tool: Tap on Files.
  3. Choose the Right App: When the "Open with" prompt appears, select Files (the blue folder icon).
    • Note: If you select Files by Google here, the specific export folder will appear empty or hidden.
  4. Navigate to the Path:
    • Tap the Menu (≡) and select your Pixel (Internal Storage).
    • Navigate to: Android → data → com.orangeorapple.flashcards → files → Import Export.
  5. Bypass Permissions: If you see a message saying "The contents of this folder can't be displayed here," tap the View in Files button at the bottom of the screen.
  6. Move the File: Once you locate your deck, long-press it and select "Copy to..." to move it to a visible folder like Downloads for easier use.

docs.title: 💡 Quick Tips
docs.text:
• Show Internal Storage: If your Pixel doesn't appear in the sidebar, tap the three-dot menu (⋮) in the top right and select Show internal storage.
  • Streamline Exports: To avoid this process in the future, use the Email export option within the Flashcard Deluxe app to send the deck directly to yourself.

docs.title: Replacing a Pixel 9 Pro Fold Under the Extended Warranty Program
Replacing a Pixel 9 Pro Fold Under the Extended Warranty Program
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Google offers an extended warranty program for the Pixel 9 Pro Fold: if your phone is affected by an issue that impacts device function, Google may replace it for free for up to 3 years from the original purchase date. This guide follows the replacement request flow on Google's Japan help pages, so the screenshots are in Japanese.

Note: Eligibility, options, and steps vary by region and can change. Always check the official program page first.

docs.title: Step 1: Find the Program Page
docs.text:
If your phone has a problem — for example, a battery icon that shows a question mark while charging — searching the Google Pixel Community can lead you to the program.

The official page is titled Google Pixel 9 Pro Fold 延長保証プログラム (Google Pixel 9 Pro Fold Extended Warranty Program). Key points from it:

  • It applies to Pixel 9 Pro Fold devices affected by an issue that impacts device function.
  • Coverage runs for 3 years from the original purchase date at the retailer.
  • If your phone is affected, you may get a free replacement — online, at a Google Store, or through a walk-in repair center that approves an online replacement.
  • After receiving your phone, Google inspects it to confirm it qualifies before processing the replacement.
  • The replacement comes with 90 days of warranty, or the remainder of the original warranty, whichever is longer.
  • Back up your data first: Settings → System → Backup → Back up now.

docs.title: Step 2: Check Your Support Options
docs.text: Scroll down and click サポート オプションを確認する (Check Support Options), then go through the process.

docs.title: Step 3: Review the Next Steps
docs.text:
When you finish, a confirmation page lists what happens next:

  1. Check your email — the return instructions arrive there. It can take about 15 minutes to reach your inbox.
  2. Back up your device.
  3. Remove all accessories and the SIM card — chargers, cases, watch bands, and so on.
  4. Wait for the replacement to ship — Google emails you when it's sent.
  5. Return your original device by following the instructions in the confirmation email. The return deadline is 14 days.

docs.title: Step 4: Follow the Confirmation Email
docs.text:
Google Store sends a 交換注文の確認 (Replacement Order Confirmation) email. It confirms the replacement order and its estimated delivery date, then lists the 返品手順 (return steps):

  1. Print the return slip (RMA) attached to the email.
  2. Use the QR code in the email to print a shipping label at a participating convenience store or shop that handles Yamato Transport shipping — FamilyMart, a PUDO station, or a Yamato Transport office.
  3. Make sure the IMEI or serial number on your phone matches the number on the RMA slip.
  4. Back up your personal information.

docs.title: Step 5: Compare the Original and Replacement Devices
docs.text:
Scroll down in the email to see the 元のデバイス (original device) and 交換品デバイス (replacement device).

Note: You can't choose the model or color of the replacement. In this case, a Pixel 9 Pro Fold in Obsidian was replaced with a Pixel 10 Pro Fold in Moonstone.

docs.title: Step 6: Erase the Old Phone
docs.text:
If the old phone won't power on — for example, because the battery is dead — you can't erase it from the device itself. Use Google Find Hub instead: select the device, click Factory reset, then click Next and sign in to your Google Account.

If the phone is offline, erasing starts the next time it comes online.

Warning: A factory reset removes the phone from Find Hub and permanently erases its data. Wait until the replacement has arrived and your data has moved over — if automatic backups were on, you can restore from the last one onto the new phone.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
• Google Pixel 9 Pro Fold Extended Warranty Program
  • Google Find Hub

docs.text:
Token Meaning {+KC_XXX} Key press {-KC_XXX} Key release {+KC_ENT}{-KC_ENT} Enter key (sends a new line)

docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

The Keychron Q11 ISO (Layer 2) has two dedicated keys for these characters, highlighted in the layout below.

  • The ~ key is to the right of Shift on the bottom row.
  • The Esc* key is at the top-left of the number row. It is separate from the standard Escape key and has a backquote engraved on it.

docs.title: Type a Tilde

docs.title: Type a Backquote
docs.text:
Note: A Keychron Q11 firmware update changed the behaviour of Win + Esc* — it now opens Command Prompt instead of typing a backquote. Use the AutoHotKey workaround below.

Use an AutoHotKey script to remap Ctrl + ' to type a backquote:

^'::           ; Ctrl + '
{
    Send("``") ; sends one `
}

Note: In AutoHotKey, a single backtick is an escape character. Two backticks inside Send() are required to produce one literal backquote.

If Ctrl + ' does not work, open PowerToys → Keyboard Manager and check whether the key combination has been remapped.

1. Go to the Home screen and open your Friends list.
  2. Long-press on the account you want to delete.
  3. Select Delete.

docs.title: Recommended: Do Both Together
docs.text:
If you only block someone, they remain in your Friends list. To remove them completely, do both in this order:

  1. Block first.
  2. Then delete.

Note: Neither blocking nor deleting sends a notification to the other person.

docs.title: Adding a New Profile on Meta Quest 3
Adding a New Profile on Meta Quest 3
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Meta Quest 3 supports up to 3 additional profiles alongside the primary account (4 accounts total), making it easy to share your headset with household members while keeping saves and settings separate.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you begin, the person you're adding must:

  • Have their own Meta account. They can create one at meta.com or through the Meta Horizon mobile app.
  • Have the Meta Horizon app installed on their phone and logged in to their account.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Put on the headset and press the Meta button on your right controller to open the universal menu.
  2. Hover over the clock icon on the left side of the menu. When Quick Settings appears, select it.
  3. In the top-right corner of Quick Settings, select Settings.
  4. Select Accounts, then select Add Account in the top-right corner.
  5. An 8-digit code will appear on the headset screen.
  6. On the new person's phone, open a browser and go to meta.com/device, then enter the 8-digit code.
  7. Pass the headset to the new person (or continue yourself). They will complete initial setup on the headset, including:
    • Logging in to their Meta account
    • Adjusting headset fit
    • Setting up Guardian (the boundary system)

docs.title: Switch Between Profiles
docs.text:
1. Press the Meta button to open the universal menu.
  2. Select your profile picture on the far left.
  3. Select Switch Accounts in the top-right of the profile screen.
  4. Choose the account to switch to.

docs.title: Enable App Sharing
docs.text:
By default, additional profiles can only access apps they have purchased themselves. The primary account holder can enable App Sharing to let all profiles access their purchased apps:

  1. Go to Settings → Accounts.
  2. Enable App Sharing.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Additional profiles can save their own app progress, achievements, and leaderboard scores independently.
  • The primary account cannot be removed without performing a factory reset on the headset.
  • To remove a profile, go to Settings → Accounts, find the profile, and select the remove option. Locally saved data for that profile will be deleted (some games may retain cloud saves on that user's Meta account).

docs.title: Displaying Your Windows Screen on Meta Quest 3
Displaying Your Windows Screen on Meta Quest 3
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Using the official Windows App + Mixed Reality Link solution by Microsoft, generally available as of October 2025.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Meta Quest 3 or Quest 3S (on Horizon OS v81 or later)
  • Windows 11 PC
  • Both devices on the same Wi-Fi network
  • A Microsoft work or school account (personal accounts are not supported)

docs.title: Step 1: Set Up Your PC
docs.text:
1. On your Windows 11 PC, open the Microsoft Store.
  2. Search for and install Mixed Reality Link.
  3. Launch the app — it runs in the background and makes your PC discoverable by the headset.

docs.title: Step 2: Install Windows App on Your Headset
docs.text:
1. Put on your Quest 3 and open the Meta Horizon Store.
  2. Search for "Windows App" and install it.
  3. Launch the Windows App from your headset library.

docs.title: Step 3: Connect
docs.text:
1. In the Windows App, sign in with your Microsoft work or school account.
  2. Select "PC near me" from the menu.
  3. A pairing code will appear on your PC screen.
  4. Look at your keyboard from within the headset and tap Pair to confirm.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Up to 3 virtual monitors in your mixed reality environment
  • Supports both local PC and Windows 365 Cloud PC connections
  • Also connects to Azure Virtual Desktop and Microsoft Dev Box
  • Passthrough mode lets you stay aware of your physical surroundings

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Can't find your PC? Make sure Mixed Reality Link is running and both devices are on the same network.
  • Pixelated display? Check for network latency — a wired Ethernet connection on your PC helps significantly.
  • Personal Microsoft account not working? Work or school accounts only; @outlook.com addresses are not supported.
  • Pairing fails? Restart both the headset and Mixed Reality Link, then try again.

docs.title: Getting a Second Phone Number
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Getting a second phone number is much easier than it used to be. Depending on your needs for privacy, cost, or convenience, you generally have three main ways to do it.

docs.title: The 3 Main Ways to Get a Second Number
Method 1: The Super Cheap Route — povo2.0
docs.text:
This is the most popular method for people who just want a backup number or a spare number for receiving SMS verification codes.

  • Cost: $0 / month (basic fee)
  • How it works: You get a real 070/080/090 number for free. You only pay when you want to buy high-speed data or call packages (called "toppings").
  • The catch: You must buy at least one cheap topping (a few hundred yen) once every 180 days to prevent auto-cancellation.

docs.title: Method 2: The Easy Route — Add a Line to Rakuten Mobile
docs.text:
If you already use Rakuten Mobile, this is the most seamless option.

  • Cost: Starts at 1,078 yen / month (for up to 3 GB of data)
  • How it works: Apply for a second line under your existing account. Since they already verified your ID for your first line, setup is fast.
  • Perk: Unlimited free domestic calls on that second number via the Rakuten Link app.

docs.title: Method 3: The Digital Route — 050 Apps
docs.text:
If you don't need a traditional mobile number and just need to make or receive voice calls over the internet.

  • Cost: Usually a few hundred yen per month
  • How it works: Download an app (such as 050 plus or My050) and it gives you a VoIP phone number starting with "050".
  • The catch: Many apps and web services (such as LINE or banking apps) block 050 numbers for account verification to prevent spam.

docs.title: How to Use Both Numbers on One Phone
docs.text:
If you want to use two numbers without carrying two physical phones, use Dual SIM.

Most modern smartphones support one physical SIM card and one eSIM (a digital SIM you download instantly) active at the same time. This lets your phone stand by for calls and texts on both numbers simultaneously.

docs.title: Connecting and Disconnecting SpaceDesk
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

SpaceDesk turns your Android tablet into an additional Windows monitor. Understanding how to connect and disconnect cleanly prevents display configuration issues.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: State Effect on Windows SpaceDesk Viewer open and connected Tablet appears as an extra monitor Viewer disconnected or closed Extra monitor disappears from Windows Driver turned off No new connections can be established

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
1. Open the SpaceDesk Driver Console on Windows and turn the driver on.
  2. Open the SpaceDesk Viewer app on the tablet.
  3. Tap your PC in the list.

Windows adds the tablet as an extra monitor.

docs.title: Disconnect
docs.text:
1. Swipe away the SpaceDesk Viewer app on the tablet, or disconnect from inside the app.
  2. Open the SpaceDesk Driver Console on Windows and turn the driver off.

The session has ended when Windows Display Settings no longer shows the tablet as a monitor.

Note: If Windows gets confused about monitor arrangement after reconnecting, open Display Settings and drag the monitors back into the correct positions. Windows sometimes places a reconnected monitor in an unexpected location.

docs.title: Understanding Why SpaceDesk Is Free
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

SpaceDesk is free for personal use because the company behind it, datronicsoft Technology GmbH, earns revenue from enterprise and OEM licensing. The free version serves as both a product and a showcase of their display virtualization technology.

docs.title: Trade-Offs vs. Paid Alternatives
docs.text: SpaceDesk SuperDisplay Price Free Paid Wireless display Yes Yes Device support Broad Focused Pen experience Varies Polished for artists Setup May require tweaking Generally simpler

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Wireless latency depends on your network quality.
  • Stylus support is less refined than dedicated drawing solutions.
  • Updates can occasionally introduce issues.
  • Support is limited compared with commercial creative software.

docs.title: Streaming a Windows PC to an Android Tablet with Sunshine and Moonlight
Streaming a Windows PC to an Android Tablet with Sunshine and Moonlight
docs.text:
Note: This document was generated by Claude Code and has not been reviewed by a human. Please use it as a reference only.

Sunshine (host) runs on a Windows 11 PC and streams the screen using the GPU's hardware encoder for low latency. Moonlight (client) runs on an Android tablet, receives the stream, and sends touch and pen input back. No cable is needed — both devices only need to be on the same Wi-Fi network.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Windows 11 PC with Sunshine installed
  • Android tablet with Moonlight installed (tested with an XPPen Magic Drawing Pad)
  • Both devices on the same Wi-Fi network — a 5 GHz or Wi-Fi 6 network works best, and connecting the PC by Ethernet helps further

Note: Screenshots were taken with Sunshine v2026.918.174827, a pre-release version at the time. The steps are the same for other releases.

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Sunshine Releases Page
docs.text: Go to the Sunshine releases page on GitHub.

docs.title: Step 2: Download the Installer
docs.text:
Scroll to Assets and download Sunshine-Windows-AMD64-installer.msi.

  • "AMD64" means a normal 64-bit Windows PC (Intel or AMD CPU) — it does not refer to the graphics card. Use the ARM64 file only on ARM-based PCs.
  • Choose the installer rather than lite.zip. The portable version can lose control when you interact with administrator-level windows.
  • If the newest entry is marked Pre-release, look further down the release list for the one with the green Latest badge if you prefer a stable build.

docs.title: Step 3: Run the Installer
docs.text:
Open the downloaded .msi file and click through the wizard:

  1. Welcome → Next

  2. License Agreement → check I accept the terms in the License Agreement → Next

  3. Custom Setup → keep the defaults → Next. The defaults include Launch on Startup, so Sunshine starts automatically with Windows.

  4. Ready to install → Install (approve the Windows permission prompt)

  5. Completed → Finish

docs.title: Step 4: Start Sunshine
docs.text: Press the Windows key, type sunshine, and open the Sunshine app. A Sunshine icon appears in the system tray, near the clock.

docs.title: Step 5: Open the Sunshine Web UI
docs.text:
In Chrome, go to https://localhost:47990.

Chrome shows "Your connection is not private" (NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID). This is expected — Sunshine's page runs on your own PC with a self-signed certificate, which Chrome does not recognize.

  1. Click Advanced.

  2. Click Proceed to localhost (unsafe).

docs.title: Step 6: Create the Login
docs.text:
The first time you open the page, Sunshine asks you to create a username and password. Any values work — they only protect this local page, so just remember them.

Note: After you click Login, Chrome shows its own native Sign in prompt (separate from the page you just filled in). Enter the same username and password again to continue.

You are signed in when the "Hello, Sunshine!" home page appears.

docs.title: Step 7: Install Moonlight on the Tablet
docs.text:
On the tablet, install Moonlight Game Streaming from Google Play. Other download options, including Amazon Appstore and F-Droid, are listed at moonlight-stream.org.

Warning: Do not install the Windows version of Moonlight on the PC for this setup. It is a client, and the PC is the host.

docs.title: Step 8: Connect to the Same Wi-Fi
docs.text: Connect the tablet to the same network as the PC.

docs.title: Step 9: Find the PC
docs.text: Open Moonlight. The PC should appear automatically. If it does not, tap + and enter the PC's IP address.

docs.title: Step 10: Get the PIN on the Tablet
docs.text: Tap the PC in Moonlight. A dialog appears with a 4-digit PIN. The PIN expires after a short time, so do the next step right away — if it times out, tap the PC again to get a new one.

docs.title: Step 11: Enter the PIN in Sunshine
docs.text:
1. On the PC, open https://localhost:47990 and sign in.
  2. Click the PIN tab.
  3. Enter the 4-digit PIN from the tablet and give the device any name, for example Magic Drawing Pad.
  4. Click Send.

When it works, the page shows "Success! Please check Moonlight to continue" and the lock icon disappears from the PC entry on the tablet.

docs.title: Step 12: Start Streaming
docs.text:
In Moonlight, tap the PC and choose Desktop. Your Windows 11 desktop appears on the tablet.

Suggested starting settings, in Moonlight's settings, before connecting:

Setting Start With Resolution / FPS 1080p, 60 fps, then raise if Wi-Fi holds up Bitrate 30-50 Mbps on 5 GHz Wi-Fi Touch mode Direct touch (the pen acts where it touches)

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The PC does not appear in Moonlight? Check that both devices are on the same Wi-Fi and that the Windows network profile is Private. Then add the PC manually by IP address.
  • Still not found? Allow sunshine.exe in Windows Security → Firewall & network protection → Allow an app through firewall. The installer normally adds this itself.
  • PIN is rejected or times out? Tap the PC in Moonlight again to get a fresh PIN and enter it quickly.
  • Colors differ from the PC screen? Turn off HDR and Night Light in Windows. On the tablet, use a natural color mode and turn off eye-comfort or blue-light filters. Try another video codec in Moonlight.

Note: Port forwarding is only needed for streaming from outside your home network — it is not needed on the same Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Pen pressure in Blender through Moonlight has not been verified. If pressure does not respond, set Edit → Preferences → Input → Tablet API to Windows Ink in Blender and test again.
  • SpaceDesk showed better colors in testing, and its Android viewer supports pressure-sensitive pens — it is worth comparing for pen-heavy workflows.
